question_text: Hello, Alvaro Serrano from Morgan Stanley. A couple of questions on the themes that you've already touched on, but hopefully with a new angle. On the US cards, to get to $40 billion, you have to grow balances. If I take out American Airlines and add General Motors, about 40% or a bit more than 40%. Can you give us a flavour, because the actual organic growth in the US market seems to be slowing down, so what is the reasonable sort of expectation of what could be organic on your existing JVs and what could be new deals? And also the 10.66% NIM to progress to above 12, should we expect it to be linear? I know you said last week that the price actions would feed into next year, but just a sense if it's going to be linear? And the second theme of question is on CCAR and US deregulation. Putting Basel 3.1 end game aside, my impression is there's an expectation that CCAR is going to be watered down. Can you help us think through how that would help you? It's obviously less capital, but is that for the Group? Is it a constraint? What would you do in that scenario? What possibly does that open up? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thank you, Alvaro. So let me touch on the US cards to start with and then we'll come to CCAR. And again, Dan might want to make some comments on the closeout of that question. So in the plan that we have, the majority of the growth, more than [two thirds] we assume was organic, so that is our objective. Within there, we do typically expect a number of partners over any particular planning period. It's also important to think about how we retain partners. So if I just take those in turn, I mean General Motors at around $2 billion is the kind of size and scale of partner that we are pleased to bring on, between $2 and $4 billion. It is really an ideal size, both in terms of the implementation and the integration of it, but also the concentration that it places within the portfolio. So expect us to be focused on both of those two things. In terms of the NIM, I wouldn't expect it to be linear. There are factors within there that will be a bit more linear. So I would call out the funding benefits that we expect to see as we continue to build out the deposit franchise and the repricing actions that we've taken already. They're already in the terms and conditions for those customers, but they have to purchase on those new terms and conditions for that NIM impact to draw through, which is why you're going to see it drift through over time. So I'd expect those two things to be more linear. There are other things which will be less [linear]. The first will be a degree of seasonality in the business. You can see that in the fourth quarter, you probably see it in the first quarter also, and then you tend to see a little bit lower as you go into the middle of the year, just running in line with borrowing behaviour in the US, remember that post-holiday season, we see a pay down, you get tax credits in the US, people use those. So there's just a natural ebb and flow to the NIM that we would expect. And then the other thing would be, as we sort of rebalance the portfolio away from the super prime travel portfolio that we have, towards more retail, both by growing the partners we already have but also the opportunity to bring on new ones. Then you should see that NIM change. I mean one of the things that we said about American Airlines is we've had a long partnership with them, a long relationship with them. That's not just actually in US cards but in the Investment Bank as well. So it's certainly a relationship that we are sorry to see go, but at the same time it's got a low risk adjusted margin. And so over time, I would hope that the portfolios that we bring on would push that risk adjusted margin up. Moving on to your second point, it's difficult to speculate about regulatory change in the US because there's clearly been a lot of commentary and we have yet to see anything formal either in terms of CCAR, or indeed in terms of Basel 3.1. So take these general comments before then. We typically perform well in CCAR because we've got a diversified business in the US. To the extent that it's watered down, it would reduce the overall capital levels that we've got in the US, but Dan, you might want to add. Generally, we operate in a position where the Group and the PRA metric is more binding on us than the legal entity capital metrics. So, certainly a watering down of CCAR would give us great flexibility in terms of capital and how we deploy it across our legal entities. But more important is the regulation and the Bank of England stress test. So it is helpful, but it's not a key driver for us.

question_text: Hi, Sheel Shah, JP Morgan. Just two quick follow-ups on the US cards business. Firstly, when you're looking at the historic partnership opportunities of $40 billion and the 15 number of deals a year, how many of those do you think sit within your risk appetite and your strategy, just to get a view on how this could look going forward? And secondly with AA going towards a single issuer model, do you think this is the trend that we should expect amongst other issuers and if that was the case, would you look to then participate in these deals?
answer_text: Okay, thank you for those. The first is quite difficult to answer really, without seeing the details of the portfolios that come up, but you should expect us, as we said, to want to do more in retail proportionately. The retail market and the travel and entertainment markets in the US are broadly the same scale. We've got a good market share in travel, I think it's around 12% from memory and a much lower, low single digit share in retail. So you should expect us to sort of be biased towards that retail side. That being said, we are very focused on the credit quality of this portfolio. You've seen over time actually, even though we've had different portfolios within there, the FICO of this business overall has been about 740 for a long time. So when I talk about a slight movement in our expectation of risk, it's not a massive wholesale change there at all. We have a relatively conservative risk appetite for this business and actually, one of the things that really works here is where we are providing consumer banking services to existing Investment Banking clients. That works extremely well for us, the Group, and again, you've seen us do that through last year. A good example is Wyndham, a long standing Investment Banking client and we renewed that early, directly with Wyndham and that one didn't actually go to market. So that breadth of relationship is important to us. In terms of single issuer, there are a small number of very large programmes in the US, so Costco, Walmart, Delta, American, and typically they do go to single issuers. Things of that scale are unlikely to be of interest to us, just because of the concentration risk associated with them. We have an appetite to grow this business, but it's capital hungry as we said, you know, we want to be able to share that risk with external partners as we went through in 2024. We can see that business being $40 billion, but I can't see it necessarily being $100 billion, put it that way. Okay, thank you.

question_text: Hi, thank you. Amit Goel from Mediobanca. I've also got some follow-ups, just on the USCB business. So one initial comment, I think you made that you'd like business to get to mid-teens [RoTE] beyond 2026. So just want to check how you think about getting there? You know, we're not getting the repeat of the gain in 2026, we've got the higher risk weights. The market seems to be getting a little bit more competitive with maybe a bit more economics going towards some of the partners. So, just curious how you're seeing that step up. And then secondly, if you give a little bit of colour in terms of the RWA regulatory impact, where I guess the estimate was unchanged post the AA piece changing. So just curious the moving parts there or how you're thinking that's going to be repaid? So that's just on the AA part. And I had a second question just on the BUK fee line, I just wanted to just check in terms of what you're thinking. I think the guidance is for greater than 250 million per quarter. Obviously that's a step down versus the kind of Q3 / Q2 rate, but better than Q4, which was impacted by securitisation. Just wanted to just get a sense of how much should I anticipate ongoing securitisation type effects? And how to think about that line going forward? Thanks.
answer_text: Okay. Thank you. Okay, it's definitely cards day today. So USCB, how do we get to mid-teens [RoTE]? Well, I think about four factors there. The first is NIM that we talked about this morning already. So the repricing that we've done already and the funding costs are the major factors there. And also this move towards a higher risk adjusted return more generally, as we morph the portfolio and rebalance it away from being quite travel and entertainment dominant. The second one is volume, as I've talked about here, you've got a relatively fixed cost base. You know a good example of that is with GM. I said we're not going to have to rebuild all the capability that we had to do for GAP. So you've got the ability, as you onboard more volume, your marginal cost comes down across the complex. The third is capital efficiency. So you're right, clearly we have some degree of regulatory drag here from the IRB model. So you should expect us to pursue further opportunities for capital and risk sharing with external parties as we did in Q1 with Blackstone which was successful. You should imagine that we're going to do that again. Finally, costs. It's really interesting to reflect on where this business has come from, as we think about its efficiency. You know, if you're running travel files with thousands of dollars per account, your ability to handle that manually is significantly higher. As you move into an environment where you inherently have smaller balances per account, you want to be more and more digital. So if I look at the digital interactions in that business, they're at 93%. Now that's improved, we expect that to improve by a further 10% this year. If I contrast it to BUK, I mean BUK would be 98 / 99% in comparison. Now you might say, well BUK is not a good comparison because it's clearly a retail bank, and therefore you're going to have current account activities that are [generally] higher, but actually our German cards business wasn't that different. So we do think there's an opportunity here for us to increase, not only the efficiency of the business, but actually the customer experience by making more of the activity digital. So it's really through those four steps that we think we can get to, first, in line with the Group. And then secondly, pushing on to the mid-teens [RoTE]. And then in terms of the $16 billion, it remains our best estimate and the reason I say that is of course, we are expecting AA to fall out of the portfolio, but I'm also expecting other things to go back in. And the thing that's somewhat uncertain is the timing. We know the timing of when we will have built that model by, but the timing of the approval of that model and therefore the implementation that I would expect to follow that. Typically, once we've got approval around the model, it takes us around six months say to implement it. So it's the timing really. So the exact size and shape of that portfolio at the point of implementation is not entirely clear at this point in time, which is why we're saying the best estimate we have is the one that we previously had, which is we would expect the portfolio to be about the same size. And then finally on your question on BUK fees. This line does move around a little bit because you've got a few things going on there. You've clearly got securitisations, you've got debt sales and various other bits and pieces. The best estimate I can give you is greater than 250, which is what we said in in the past. I wouldn't expect a lot of securitisation in this business. And Dan might want to comment on this. This is part of the portfolio that we have around risk transfer. It's at a true sale risk transfer. So expect us to do it episodically, as we dynamically manage the balance sheet, but Dan you might want to add. I think periodic is the right sort of thinking. Obviously the one in Q4 was specifically on a particular bit of the mortgage books, stage 2, stage 3 loans. And we'll do that on occasion, just to make sure that the risk profile is in the right place. But again, we'll call out, you know, as and when we expect to do so.

question_text: Andrew Coombs from Citi again. Just to clarify two of the points you've made. So one on the costs. Thank you for saying you're comfortable with where consensus is for 2025. Just off my memory, I think there is a step up in cost in 25 in parts because consensus has higher litigation costs in. So could you just talk about if consensus has the right mix of costs as well? I'm pushing my luck here, but thank you. And then secondly, just coming back to the USCB, the gain [on sale]. You've always talked about this J-curve effect on the US card revenue portfolio and obviously what we have is a gain is going to drop out in 2027. You're guiding to the same level of receivables as you were previously, but now because you're going to be on boarding a lot more, is there a risk that actually the return profile in USCB, and even potentially the Group, goes down in 2027 versus 2026?
answer_text: So in terms of 2025 costs, I would say I'm comfortable with the total. I'm not going to make any specific comments around litigation or otherwise, but broadly comfortable with where the total consensus is. On the USCB gain and the J-curve. We do expect a J-curve as we onboard new balances in the US. Typically what happens is you've got upfront marketing, you've got day one impairment and then obviously the capital going out on day one and the earnings come thereafter as the customers build their balance. What creates lumps and bumps, if you like, in the RoTE profile is where you stop and start that acquisition flow. So to the extent that we continue to actively acquire as we have been doing in the market, I would expect that to be less impactful. The specific impact of bringing on new partners, it depends. So in some cases, you're bringing on a back book where you've already got a portfolio which is earning at a reasonable RoTE, as we did, for example with GAP. And then there are some like Breeze, they start from scratch. So it depends on the specific pathway. In terms of RoTE aspirations for 2027 versus 2026, I'm clearly not going to give you additional guidance here, but you should tell from our overall tone that 2026 is not, we believe, a resting place. We're ambitious for the business and we want to keep pushing the RoTE on a consistent basis upwards.

question_text: Thanks so much. Can I come back to the whole issue of growth and I guess growth in the UK economy, growth in your lending. It's obviously a huge theme with the new government. And I was talking to one of your peers last week. I don't want to put words in their mouth, but broadly speaking, they were saying there's nothing the government could do because there's no demand. So, however much regulation changes doesn't make any difference, which I guess the government will be quite surprised by. So, if I look at your lending growth, even in the second-half, if you annualise, it's only 1.5%, which is very little. Provisions across the sector is near zero. Everybody is massively below their normalised provision rate and I guess looking at that, a man from space would look at that and say clearly you're not lending enough. Clearly you could lend more, take more provisions, support the economy more. The UK would grow more. What is wrong with that analysis and if it's not wrong, what can be done to actually get the sector lending again? And by lending, I mean 3, 4, 5 percent a year, not 1.5%.
answer_text: Good question Ed, one that we've discussed actually with quite a few in investors on the road. You know we remain optimistic about our ability to grow within the UK economy. In part, because we are pushing on areas where we have lost market share. Or indeed didn't have it, for example, like High Loan to Value mortgages. You can see that in our ability to pull in additional volumes in cards. I mean, [bringing on 1] million [new] cards is the most cards we have written since 2012, in this environment. And that was actually through us improving our customer journey. So this is not just all about pricing and risk, it's actually about the ease in which you interact with your customers. question_text: Hi, good morning, everyone. Thanks for taking the questions and a good set of results today. And in terms of the growth as we look forward, the strategy is predicated on very much growth in the business, but I think a lot of people would understand you being a little bit more circumspective, delinquency trends look like they were deteriorating. So my question really is sort of how wedded are you to growing the book meaningfully as planned and into higher-margin, but slightly higher-risk segments and how easy would it be to pause that growth, if you like? So trying to understand how you weigh up balancing that strategic outlook with the current uncertainty? Thank you.

I'm glad that's helpful. That's on page 38 and it's a bit more of a holistic view of what's going on in the US market generally, but also in our book. But really what happened in Q1 is as a BAU matter, you've got a slight seasonal elevation in the impairment charge. We normally see that in Q1, and it's just reflective of the high levels of consumer spend that we see in Q4 through the holiday season. Typically, what then happens is you start to see that reverse in Q2 and beyond. So far, very straightforward. In terms of the PMA, it's worth stepping back and thinking about what we consider when we book impairment and we're looking at two things. The first is consumer behavior. And the second is what we expect to happen in the macroeconomic environment. On the first, in consumer behavior, we see no change. And you can see that clearly on the charts, delinquencies are relatively low and stable. Actually, we see no change on the second. So, US economic consensus forecasts are actually relatively static, and they're very similar to where they were at the full-year. But we think that's likely a timing issue, and therefore, it's reasonable for us to assume that they will change in the coming weeks and months. And therefore, we're trying to get ahead of that. So we're being thoughtful and methodical. So what we've done is essentially skew the downside bias in the impairment charge to accelerate a bit of coverage here. But just as we step back, the performance of the book itself is extremely robust. Venkat? Yeah. So I think I've said in the past when I look at the book overall, there's about 20 corporate clients, 20 million underlying customers. The second is, related to that, what's the industry? We've had a bias towards travel and we are looking to diversify out of travel. We added GAP, we added General Motors and we chose not to renew our share of American [Airlines]. The third is the size and renewal rates. So we like to have a mix that is [smaller, relative] to our overall portfolio, and not a lot of renewals coming in at the same time. And the last one is the actual underlying creditworthiness of the borrower. And through this combination, we like to create a business with a stable and high risk-adjusted return. So when you take all of this together, we are continuing to want to grow this business. We do think the opportunities are great. Obviously, we will factor in the consumer environment when we do the actual risk selection of customers and look to get good risk-adjusted returns. question_text: Good morning, both. Thank you for taking my questions. Both are really around regulations. Barclays has been a market leader on [Significant Risk Transfer] transactions. And in April, the regulator wrote to all UK banks highlighting concerns in this area. Is there any headwind to capital that we should be considering as a result of implementing any relevant changes that are identified in that letter? And secondly, some of your peers have written to the government asking for a softening in the ring-fencing regime. How material could a change in regulation be here for you? From the outside, it feels like you'd be one of the large beneficiaries of any change here. Thank you.
answer_text: Thank you, Ben, and good morning. Again, I'll take the first and then hand to Venkat for the second. On SRT, the Dear CFO letter that we and others received recently did deal with SRT, but it was actually more focused on the financing of SRT. And to be really clear, we do not finance our own SRT programs. So we're not extending financing to investors who are then ongoing investors in our SRT. So we think that's the focus. And from our perspective, we've run our Colonnade program since 2016. We share the details of each tranche of that with the regulator in order to get capital relief, and we manage the reinvestment risk around that very, very carefully as we've outlined before. So we're comfortable with our position and wouldn't envisage any capital consequences. Venkat? Yeah. So on ring-fencing, I think you know, that of the major UK banks, we have been opposed to any change in relaxation in the ring-fencing regime. So while I agree with what others say that there is friction in the system, there was obviously a high cost to set up the ring fence, let's call it a sunk cost now, and there's a little bit of trapped capital and liquidity. And if you release that in the short-term, it would be good for banks, and let's argue, for some customers. But I think in the long-term, it weakens the system because it weakens deposit protection. I think the ring fence is an extremely strong and secure form of deposit protection in the UK and while [the relaxation of the ring fence regime] might be short-term attractive, I think in the long-term, it weakens the system, it weakens the participants in the system and that includes Barclays. That's why on balance, I do not think we should change the ring fence regime and I'm a strong supporter of it in its current form.

So, if you look in the disclosures, you'll see that credit risk RWAs are down, market risk RWAs are up and counterparty credit risk RWAs are up. question_text: Good morning and apologies if you've already touched on this because I turned up a bit late, I was multi-tasking. On US cards, I think you have the $40 billion receivables target you've maintained for 2026. I just wonder that with the sort of broader discussions around US cycle, you obviously need to sign on new clients, new [Joint Ventures] on to get to that. Is it the right time? And do you feel there's enough visibility to take on significant portfolios to achieve that $40 billion or would you need to wait, just to think about that sort of medium-term target? And then another one on the IB, on general activity. Could you maybe give us a bit of colour on how the Investment Bank has done during the quarter or maybe even April or by region? What I'm trying to get to is, obviously Q1 is very good, but if volatility comes down, are we suddenly going to see a very quiet sort of performance and how much of the activity you think, how much visibility you have on for the rest of the year. It's a difficult question, but any hand-holding or colour would be much appreciated. Thank you.
answer_text: Alvaro, hi, I'll start with cards, and we've covered a little bit of this, but I'll go over it again, and then Anna will talk about the Investment Bank. So on the US cards portfolio, the growth is going to come in net receivables from three things. One is the organic growth in our existing portfolio. The second is how we choose to flex the lever that we have used of risk transfers. We can do more or less and if we do less, the receivables are there on our book. And then the third thing is portfolio changes, which is new accounts or accounts leaving. So on the first one, which is organic growth, we are fairly comfortable that we will continue to see organic growth. And we have a very-high credit quality portfolio. We're looking to diversify it among certain sectors, but it's a high credit quality portfolio. On the second one, which is risk transfer, there's always a question at the time of what capital benefit we get, what's the price at which we sell it, and whether it suits our risk management. As you say, given that we've chosen not to bid for our portion, for a renewal of our portion of American [Airlines], all else equal, we would want to keep things on our balance sheet. Third is acquisitions or other disposals. We've renewed a bunch of our other accounts through 2024. I think we mentioned that in our previous full-year earnings. And then we continue to look in this environment, especially in this environment at good-quality portfolios that we think rounds out our business. And these things are very long-term decisions. A typical portfolio takes two to three years to decide to bid and to come to you, and then it's there with you for hopefully seven years. So these are long-term decisions, and I wouldn't let the short-term stuff in the market affect that decision-making. Anna? Thanks, Venkat. Alvaro, the only thing I'd add to that is that, achieving the plan and the returns that we want in USCB is not just only volume either. We're working very hard on margins. We're working very hard on cost and digitisation of the business and also the capital efficiency, as Venkat said. So a plan of many parts. And let me talk about the IB, sort of generally in the quarter, and then I'll pass across to Venkat, he might want to add at the end. If you think about what should have happened to our IB in the quarter, given the volatility that we've seen, we should see strong Markets revenues and a more subdued [Investment] Banking environment. And that's exactly the shape of our results, very much in line with the market more broadly. And as I look at Q1 in particular, we've been investing in this business for some time and investing to create a franchise that allows us to perform in a range of environments and you see that. So the FICC result is very strong and I think that reflects our investment in Securitised Products. It reflects our investments in our Rates businesses and Equities is strong. Actually, you'll recall there was a one-of last year, but our Equities position has been very much driven by the investments that we've made in Equity Derivatives. So we feel like we're facing the market with a much more complete franchise. And of course, our Financing business has stability and it's probably less impacted by volatility, but you can see good growth in there that's obviously also underpinning FICC and Equities. I said we would have expected the IB to be a bit softer. And of course, our Investment Banking to be a bit softer in Q1. And of course, it has been, we feel that's in line with the Street. So you see good cost control, and you'll also see very, very good risk control. We've disclosed today for the first time consistently, both our [Value at Risk] progression and indeed, our loss days. And you can see we're not taking outsized risk. I should have actually mentioned also a very good performance within the International Corporate Bank within [Investment] Banking. So Financing and the ICB are both less impacted by volatility. Venkat, do you want to comment? Yeah, I'll re-emphasize what Anna said at the beginning, which is that if you see the first-quarter results, you see the performance you would expect to see in the places you'd expect to see them. And obviously, we can't talk about the second quarter. We don't. We are about a month into it. But again, re-emphasize what Anna said on the Markets side. When there is volatility, we aim to put our clients first and to do intermediation and risk management for our clients. And that is what we strive to do and it can be profitable as long as you manage your own risks well, which is what we strive to do. And Anna gave you the data on the first-quarter results of that. So that's what we strive to do every day. And on banking activity, people will wait for clarity until they resume, it could happen sooner than we think. But the overall business is pretty well-diversified, whether you look at the Investment Bank and you look at deposit growth in the International Corporate Bank, you look at the business in the International Corporate Bank, you look at Markets or even the whole bank as a whole.

question_text: Yeah, good morning, everybody. Thanks for taking my questions. Two quick ones. So given the conservative banking wallet already embedded in your planning assumptions, which I guess you just referenced. Are there any initiatives, either on the cost side or the investment side, that you would need to either undertake or delay should 2025 indeed play out as per those wallet assumptions? That's the first question. And then second, you mentioned the substantial increase in Transaction banking deposits in the US. How has that trended post-quarter end? So companies are maybe building liquidity, delaying some investment spend. Are you seeing that show up in your deposit volumes? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thanks. Thanks, Chris. Thanks for the questions. I'll take the first one and then I'll hand across to Venkat. Look, as I said, that was our assumption for Banking. And actually what we're seeing here is the diversification of income working really well across the bank, both in terms of [being] more than offset by Markets activity and also the strength that we're seeing coming through in the UK and the UK complex more generally across deposits that's underpinned our upgrade today. So the revenue line appears to be very robust and we have confidence in it. That said, that does not undermine our focus on costs and it's what we're doing every day. It's a key part of the strategy. You can see that all the way through the P&L today. Income up by 11%, profits up by 19%. The plan is to create operating leverage, not just at the Group, but across every single business within the Group. Overall, I still expect what I expected at the year-end, which is for incremental investment to underpin the longer-term growth of the plan and inflation to outweigh our growth efficiencies for the year and for us to see an uptick in costs. All of that is contained within the most important cost metric, which is cost income ratio at 61%. That is the number that we are most focused on. It's likely that we'll see some movement in absolute costs. I'm happy with consensus as it currently starts, but it is FX sensitive and it is performance and volume sensitive. And therefore, I'd really urge you to focus on the cost income ratio target that we've given. We feel like 57% in Q1 is a good down payment against that and should show you how focused we are on operating leverage. Venkat, Transaction banking? Yeah. So Transaction banking has been an area of great emphasis for us in the last few years. We spoke about it last year. We've spoken about it at our year-end earnings. People choose us and the quantum of deposits is based on two factors. One is the growth in our overall Transaction banking business or relationships generally, people's choice of us as a counterparty, which is increasing. And then ultimately, their needs for cash and their use of cash. In this period, we continue to see happily people choosing us as a counterparty newly, and that's good and that's improving again. And then I think on cash, what you're seeing is growth in deposits, in part, what you would expect when people are being cautious on the deploying of cash for transactions. So you're seeing deposit growth, whether it's individuals or it's institutions. It's all what you would normally expect in this environment. Okay. Thank you. Thanks, Chris. question_text: Hello, good morning, both. Got a couple of questions. The first is a follow-up on Ed's question on capital. You came into this year at 13.6% [CET1] ratio, 13.3% adjusting for the buyback. It does sound increasingly like you want to operate closer to 14% moving forward. Can I just confirm that is how we should be thinking about it? I'm just wondering whether there's an element of this relating to the fact that UK RWA growth, your target for end of next year looks increasingly stretching, and maybe you're thinking about some sort of inorganic bolt-on, which obviously would consume some capital in a one-of sense there. So that's the first question. The second question is on sensitivity again, particularly in the US card book. If I look at your full-year downside scenarios, even on downside 2, which has got GDP falling over 1 percentage point this year and next year, unemployment moving to above 7%, the models are telling you that your required Stage 1 and 2 ECL builds would only be about £177 million, which feels very low given that set of macroeconomic assumptions. I mean, I guess the models are telling us what the models are telling us, but how robust do you think the models are? I guess into COVID, IFRS-9 was quite new [...]. We're seven to eight years in now and this obviously applies across the Group as well, because the sensitivity to downside one and two scenarios is very limited given the severity of those. So comment on that would be useful. Thanks.
answer_text: Okay. Thanks, Jonathan. Okay. So let me start with capital. Venkat may want to comment on this also. You're right, we're generating a lot of capital. But as I said previously, that is an outcome of the plan and it is intentional, it is deliberate, and it's what you should expect going forward. We did indicate at the full-year that you should expect us to operate towards the top half. And I'll just reiterate that as our formal guidance, but just reflecting on the fact that we are generating a lot of capital. And just on the utilisation of that capital, we're very focused on deploying £30 billion in the UK. That plan is intact. As I look at where we are now, we've deployed £14 billion of that, recognizing, of course, that a large part of that has come from Tesco, but you can see good loan growth in the quarter, both from BUK and from the UK Corporate Bank. If I look at the specifics of lending, the consumer preference at the moment is for secured versus unsecured lending. That's very clear. That's okay. And then as I look at the lending as it's developing in the Corporate Bank and Private Banking and Wealth Management, actually it's very high quality and that's reflective of our portfolios. So, Q1, if I look at that in isolation, the lending is happening, maybe the RWA weighting is a little light. But over the period of the plan, that plan is intact. And I'd particularly point you to the momentum that we've got, both around mortgages and cards on the leading indicators on Slide 15. We're going through that J-curve in cards, you're going to see interest-earning lending and RWAs growing from the back-end of '25, with all of that maturing through. Venkat, do you want to comment more on RWAs? No, look, I think Anna has covered it all. I'd also remind you the environment in which we are. You would expect us to be on the general side of prudent in our capital [deployment]. Yeah, absolutely. And then on the second point, I would take the disclosures on IFRS9 as a sensitivity. They're not predictive. They essentially say, what happens if I take my current static balance sheet and I push through a different set of macroeconomic variables? What it doesn't take into account is clearly the kind of stage migration that you would see into Stage 3. It doesn't take into account any increases of exposure at default. So the fact that customers may draw down, as they become more financially pressed. But also the other thing that it doesn't take into account is credit actions that we might take in order to manage that position. So I wouldn't think of it as a scenario. I would think of it as a sensitivity and it's quite a straightforward sensitivity. I don't think it's intended to be predictive. The same is true of the PMA that we've taken. That's really just a downside bias at this stage.

question_text: Morning, Ben Toms from RBC. Thank you for the questions. The first one is on consolidation in the UK space. You've been quite clear before where you've talked about how you wouldn't want to undertake into any transactions that potentially would disrupt the strategic plan. But if others consolidate around you, is there any potential for that to change your view on how you think about consolidation in UK? And then secondly on net interest income. Can you just talk a little bit about how you see the cadence of net interest income developing as we go through the year? Is it a little bit up each quarter? Is that the right way to think about it? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thank you Ben. Just to reflect on the UK market, we think that there are clearly some factors here which are driving a degree of consolidation in the market. Clearly the economic environment, the rapid rates up, rates down scenario can put pressure on some business models. Equally, the pace of regulatory change, and I would say both prudential and conduct regulation, again, puts pressure on business models, and we've seen that in some of the transactions that have happened, whether that be Tesco for ourselves, Sainsbury's, Co-op etc, so we see that running as a theme. However, our position remains the same. Our plan is an organic one, and our objective is to use the now multiple brands that we have in BUK in particular, but also a refreshed momentum that we have in the other businesses really to grow in line with the plan that we've given you, and we really don't want to distract the businesses from executing the plan that they have in hand, which is not unambitious. We've still got £16 billion to go and we think that we've got the momentum there to deliver that. So we don't want to distract [the businesses]. The exception to that would be if we saw something that was not distracting and added to our capability or accelerated our existing plan. So Tesco would have been an acceleration of that existing plan and Kensington gave us the capability that we didn't otherwise have. So that's how we think about it. I mean, we certainly don't lack scale in the UK and we're really watchful of the environment around us. On net interest income, you can see what's happening here, because now almost one of the factors is out of the way, because previously what we had was that downward pressure that was coming from deposit migration and deposit margin compression. And what we've really observed towards the back end of 2024 and into 2025 is real stabilisation of that position, which is why we've now upgraded our net interest income. We believe that that stability will continue, that's why we are now guiding to the hedge notional being more stable and again that provides that momentum. So what we're really looking at here is continued tailwind from the hedge, and we would expect that to build with successive quarters all the way out to 2026 and indeed beyond. And then at the same time, what you've got is growth in the asset base which is ticking over very nicely, going at the kind of scale and momentum that we would expect. So we are expecting progressive increases in net interest income. Now of course there's some calendarisation in there, so Q1 tends to be a little bit lower.

question_text: Hello, Perlie Mong from Bank of America. Can I take you back on capital? So, I guess there's now a little bit of a divergence in terms of you know some of your peers saying they're going to go down 13%, and others being very clear that they're comfortable with the full range. So the upper end of the range is the guidance. I understand that some of that is to do with general uncertainty, and some of that is to do with the timing of the regulatory change. But even then, the [Maximum Distributable Amount hurdle] move was only about 20 basis points. So just wondering how you're thinking about that. On the call a few weeks ago, you also said that it is not inconceivable that sitting at [13.9%], in the next couple of quarters we might go through that range. So would you stay there, or would you always pay back to the top end of the range as it were? So that's number one and number two is on US cards. So I guess maybe the dust has settled a little bit since liberation day in terms of consumer behaviour, what have you seen? I guess the question is less about asset quality, but more that in the past, certainly the full year, there was some guidance and ambition about growing more in the retail segment of the consumer market. Is that still where you're comfortable going? Is that where consumers want to spend? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thank you Perlie. So at the full year, what we said was you should expect us to operate towards the upper half of our target range of 13 to 14%. The reason we said that was really two things. Firstly, it was the Pillar 2A impact of IRB, but it was also the fact that some of the reductions that we might have anticipated in Pillar 2 are now further out, because the implementation of Basel is further out. But we also said that would leave our distribution plans unaffected. So you should take from that that we'd always plan to be in that kind of zone. We were just being clearer with you with that disclosure. In terms of where we are now, I would distinguish how and why? So how are we there? We're there because that is what the strategy is designed to do. The strategy is designed to create higher, more consistent levels of returns, that will in turn generate higher levels of capital. So we shouldn't be surprised by the capital trajectory in the firm. That is the modus operandi of the plan. So now we find ourselves here, what does that mean? We are clearly reflecting the uncertainty in the economic environment, we're very mindful of that. And as we make decisions about how to deploy our capital, we are still very mindful of the hierarchy that we gave you, that remains intact. So it's number one, ensuring that we are robust from a regulatory perspective. Number two, delivering our distribution plans, which is at least £10 billion over the three years and number three, investing in our businesses. So from our perspective, the outcome and what we see now is very much in line with what we originally planned. It's conceivable that we go through the top end of our range, but again, that would be in the context of the plans that we set out for you and the priorities that we've given. So I wouldn't add any more than that. In terms of US cards, our book is biased, if you like, towards super prime. That is a great position from a credit perspective, but actually leaves us with some opportunities as a risk adjusted margin matter. You should expect us to continue to seek out retail partners as we have done in the past. That is a long term strategic goal, to rebalance this portfolio away from the concentration that it currently has in travel. Clearly, we'll be very thoughtful about that, but that strategy remains intact. And we do look at risk adjusted margins, that's really important to us and we believe that by doing so, the risk adjusted margin of this book will continue to increase, that's our opportunity. In terms of customer behaviour, no significant change, only what we called out, I think, for a couple of quarters now, which is customers continue to repay at very high levels. So if you look at customer repayment rates [on slide] 38. If you look at the customer repayment rates, they're at 32%, which is significantly elevated still versus the pre COVID position, even after all of the credit normalisation in the US. So if it's having any effect at all, it's probably having a bit of a drag effect on the ability to build balances, but we're happy with that balance at this point in time.

question_text: Sanjena Dadawala from UBS. Two questions. First on IB, specifically around cost. So revenues beat by 9%, but cost miss is only 1%. So how should we think about costs in the IB, and in relation to revenue, and maybe phasing? Then secondly, I just wanted to clarify the position on ring fencing and reform, what's the customer protection which the firms cannot achieve on their own, so their own measures which that provides, and the other factors which stop you from supporting any reform?
answer_text: Okay, thank you. Let me just start with costs in the IB, I mean not cost, but efficiency. So efficiency is a really key part of the plan to create higher and more consistent returns in the IB. So you're going to see absolute costs flex up and down depending on how the growth of that business continues. But ultimately it has to have a cost base that would support a return in line with the Group in a range of environments. So, expect us to continue to drive operating leverage in the IB, that's coming through both from good old fashioned cost control but also our technology plans, our efficiency plans to look at this business from end-to-end and drive out pockets of ineffectiveness and inefficiency in all of the processes. Ultimately that has a very strong client lens as well. We're trying to make the businesses better, cost is an output. So that's how you should think about it. I would expect this business to deliver positive jaws more often than not. It won't do so in every quarter, just because of the nature of the business, but I would expect it to do so [more often than not]. I won't call out its operating cost trajectory from here. I'd make two comments though, which are perhaps a little bit offsetting. The first is we accrue our [compensation] in line with the returns of the business. So you typically expect Investment Bank [compensation] to be a bit heavier in the first half of the year, but equally we also called out that our structural cost actions were a little light in the first quarter across the bank. That's not an IB comment, but across the bank as a whole. And therefore we would expect to spend in line with our normal levels, so between £200 million and £300 million for the rest of the year. In terms of ring fencing, our position is, as Venkat set out on the day [of results], we believe that at the heart of ring fencing was a desire to protect customers in the UK. Consumer deposits and specifically the deposits of retail investors and small corporates. And the regulation enshrines that around corporates of £6.5 million and lower, they have to be within a ringfence, and that is how our ring fence is constructed. So it's constructed specifically with that in mind. Having gone through the process of ring fencing, clearly there are inefficiencies that [it] drives. You would recognise that [in] what some of the other firms have said, it's certainly apparent, but now the ring fence is in place and firmly established. That is part of the way that we now do business and actually it's not significantly different in its intent from some of the provisions that we see elsewhere in the globe. We have an [Intermediate Holding Company], we have a ring fence, liquidity and capital position within Delaware, so it's just part of the complexity of running a large international group. And from our perspective, what trumps everything is the deposit of protection in the UK. Okay, thank you.

question_text: Good morning, Guy Stebbings from BNP Paribas Exane. The first question was on the US consumer, on the deposit side. Slide 25 shows some really good growth, particularly in the core segment, so just wanted to get an update on what you're seeing there, and anything in terms of the economic, in terms of the funding cost benefit you get there, versus the other deposits in that franchise. The second question is on UK mortgage flow, if you're able to give us a sense as to how much is coming from Kensington versus the heritage book and any sort of economics around that, particularly interested in terms of the spread difference you would see on that business versus the other business and wondering if it means that Barclays could even see mortgage spreads expand or least be flat, which isn't necessarily something we've seen for smaller banks.
answer_text: Okay, thank you. So we're pleased with the progress of deposits in US cards. So the difference here is really we've gone from something that was essentially a funding objective to something that is now much more strongly a retail proposition and specifically dealing with our partners. So I'd call out AARP (American Association of Retired Persons) and the launch of a tiered savings product that happened in Q3 of last year, to underpin our strategy to drive retail deposits up to around 75%. So it's a really core part of our desire to grow the NIM of this business. Because when we set out on our plan, there were a couple of things that we really noted about our business. One was, as we compared it to our US Peers, was really the comparative margin and risk adjusted returns, and the COVID experience is what's drawn us to seek more diversification across partners, but the funding costs were higher for us. Now I would expect them to be higher than a money centre bank, but I wouldn't necessarily expect them to be higher than many of the solo card providers. So that's really what underpinned this strategy. I won't give you the differential between the different funding types, but it is significantly cheaper than the brokered deposits that we have, but all of that is contained within the NIM guidance that we've given you of getting to greater than 12%. So we expect to continue to drive that strategy, completely digitally, of course. It's been very successful and, if anything, probably a little bit more successful [and] faster than we might have anticipated. And our Treasury colleagues have found themselves with a little bit more funding than they might have expected there, which has clearly had some downward pressure on NIM that will dissipate. In terms of mortgage flow in the UK, if I deconstruct our book, clearly we are now taking a much stronger flow from Kensington. We bought that at a point in the cycle where it probably wasn't going to come to the fore, now it is. That's helping us to fulfil our desire to take on a bit more high loan to value mortgages. I think previously we said it's around 15%, now it's 22% in our first quarter, so a much stronger part of the flow. That does have an impact on the blended margin coming through, clearly makes those margins higher. And at the same time, we do not have a significant churn effect from the back book. So from our perspective, despite the fact we've seen some volatility and swaps, and that played through in some tightness in spreads generally, the forward momentum in terms of mortgage margin is positive. Thank you.

question_text: Good morning, Rob Down from HSBC. Two questions please. The first, just a quick one, UK corporate, as you mentioned earlier, we saw pick up in loan demand coming through Q4 and into Q1. Can you talk about the loan demand, and what picture you're seeing today, whether or not we can continue to see that growth coming through for the remainder of the year or whether you're seeing counterparties perhaps postponing their lending? And then the second question, I know we're already halfway through the current programme, but given you started talking about 2027, can I just ask you a couple of quick questions there? You've got structural hedge tailwinds coming through that you mentioned, I'm guessing you're expecting to see loan growth and deposit growth continuing, assuming base rates don't fall, that should give you a healthy revenue picture. You talked about cost efficiency within the UK and the IB, so I'm assuming we're talking about positive jaws, so you get the operational gearing effects on the bottom line. What we haven't really talked about is capital and the capital mix. You've also got an ambition to get to 50% RWAs in the IB by the end of 2026, how do you see that playing out further on? Will we see more investment going back into the IB? Will the efficiency gains from capital perspective have expired then, or do you think the 50% could continue to shrink as part of the Group? Because I think that's important when I look at your UK domestic peers, I think we're probably all forecasting high teens RoTEs for 2027. I guess you're [>12%] for 2026. So can you close that gap in 2027?
answer_text: OK. Thank you. Let me start with the UK Corporate Bank. So we are seeing momentum in UK Corporate, as you call out. There's normally a fairly significant lag between putting the facilities out and corporates drawing down on them. If I were to call out any particular behaviour at the moment, I would say that's perhaps lengthening out a little, so it's not a change in demand as such, maybe just a slowing of the process. Obviously, when you get into individual sectors, that picture will be different. If you get into sectors where they have a significant exposure to import-export, then clearly they will be more cautious. But as the sector as a whole, I wouldn't say we see anything more meaningful than just a slowdown in the pull through. When I get to 2026 and beyond, I'd call out a couple of things. The first is, 2026 was designed to be a point in time. We gave you a three-year plan, it's not deemed to be an ending point for any of the metrics that we set out for you, whether that was RoTE, whether that was the proportion of capital deployment. The plan had the ultimate aim of raising the returns of the Group and making them more consistent and we believe that is driven by deploying a greater proportion of capital in the Group towards the higher returning, more stable businesses. That plan remains intact. So I wouldn't see the 50% or the 12% as being a resting point, you should expect them to progress beyond that. I'm not going to give you numbers now, I can't give you the endpoint. Think of it as a sense of direction and momentum that we would expect it to continue. Really importantly for us, we see value in having a diversified business that allows us particularly to perform in a range of environments, but we have to get the right capital balance across the Group and we're on a journey. 2026 is a staging point, that is the one that we are 100% focused on delivering right now and we'll come back to you in due course. Thank you.

question_text: Kian Abouhossein from JP Morgan. My question is around the US cards business and you've discussed in the past the diversification effect of the US cards business, on the CCAR process and capital requirement in the US. We will get transparency most likely in the summer around CCAR, and you will see at least, maybe we will see as well, what capital diversification effect you will get. I don't know how much detail you get today, but is there any thinking around, if the effect is actually not that material, [how] that changes your mind around the US card business? How do you think about this optimisation element, considering we will get that detail, and hopefully on the on the public side, we'll get it as well?
answer_text: The fundamental value of this business is we believe that it delivers business diversification, I will come to capital diversification in a minute. But it delivers us the opportunity to participate in one of the largest consumer markets in the world, where we have, we believe, sufficient scale. But we still have room to grow in terms of market share, and the opportunities that we have around us. So I've talked to Perlie before about the balance between, the non-retail and the retail parts of the book. Retail is a much bigger partner market in the US, that gives us real room to grow. But a key part of that is getting this business back to a position where it delivers, first, in line with the Group and second, to a point where we believe it can deliver a mid-teens result as it has done in the past, even after IRB. That is our objective. We're confident we can get it to that place, and on that basis it provides a business diversification to the Group. Beyond that, it also provides a degree of capital diversification. You're right, if there's a change in US stress testing, of course we need to refresh our understanding of that. But it seems unlikely that the stress test will change significantly in nature, as in the diversification benefits that we get are the same as those as we enjoy in the UK, which is first, you tend to get a market stress, then you get an unsecured stress and then you get secured stress. And to the extent that you have a diversified business, you have your businesses being stressed and then recovering at different rates, and that provides you with a more robust revenue position all the way through any stress environment. Barclays was the only UK bank that did not make a loss in COVID. So we believe that diversification works. The current discussion around US stress testing is more about transparency than changing the nature of it, and the transparency of the process. So we need to wait and see, but I would really distinguish those two things strongly. Business diversification, reaching mid-teens, of course, if we're unable to do that, then we should look at it very, very critically. But if we can, then we think there's value to the group. And then beyond that, just being clear about the additional strategic capital diversification this gives us within the US.

question_text: Sheel Shah, JP Morgan. First, in the US cards, coming back to the NIM. Can I ask if you think that greater than 12% is still achievable for 2026, given you're holding maybe a bit more excess liquidity from deposits, revolver balances are maybe a little lower than you'd expect? Secondly, on the markets VAR, the £23 million in the first quarter, that's a lot lower than your 2024 average of around £26 million, or even lower than your 2023 average. What are you doing behind the scenes here? I know that inventory risk is lower, using capital more efficiently, but any tangible examples you can give around this?
answer_text: Let me start with US cards, yes, we believe it's [still] achievable. What you're seeing in Q1 is a slightly odd picture, impacted by a couple of things. The first is, as Fed rates reduce in any particular quarter, you're going to see some degree of compression in NIM, but then offset in non-interest income. We've got floating rate assets, largely fixed rate liabilities that take time to reprice. We do hedge the position, but it's not the kind of structural hedging that you see within BUK, and the income from that hedge actually flows into non-NII. So it's a little bit messy, but you can see year-on-year that non-NII is much stronger, and that's really the effect of that hedge. But on an underlying basis, no real pressure on income. The other thing that's going on in Q1 is, what I would describe as a full NIM, it's not a banking NIM. So we have some cash sitting on the balance sheet ready to do a securitisation repayment, and that's undermined the NIM by creating a larger denominator. [The] pathway from here, I can see clear building blocks to get us to that greater than 12% position, and they come from all of the areas that we talked about before. So, the repricing that was completed last year, and flows through into NIM as customers use those cards and pay down the pre-repriced balances. The second thing is the deposits that we talked about previously. Thirdly is just the overall risk mix, clearly we'll get another move on again once we onboard [General Motors] later in the year. The building blocks are still in place, Sheel, so we're comfortable with that progress, it's a really key part of our plan. In terms of Markets VaR, I wouldn't call anything [out] in particular, because it's actually a business style and philosophy across the entirety of the market business. Again, it reflects the strategy that we set out at the beginning of this planning cycle for you, which was a real focus on the fact that we had deployed a lot of technology into the Markets business. That means that we're taking more risk intra-day, not so much in terms of inventory. So that's really the thematic, you could see that across a number of businesses, and it's really a reflection of the investments that we've made. So when I say we've monetised the opportunity within the current environment, that's really what I'm talking about here, and we have been really nimble in the way that we deployed capital. So I wouldn't say anything more specific than that. Thank you.

question_text: Morning, Andy Coombs from Citi. Firstly is on the Fixed Income result. You correctly pointed out that there's this big year-on-year improvement greater than your peers. Why that reticence still?
answer_text: So, how do we feel about FICC? I would say a couple of things, the first is we are definitely performing better across a range of products. Our European Rates business, as we said, has been an area of focus for us. That was very strong historically, we lost market share. We started of focusing on building that market share back through last year, it was definitely a journey through last year and it performed much better in Q1. The other thing I would call out is Fixed Income Financing within here, equally as part of our Financing businesses, are a much more stable source of revenues and Financing in general is a business that we've invested a lot in. We see good balanced growth and robust margins. So I would say the underlying position is objectively good. In any particular quarter, your [comparators] will either help you or weaken your result, that is just the nature of this business. I would say Q1'24 [was] maybe a little bit weaker, but then if you look at the trajectory and exit rate from 2024 into 2025, I think that would take you back towards this stronger position. From our perspective, what we're really focused on is, are those businesses performing well and in the way we would expect them to, [with] the market share as an output. On the structural hedge, I think Robin touched on this on the day [of results], I'm going to say the same thing again, we said broadly 90% as a planning assumption. question_text: Good morning. Alvaro Serrano from Morgan Stanley, a couple of questions please. One, maybe an uncomfortable question, on Dealogic data and the quarterly run rate at the moment. It does look pretty weak, it did look pretty weak in Q1 and then it turned out to be okay. Obviously April was quite a meaningful month. So I'm guess I'm trying to ask for some help to how to think about that market data that's coming through, because in Q1 it turned out to be, I think, wrong. So if there's any hand holding you can do there to help us interpret the data. Second, is on RWA efficiency, the large leverage finance position, Twitter / X, was largely disposed of. Are there any other legacy positions or any other low hanging fruit in terms of RWA efficiencies that are left, that you think there's more to go? Or you are where you want to be in terms of leverage finance appetite? Thank you.
answer_text: In terms of Dealogic data, clearly there is a subdued Banking environment. We saw that through Q1 and it's, if anything, more intense in April and particularly in ECM and M&A, there's probably a lot less activity than perhaps people expected at the beginning of the year. From our perspective, we planned for a market that was 10% down year-on-year. Q1 was broadly in alignment with that. What we have focused our businesses on is, clearly the scale of the market will go up and down. We are focusing them on making the market share gains that we've asked them to make, so even in a lower market [environment], are they making progress? So that's how we are thinking about it. And so far, we would say that things are getting postponed [and] pushed out, rather than cancelled. So that's what we see. There's just uncertainty in the market and therefore you can imagine the CEO community are reluctant to progress. It's very difficult to say anything more than that.

question_text: Hi, Priya Rathod from Jefferies. Just a few questions for me. So first is, going back to your comment on March being the strongest month for application and completion in Kensington. How much of the strength was driven by customers moving ahead of the stamp duty changes? And do you have a view on what the sustainable rate is going forward? And secondly, going back on to Brookfield, and I appreciate the insight you've given already, but if you could just remind us of the strategy and the long term benefits of that partnership, please? Thank you.
answer_text: There was undoubtedly a degree of pull forward into Q1. I think we've called that out and I think many of our competitors have done also, and you can see that in the strength of the data. That said, there is general momentum in the housing market in the UK and mortgages goes hand in hand with that. That comes from real wage growth, relative economic stability, relatively low but robust HPI and all of that flows through into good real housing activity. So, as we go forward from here, you might see a little drop back for a while, just reflecting that pull through. But generally speaking, there's momentum in the market and that comes from both sides of it. So you're seeing both purchase activity happening, both first time buyers and house purchase. That's good because it drives real economic activity in the wider economy, and it also tends to be slightly higher [loan-to-value], so slightly higher margin [versus] other participants in the market. Also, there's a pretty robust remortgage market as well, because what we've seen in the last few years is a shortening of terms, so there's definitely quite a remortgage churn in the market too, which gives us a good gross market to operate within, so some step back, but generally good. I would say in terms of Brookfield, how do we feel about this business? We feel that it is a really important service delivered to our clients and that is from the largest corporates all the way through to SMEs in the UK and about a third of the payments in the UK flow through that process every day, so it's a large scale business. However, it is also, (a) a scale business; (b) a low margin business and (c) one that has high technology requirements. And our view here was that we wanted a partner who could help us scale the business and help us deploy technology effectively across its waterfront. So, particularly into the smaller participants in that market, so the SMEs, where the technology has changed quite markedly over the last few years and arguably we have not kept up. So we didn't feel like we were the best able to do that on our own, particularly with the technology in mind. So that's really what's driven our desire here for a partner. But from our perspective, it's a business that we feel with Brookfield, we can deploy that technology. They also have businesses elsewhere in the globe that are using similar types of payment rail, so we can leverage that. The expertise that they have for us to bring this to a level of return, commensurate with what we would expect one of our businesses, because it's not there at the moment, it's marginally loss making, so it needs to be turned around with that partner. Then ongoing, reflecting our commitment and our interest in this business, we would expect, even after an exit, to retain 20% of it. So that's the general plan.

question_text: Thank you. It's Amit from Mediobanca. So two questions, one follow up from the [Q1 results day] call. I want to check again on the maturing hedge yield as you look out beyond 2026. It's just because some of your peers have slightly lower maturing hedge yields ahead of 2027, and then they have to step up. So I just want to check that there's nothing in particular, when thinking about what that maturing hedge yield will be, driving the continued growth in the hedge income. And then secondly, just coming back to your points on USCB in terms of risk adjusted margin. At the moment you're targeting something like 8 percentage points between NIM and loan loss provisions. So as you look to pivot the book a little bit more away from travel, and you look beyond, just curious where you think you can kind of get that to, whether that's nine or ten, or how you think about that? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay Amit, why don't I start with the second one and perhaps Dan can come back to the first. So we haven't given a target for risk adjusted margin beyond 2026. I mean, you're right in terms of the maths for 2026. The disposal of the [American Airlines] portfolio alone will move this, so we haven't changed our targets at this point in time, because we're still reflective of the exact timing of that [American Airlines] deal and what we do in terms of filling in the volume behind it, if you like. But [American Airlines] disposal alone will increase the NIM, but also increase the loan loss ratio from the numbers that we've given you to a more beneficial outcome. So it would be higher than eight, where it actually ends up obviously depends on the timing of that sale. We do expect it to be in 2026, but then the onboarding of GM, the onboarding of potential other partners, organic growth. So we'll update you in time, but I think you should expect us to grow it beyond the number that we've given you already, and actually onboarding GM and of boarding [American Airlines] will do that all on its own. Dan? Yes, we obviously haven't given you much guidance from 2027 and beyond, but obviously we have given you the locked-in income for 2025 and 2026. And we've also said that the structural hedge will continue to provide momentum beyond 2026. So I think you should just look at the five year sterling swap level and then the average yield on the portfolio, and you'll sort of just see that is the potential that will continue to create momentum, and that momentum will be beyond 2026. question_text: Chris Hallam from Goldman Sachs. So the first question on the banking wallet, a bit of a follow up from Alvaro's earlier question. I guess we should continue to think about the wallet assumptions, -10% for this year, +5% for next year, 2026 being lower than 2024, as more sort of prudent planning scenarios and assumptions rather than a forecast. But what is your best sense of what will actually happen? Or how would you assess client readiness to transact, given the backdrop this morning is different to the backdrop two weeks ago? Secondly on US cards, I appreciate the comments on the resilience of the business through April, in line with the industry more broadly. But I guess in the last few weeks you must have done quite a lot of fire drills around potential macro scenarios, potential adverse outcomes. Has any of that work changed at all how you think about where you want to grow the business or how you want to put more capital to work? Thank you.
answer_text: Thanks, Chris. So, the way you characterise Banking is the way you should characterise how we approach business in general, which is that we will plan on, I would say, a reasonable basis and the $80 billion for the current year is roughly the 10 year average, well actually $84 billion is the decade average. So it's nothing more than that, it's not scientific, we just think it's a reasonable number for which we should plan. In doing so, we're trying to put some operational tension into the businesses, because clearly I want them to reach the returns goals and by doing so, that must be on the basis of a blend of market share gain consistently delivered, prudent management of risk and driving the efficiency and effectiveness of the business. It cannot be on the basis of a heroic or high market assumption, so that's why we do that. But it is a prudent assumption, [and] you should expect us to monetize at any environment around us and that's why we've invested in the business. Again, expect us to be ready as and when the market picks up. It feels like that readiness to transact, if you like, won't be universal because different sectors are clearly getting clarity at different stages of time. Different geographies are getting clarity at different stages of time. So if you're running either a US corporate or a large global corporate, it actually depends on the specifics of your business model, and we hear that very strongly as we talk to clients. So I think it feels unlikely that we'll wake up tomorrow and the world will have gone back to wherever we thought it was in Davos. But as clarity emerges in different geographies and sectors, hopefully we'll see some coming back, but in the meantime, we continue to drive operational effectiveness. In terms of US cards, this is a business that we've run for 20 years, so it's not new to us. This environment is not new to us. Therefore, what have we done over the last few weeks? The answer is nothing significantly more than we would do ordinarily in this business, because that's just the way we run it, that's the way we understand it. So as you can imagine, even back in 2023, we were cutting unused credit lines, because we knew that unemployment was bound to rise in the US because it was at such low levels. We've been extremely cautious about the lower FICOs. You can see that around 13 percent or less, is less than 660. And actually, if you look at [slide] 38, you'll see that the flow into those lower FICOs is lower than the stock. So that tells you that the credit risk decisions that we're making on the margins are very thoughtful. We are fully staffed in our collections capability and we're really thoughtful about that. So when we see a change in consensus, as we saw in 2023 and 2024 for US unemployment, we don't just change our IFRS9 result, we actually deploy the business to do something different. So whether that's the way we interact with customers, or the fact that we might be putting more people into that collection capability. So we're ready, but the business is very calm and very confident because we've weathered this kind of environment before. We're also very focused on these other [areas], which is deploying the deposit strategy, deploying the efficiency strategy, because from their perspective the most effective thing they can do is improve the returns of business.

question_text: Thank you. Nicolas Payen from Kepler Chevreux. I have two questions please. The first one, coming back on the IB and the capital efficiency. We have seen a strong improvement in the revenue to RWA by almost 120 basis points. If I look at the mix actually, Fixed Income was very strong and usually it's a bit more capital intensive than M&A and ECM, which were kind of lacklustre. So just wondering, if we have a market coming back on ECM and M&A, should we expect another very strong improvement on that front? The second question on BUK, I appreciate we have already discussed in the call, but the non-NII line was actually kind of weak, if you look at [it on a] historical basis. So just wondering if there is anything particular in that line? Thank you.
answer_text: Let me take the second one first. Absolutely nothing to call out in there. That line can be a little bit lumpy, because you can get some one-ofs in there. But we would reiterate the guidance that we've given you, which is greater than £250 million. There's nothing specific I would call out in Q1. Just [to] remind you that sometimes Q1 seasonally can be a little bit weaker, because some of the income that flows into there, you've got some interchange income going in. So typically Q1 transactional levels are a little bit lower [from] day count [and] seasonally lower as people recover from the holiday season, so a little bit of that going on in there. In terms of the IB and return on, or revenues over RWAs, I mean you're right about FICC, but at the same time, remember that [has] a Financing business within it. And you're seeing strong growth in Financing, and Financing is RWA light, albeit leverage heavy, but it's RWA light. So the growth in that will be driving revenue over RWAs, plus what I've talked about before with Sheel, which is just general recycling of RWAs and the velocity of capital, within the Markets business more generally. But you are right in terms of, if I go back to the strategy of our Banking business. Just to remind you, there are two parts of that in terms of the rebalancing, both designed to make that business in and of itself more capital efficient. The first was M&A and ECM, which you rightly call out are lower RWA, but also the growth of our International Corporate Bank within there. So you're getting Transactional banking income coming through. For very much the same reasons as you're seeing in the Corporate Bank in the UK, so strong deposit flows there. Again, that is deposit income. So to the extent that you see a recovery in economic activity, because as you can imagine, trade finance etc, is a little bit subdued at the moment, both in the Corporate Bank and in the ICB. You would expect that also to pick up and that's also capital light. Okay, with that I will call the breakfast to a close. Thank you very much for joining us. Really appreciate your time and we will see some of you very soon over the next day or so, but thank you and we will see you again in Q2, which is not long. Have a good day.
