question_text: Hi, good morning. A couple of questions, please. First of all, on capital and then one on the Investment Bank. On capital, you are at 13.7% after the buyback. That's a pretty comfortable position given [your 13-14% range]. [Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB)] has been delayed, when you think about your capital position versus the over £10 billion distribution, and obviously M&A options that have appeared in the press, how do you see upside to distribution versus additional firepower for M&A? Whether that's a portfolio in the US or something else, if you can maybe walk us through your thinking. And second, on the Investment Bank, obviously Trading, you have explained Anna, very strong. Clearly doing better than US peers and that's worked very well, but Investment Banking fees not so well. So in a world where we seem to be heading, famous last words, to a low volatility environment, I know you've touched on it at the end of the quarter, but if you can elaborate, if the low volatility banking fees picking up thesis has held at the later part of the quarter, as we look in the rest of the year, can we still expect sort of decent growth in a low volatility environment, i.e. Banking fees making up for whatever sort of normalisation of Global Markets we might see? Thank you.
answer_text: Good morning, Alvaro, thank you very much for kicking off the call for us. I'll take the first question and then I'm going to hand to Venkat. Our capital position just reflects the execution of the strategy. The strategy is designed to create higher and more consistent returns, which in turn allows us to return more to shareholders and indeed invest in the business, and that's really what you're seeing here. It's exactly what we expected. As you call out 13.7% post the buyback, we indicated at the beginning of the year that, actually, we expected to operate towards the upper half of our capital range just because of the Pillar 2 that we're carrying in advance of the US model being implemented. So we're exactly where we expected to be. And the broader aspects of your question, I would say the capital hierarchy remains completely intact. So, we're generating higher levels of capital from more consistent and higher returns. And our priorities are: number one, of course, regulatory. Number two, distributions. Those distributions are up 21% year-on-year. The buyback is up 33% year-on-year, and we said that the distributions should be progressive in 2025. That's what you're seeing, and our guidance and target for the three years is at least £10 [billion]. So, that all remains intact. Finally, continuing to invest in the UK businesses. We do believe our plan is an organic one, and you can see at the halfway point, we put down £17 billion of the £30 billion RWAs that we are planning to [deploy]. So, that's how we feel about capital, really no change, just the execution of the strategy. Venkat? Yes. Thanks for the question, Alvaro. On the Investment Bank, let me give you a longer term view and then I'll come to your very specific question. So, on the Investment Bank, over the last six quarters, in fact since before then, we've been obviously investing in our structural capabilities. What you see in the results in the Investment Bank is a combination of deep structural improvements, which we think are sustainable over the long run, and then cyclical aspects which benefited the [Markets] business and may have been a headwind for the Banking business. On the structural side, you're seeing deeper client engagement. One of the statistics we put out was we're a number six Investment Bank. Of our top 100 clients, who are we in the top five with? That number was 49 before the plan started, our target is 70, we're at 60 now. You can see it in the market shares which we have in Global Markets. Financing is up 23% year-on-year in US dollars. Our three focus areas are up by one percentage point, 2024 versus 2023, and that's the latest data we have. And then I mentioned the top five client [rankings]. And then when you look at Banking, capital discipline has really taken root, return on risk-weighted assets is improving and market share has improved, although a little slower this year. So that is the structural benefit that we see, and you can see it in the results. When you look at the [Global Markets] performance versus consensus, for six quarters now we've beaten consensus. The size of that beat has been growing to about £300 million this quarter. So I think what you're seeing is the combination there of both structural and cyclical. Let me come to cyclical. Cyclical in the Markets business has been helped, obviously, by volatility. And that's been a tailwind. And in Banking, as you point out, as decision-making has slowed, that volatility has been a bit of a headwind. Now, looking forward, we are seeing that headwind in Banking dissipating as there is more deal activity and we expect that to continue. As for Markets, I think a lot of the positioning that's taken place in the last six months has been in reaction to immediate volatility. So, what I would call shorter-term risk management and that has obviously delayed longer-term decision-making, which drives Banking. Now, though, in the Markets side, you could see more longer-term positioning and decision-making as people take a clearer view on different asset classes and rotation within asset classes. I hope and expect, given all the structural improvements I outlined, that we will benefit from that. Thank you, Alvaro. Perhaps we can go to the next question, please.

question_text: Hi, morning there. Two questions, if I may. The first one was on Barclays UK, I was wondering if you could expand on this historic swap maturity impact that landed in H1, that comes out in H2 and should support expansion in the product margin in the second half. I don't know if you can frame the size of that, perhaps. Then attached to that, looking at your full-year guide and talk to quarter-on-quarter growth, it looks like we're getting to an exit quarterly run rate of about £8 billion or so on the NII for Barclays UK. Consensus is at £8.3 billion for next year, it doesn't feel overly challenging versus that exit rate. So can we infer that you're comfortable with market expectations next year, perhaps even some upside, despite the miss in the second quarter? The second question was on the US Consumer business on the impairment side, encouraging to see that step down in impairments in Q2 and the lower 30-day delinquencies. Perhaps I can invite you to comment on how you think about impairments in the second half and beyond in that book. I mean there had been some scepticism that the 2026 impairment guide could be challenging to get to 400 basis points in the long run, so are you more confident on delivery there today, than perhaps three, four months ago? Thank you.
answer_text: Thanks, Guy. Why don't I take both of those and I'm sure Venkat may add on the second. Let me start with BUK NII in totality. So we are confident in the greater than £7.6 billion and when we gave you that guidance we were clearly aware of the swap matter that you're talking about here, so the phasing is panning out as we expected it to. Therefore, that means by definition, we're expecting income to be in excess of £3.9 billion in the second half of the year, and within that, I would just add for Q4 to be higher than Q3 and I'll come back to the second part of your question in a minute. So, what really drives that? There's clearly the things we talked about which is the structural hedge, loan growth, so you can see the momentum in BUK. The other thing I would just call out as a product margin matter is, it's not just this swap effect but it's also the fact we expect to see maturing promotional cards balances in the second half of the year and obviously we expect to see deposit trends to continue to mitigate. This swap point, it's a historic matter, it's an accounting point and it's accounting timing. It relates to the maturity profile of historic swaps versus how we recognise swaps against products internally, it's purely timing. To try and put some quantum around it, it's probably most of the consensus miss in Q2 and it was relatively similar across Q1 and Q2. It's a H1 versus H2 point, it's now behind us, it's not operational, purely accounting timing. From 2022 onwards, we're now booking our swaps in a different way, so I'm not expecting this will recur. In terms of the jumping off point, as I said in my prepared remarks, please use H2 as a jumping off point for NII next year, and within that, note the Q3 and Q4 momentum. It's a bit too early to talk about explicit numbers or consensus for next year, but please note from this our confidence in terms of building NII momentum, not just in meeting 2025 guidance, but underpinning RoTE in 2026 and having momentum even beyond that point. Let me now come to US Consumer impairment. It's fallen quarter-on-quarter, as we would have expected it to seasonally, and you can see that 30-day delinquencies are down 20 basis points, so it's performing well. Interestingly, within that, the lowest three FICO bands are also down year-on-year in delinquencies, which I see as encouraging. What we expect in the second half is obviously normal seasonal trends. You tend to see a build towards the back end of the year, just as holiday spending picks up. The only other notable thing I would call out is in Q3, we onboard the General Motors back book. You should expect to see £100 million day one charge then. And then you're going to see some migration effects, probably about £50 million per quarter for a few quarters, just because we onboard things at stage one. Overall, within the context of the group guidance of 50 to 60 basis points, we're very comfortable. Venkat, anything you want to add? Look, I'll just add at a broader macroeconomic level, it has been remarkable really, how resilient the US economy has been, and indeed the UK economy, to everything that's going on [with] tariffs. Obviously, there is inflationary pressure, but employment remains very strong. The [Federal Reserve] is having a meeting tomorrow, but it's not cut [rates] once so far this year. I think we have to see how that plays out, but I would say at a macroeconomic level, there is room for hope in the strength of the economy, especially as the frequency of tariff announcements and the amplitude of tariff changes reduce, both frequency and amplitude. Okay, thank you, next question please.

answer_text: Okay, thanks, Rob. I will take those. I'm not going to go into the details of [Effective Interest Rate] assumptions. question_text: Good morning, thanks for taking the questions. I had a couple on regulation, please. So firstly, thinking about what's happening in the US. If we get these [Enhanced Supplementary Leverage Ratio (eSLR)] changes and your US competitors have effectively significantly more leverage balance sheet capacity handed to them and they seek to deploy that in markets. How should we think about the effect of that on the IB growth you've seen over the last five, six years, particularly around Financing? Do you see that as a competitive threat and what can you do about it if those peers now have more capacity to muscle in? With regards to [Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR)] and the US Consumer business, the reasoning you've given for retaining that business in the past is partly because it helps your CCAR performance. Obviously, CCAR is getting more benign. Do you now feel less compelled to retain that business? What is the argument for keeping that? On the UK side of the fence, if I could just invite you to comment on what, if any, outcomes we might expect from the current UK capital framework review that's happening in the background. Are you expecting that to be a positive, and Venkat, I know you've expressed some views contrary to your peers at other banks around the ring-fencing regime. What are your updated thoughts given the changes we may see there? Thank you.
answer_text: Thanks, Chris. So I will start on the first two of those and then I'll hand to Venkat for the third point on the UK capital framework. Look, on SLR, we note peer comments. We're confident in our ability to continue to grow our Prime business and indeed our Fixed Income Financing business. We're seeing that continue, good balance growth, good spreads and actually expanding into Asia, which is relatively new for us. So very much open for business and confident in our ability to grow, and really what's underpinning that is a couple of things. Firstly, as we look at our US peers, it looks like the leverage is not binding for all right now. So this may or may not make a significant amount of difference. Secondly, we look forward to what the [Financial Policy Committee (FPC)] might do in the UK as it looks at the framework more holistically, as you point out, so no specific concerns. On CCAR, Barclays in the US typically has a good CCAR result and has exactly the same this year. A low point of 10.8%, a stress buffer of 3.3%. And we still see that diversified banks across that CCAR stack get a better result. That is very clear. There were some aspects of this year's CCAR stress test where the market shock component was a little lower than we might have previously seen, we can't always anticipate that that will be the case. So, it's important that we don't react to one stress test in isolation. Just stepping back, this is a business that we believe we can improve the returns on. You can see that we believe we can get the returns not just to be in line with the Group, but more towards mid-teens. And it offers, income and geographic diversification, as well as the particular capital efficiency point. So that's how we feel about CCAR. Venkat? Yes. Moving to the UK, first of all, I welcome the broader capital framework review that was announced recently. And I welcome it in two ways. One is it's an important topic, and the second is it's looking at the entirety of it, which is not just capital rules itself, but stress testing and everything that goes into the final number. The way I think about it is that capital and capital regulation is an important part of a healthy banking system and of growth, and it is what you do to run a robust banking system. The ring-fencing is an important bedrock of deposit protection, and what it helps is with the so-called gone concern. If a bank has a problem like Icelandic banks did in 2007-08, then how do you make sure that depositors get their deposits back over and above the protection scheme? And what can you do in terms of the assets that are attached to those deposits? The Governor of the Bank of England a few weeks ago spoke at the Treasury Select Committee and he made a point that about 99% of assets from ring-fence banks are deployed within the UK and 32% of the corresponding assets from non-ringfence banks are deployed in the UK. That's the illustration of the problem. So that's why I continue to believe strongly in the maintenance and sustenance of that ring-fence as it is structured. I mean, let's see what comes out of the government review, but that's my view, certainly. And then on capital, as I said, that is part of growing the economy and growing the banking system. Now, the Governor made another point last week at the Treasury Select Committee where he said there's no trade-off between financial stability and growth. He's absolutely right. Financial stability is a [inaudible]. It's a necessity, but not all regulation necessarily contributes to financial stability and that's where the debate is to be had. Which regulation is excessive, superfluous, gilding the lily, in the whole capital framework? And can you relax some of that regulation and improve growth? I'm optimistic for those outcomes. Thank you Chris, perhaps we can go to the next question please.

question_text: Good morning everybody. Two questions on RWAs and the Investment Bank. I guess the dynamics here in Q2 feel similar to what we saw in Q3 last year, so US dollar depreciation quarter-on-quarter. Last year, you let that feed through to lower headline RWAs. This quarter, that hasn't been the case. So I guess, what's changed there? This quarter, without reinvesting the FX tailwind, you would have obviously seen a step down in RWAs as a percentage of group towards the target. You would have seen the CET1 tailwind, but then you also, I guess, would have missed out on some commercial opportunities I suppose. Being there for clients on the Financing side continues to be an to be an important part of the rankings improvements you flagged so how are you thinking about juggling those priorities given that they may be at the margin a little bit mutually exclusive? Do you feel comfortable saying 56% is peak and it trends down from here? Secondly, just a confirmation I think on RWA productivity, there's a tick down in the second quarter, obviously Q1 was quite a high number. Anything you want to call out in the quarter, maybe it's the ICB one-offs quarter-on-quarter, and it feels like that level of RWA productivity is a level that would support the RoTE target for next year. So I just wanted to check that you agree with that. Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thanks Chris. Step back for a minute, the RWAs in the IB have been broadly flat for three and a half years. That is our clear strategic intent and what we keep coming back to quarter after quarter after quarter. It's a key part of the plan and the capital discipline that we talked about. What you might see in any particular quarter is either higher or lower levels of client activity as we pass the quarter end, and it's honestly nothing more than that. You can see that we are very disciplined in the way that we manage our risk. You can see that in the VaR and in the loss days. If you look at the distribution of trading income, that's all on page 37. So we deployed more RWAs to support clients, not really in taking materially more risk. That's what you should expect us to do, and we really don't feel that RWA discipline and growth in the IB are mutually exclusive. So since the beginning of the plan, the IB RWAs, well, more than the plan, for two years before the plan started, have been flat. And we've got an income CAGR of 9%. That's what we're trying to do here, and I think you're seeing that flow through into the second part of your question, which is really about RoTE productivity. There's a clear seasonality to the IB generally, higher in Q1, higher in Q2, than Q3 and Q4 typically. And so you're seeing nothing more than a seasonal change year-on-year. It's up meaningfully, I think, 80 basis points year-on-year. So what we're doing here, which is driving capital discipline in Banking and driving our focus businesses in Markets, is working. And what's really important to us, and it's probably the most important part of the plan for me, is not just the returns in the IB, but the consistency of those returns. That's really important. So you're going to see that, hopefully, in the coming quarters. I''ll just add not just consistency, but quality. So consistency and quality go together. As we do more in Financing revenue, as we do more in Corporate Banking revenue, you get the consistency, but you're also getting more predictable, high-quality revenues. So I endorse everything Anna just said, obviously. Okay. Thank you. Thank you very much, Chris. Perhaps we can go to the next question, please, operator.

question_text: Good morning. Thanks for taking my questions, one on the UK and one on the US please. On the UK I just wanted to come back to the deposit trends. And then secondly, on US Consumer, I wanted to ask about mix shift and what it means for your targets. If I look at your NIM in US Consumer, impressive QoQ improvement, up 30 basis points. At the same time, you're talking about a £50 million additional charge over the next few quarters from Q4 on post-acquisition stage migration from General Motors. Just given that mix shift that you've seen with AA coming out, General Motors coming on, what does it mean for your targets, the $40 billion receivables, the greater than 12% NIM, the 400 basis points cost of risk in that division? And they are now subject to slight change. Thank you.
answer_text: Thanks, Andy. I'll take both of those. So, look, we had a similar question on deposit trends earlier in the call. There's nothing specific going on here. We feel like we're broadly following our peers in terms of market share, particularly in current accounts, and you can see that, as I said, in the roll of the hedge. Let me specifically speak about fixed-term deposits and the ISA season, which I think is probably what's underpinning your question. So, look, the ISA season was very, very different this year. We can all, I guess, have a view about why that might be the case, but it was bigger and earlier than we've ever seen before. And if you look at the quantum of flows during the early part of April. I think the second week of April, the flows on those products were around £6 billion, not for us, but for the market. Then, if you look at the average of May and June, that's more like £1 billion a week. So that gives you an idea of the scale of flows. The pricing, we felt, was not economic, and therefore we stepped back from fixed-term pricing in that ISA season and remained disciplined. We did, however, grow our ISA balances year-on-year and feel like we had a good season. So where we think it's important for the relationship, we do step into pricing, and you can see there's a divergence between our core pricing and our relationship pricing. So it is important to us, but, we're not going to price uneconomically in the market whilst we have a stable underlying base. answer_text: Okay. Thank you, Perlie. So we're pleased with the £10 billion organic growth in the UK and you can see from slide 13 that that momentum is picking up, not just in BUK, in the areas that we've talked about before, which is cards and mortgages, [which] we talk about a lot, but also in UK Corporate. So we've had three successive quarters of growth in UK Corporate. And you can actually see BUK Business Banking now starting to turn. And when we set our plan, we focused that plan on areas where we were either underweight or we felt we had opportunities to grow because we'd lost market share. So that's true of, for example, high loan-to-value mortgages, or Corporate and Business Banking, where we have had a much higher loan-to-deposit ratio than our peers in the past. We're around 73% [core deposits] now and we expect that to get to over 75%. That's our objective and you can see that on the slide and there is a differential in margin between those broker deposits and direct to retail deposits. Slide 25, if you want to have a look at that. I think it's the chart in the bottom right-hand corner. So, the other thing that's going to help us progress Jordan, is, bringing on GM. So, GM is a higher margin because it's a retail book, but the risk adjusted margin is very good. So, you can see that, remembering Q3, we're going to onboard the back book of GM. We're already originating on the front book, so you're going to see further progress from here I think, in terms of that NIM. question_text: Jan from Citi, just one quick question on the IB. So, you talked about beating consensus for the last six quarters. How sustainable do you think that would be going forward, particularly in the trading, FICC and Equities, because I know some of your peers have commented on that. And then secondly, on lending, have you seen any sort of uncertain distress from corporates based on the macro environment, particularly after tariff regime in US or is it, mostly a wait and see moment or is it just business normal?
answer_text: Well clearly beating consensus, is a tale of two halves. So, I can't really comment on that. What I can comment on is the fact that we are confident in our ability to grow the IB, generally speaking. And that's really coming from our objectives to grow and stabilise. So, you can see the momentum we've got in those stable sources of revenue. We talk about Financing a lot, we talk about the International Corporate Bank less so, and remember they perform similar roles in those different parts of the Investment Bank. So, expect that to remain our focus. Expect us also to want to continue to mature out those focus businesses that I talked about within Markets. And we do feel like we are taking share. And expect us to continue to want to take share in Investment Banking fees. So, that ambition remains there. We still want to get this business to be in alignment with the group RoTE in 2026 and to make some progress in 2025. So, you should expect us to want to keep pushing that income momentum. Now, clearly what we saw in Q2 was a degree of volatility particularly in April and so we saw our daily run rates in April pretty elevated. But actually in May and June they were higher than they were in the previous year and that's really coming from the stability of that Financing business. What we are not assuming in our sort of c.11% is that there is market volatility in the year to go. Clearly if that occurs then you should expect us to monetise it, but that's not something that we are relying upon. On your second question, lending, as I said in in my question before, we don't see any sort of significant points of distress in either the UK or the US relating to tariffs or national insurance changes or minimum wage changes in the UK. They're very idiosyncratic where we see those points of pressure. Of course, we do use SRT as a credit relief mechanism and we focus that on specific sectors where we have concerns at times, but really nothing to call out. There's a little bit of wait and see, and it's very industry sector specific as you're probably picking up. But at the same time I think the general economic pressure and the desire to grow productivity is also leading some corporates to want to invest. So you see both extremes really and it is very corporate specific.

question_text: Hi, this is Priya Rathod from Jefferies. Just a higher-level question on your cost target. So, you realised £200 million of the expected £500 million, for FY25. So, £1.35 billion through that £2 billion and we've got a good line of sight here in relation to the execution of that. question_text: Elise Yu Ge from KBW, thank you for taking the questions. I've just got two please. So, first is on margin for US consumer, which has been improving Q2 to 10.8%. So that's my tricky way to combine the two questions, but hopefully it's some way related. And then second one is on capital. Clearly the onboarding of clients like GM really help that and the continued rebalancing. To give you an idea, at the moment we're about 15% retail, post GM it will be 20%. So that really does start to push the NIM but really importantly, a higher risk adjusted margin. So, the, increase in NIM more than compensates for any increase in a loan loss rate that we might expect. On corporate loan pickup. I'd sort of nest it in the context of the discussions that we've already had around credit. So it really is I would say an improved supply side on our part. And if you go back to the deep dive that we had, with Matt Hammerstein last year. He was really focused on working with the clients we already have with whom we've got deep cash relationships or merchant acquiring payments relationships. So, we know them well. Really sort of reinvigorating our appetite to lend to those clients and you can see that coming through and that's product, its process, it's digital engagement. So, all of the things that we talked about is just the strategy. I think the other thing I would call out is that we are growing our client base, so we onboarded 550 new clients last year, 330 this year so far. So, we are actively acquiring clients, and we can see that our market share of both lending and deposits is going up. So Pillar 1 is going to go up, we might expect a degree of offset and Pillar 2A, but we don't know what that is yet. And therefore, we are very happy running where we are. The business is highly capital generative. So, we are both generating good returns and improved returns, but on a higher capital base and we're comfortable doing that because it gives us options in terms of redeployment and distributions. As you've seen distributions are up significantly year on year, 21% up and that buyback is up to a billion. So, immediately on the day that we announced, obviously the capital drops to 13.7%, so it's in the zone that we said it would be and we are happy there until we've got further clarity.

question_text: Okay, great thank you, Sheel Shah, JP Morgan. I've got one on UK NII and then a few on cards please. So, on the UK NII it seems like there'll be a hockey stick effect for the third and fourth quarter. I know you've spoken about the card balances coming online in the second half. The hedge contribution in the first quarter was about £50 million increased quarter on quarter. The second quarter was about £75 million quarter on quarter. Is there some lumpiness in this that we should be expecting for the third and fourth quarter or is it going to be a bit more linear between them both? And then for the cards, just a few there. You've spoken about the asset quality environment in the cards business UK and US. How should we think about the stage two ratio? Normally that, at least on the US side used to run above 30%. I know there's some moving parts from book sales and Tesco coming online, but should we be going back towards that sort of 30% in the US and sort of mid-twenties for the UK? And then just one more on US cards with regards to, there was a deal around Apple Pay, earlier in the year, it seems you may have lost out to at least. I'm just wondering how you're thinking about competition in the cards market. It seems to be quite competitive. Is this a pricing market? You know, what's the main source of competition in this market? And keen to get your thoughts on the market overall?
answer_text: Let me start with UK NII. I think a hockey stick is too strong an expression. You know, clearly what we called out is that there was some headwinds in NII in the first couple of quarters really from these maturing swaps. The timing on the accounting, which then neutralises in the second half. And remember you've also had some base rate reduction effects in the first half as well, so, you get that sort of repricing timing coming through. So specifically what you should be modelling is that the negative factor in product margin in that sort of diagram that we've given you goes from being negative to neutral to positive essentially in the second half. So, I'm not looking at any particular lumpiness. Really what you've got coming through is continued role of the structural hedge, continued asset growth, but then the margin matter, really that hedge effect dissipating and also the maturation of cards starting in the second half. So not lumpy. On the second point on cards, it's difficult to call out a specific percentage. Essentially, what stage two is that's the real sort of procyclical element of IFRS 9 is the way I think about it. Because they're almost certainly not delinquent, but your model is telling you given the macroeconomic environment or your macroeconomic assumptions that they may well become delinquent and therefore you start providing for those. So, there can be movements in and out of stage one and stage two purely on the basis of a change in consensus, macroeconomic consensus, which we use to drive our IFRS9 models. So, it's difficult to call out a specific percentage, but if you saw an expected deterioration in the macroeconomic environment, that's where you'd see the increase in charge coming through a higher coverage of those stage two balances. The other thing I would say is perhaps two offsetting things. Given that the level of indebtedness is such structurally lower, not just in the UK but in the US, clearly that also feeds into whether someone is stage one or stage two. Because the more sort of borrowings you have, the more likely it is that we regard you as a stage two borrower. So, a general level of reduction in indebtedness across both markets will feed through into a generally lower level. Conversely to that, if you start to see a pickup in spending that comes from economic confidence, even though the environment might be better, if customers start spending more, then that can also trigger them into stage two. I often say to my colleagues, if they go and buy a new house and start buying stuff for the house, they will certainly become a stage two customer irrespective of whether or not you feel you are a credit risk. So, it's quite sensitive really to nuances and customer behaviour. So, I won't call out percentage but a few things to think about there. And then finally in terms of the US cards book we continue to look for new partners in the US and you should expect us to do so. We see really our sweet spot probably where we have a competitive edge around a slightly smaller portfolio, say between £2-4 billion. We like that because typically, it doesn't put a huge concentration in our book, which we're always mindful of. So, we don't want very, very large books within there, just because of the scale of our business. So don't expect us to pursue a Walmart or a Costco or anything like that. Simply the book isn't big enough to house that. We wouldn't want the concentration risk. It is always a balance between price and the rest of the service that you can give those businesses. Remember for us we do not have our own brand in terms of cards. That makes a difference to partners. We are not competing in the wallet against them with our own card. The other thing is we carry their brand. So the service and the operational stability that goes with it is really important. So we continue to invest in digitisation of this business. And in fact, the customer facing and customer engagement digitisation is probably the best in the business, not necessarily at the operational end, but in the way that you interact with us. So we think that's also important for partners. So it's not just price, it's very multifaceted. And you can see that in our retention. In the last year we've won not only the GM, but we've retained four. So, it does come through in the retention stats. We're able to build those businesses very successfully, retain clients, provide a really high level of service. And you can see that in the satisfaction of the partners that we work with. So very focused on that.

And within that sort of really using the full breadth of the range that we've got with Kensington, which I'll come back to. Cards very similar. You can see the run rate that we are going at now deploying not just Tesco into the market, but also Amazon and Avios. So, remember, we're running essentially four brands, now as we address that market and that's really helping us target different types of customers, different products. Corporate lending you can see is picking up some momentum. What happens there is we put the RWAs out and then you subsequently see the drawdown. So, there's some timing disconnect between RWAs and lending in corporate. Typically, we've put those facilities out, we've seen subsequent drawdowns. And then the last one I would call out is just Business Banking. So, worth looking at the bottom left-hand side of page 13. So, in Business Banking remember it's still got a lot of these COVID era loans within there, that are in run-off. So you've seen those declining over the last few quarters and really what you should be focused on is the darker blue area at the bottom, which is probably too early to call it a trend yet, but we are pleased with that progress in terms of Business Banking lending really starting to turn and expect us to focus on that more. Kensington is a standardised portfolio, at this stage, so that should give you some ideas to as to how the risk weights are relative to the book as a whole.

And then secondly, with the US deregulating, what do you think the UK PRA will do in response? Are there any lines they will not cross or how would they ensure competitiveness for UK banks? I won't obviously call out names, but as I said before, where we see issues, they are idiosyncratic. So they still do occur, they're just not systemic across the book. So, it's not really inconsistent with my comment around overall credit quality. The other thing that's going on in there is we do put the cost of hedging through there. question_text: Hi, it's Perlie, Bank of America. So just a couple of final questions I suppose. TSB, I guess no one would say that the price they went for was particularly cheap, but I guess nevertheless they managed to come up with a pretty attractive RoI, notwithstanding the fact that they're using a 55% synergy assumption which is quite high. I guess any comments you could give in terms of why in the final rounds you did not go for it, and maybe just a wider thinking of what level of RoI do you think would be worth it if you were to do an M&A transaction? And then a couple follow ups on the [US] cards side. Note that you said that you are mindful of the concentration risk. I think there are maybe some portfolios that are maybe a bit more at risk of maybe having a combination. I guess Hawaiian Airlines you might have in mind. I know you said that you're [continuing] that partnership and nevertheless there's some conversations around that. So, does that mean that if that were to happen in the next few years, you would not want to chase that volume because it would present too much concentration risk? And I guess the other follow up to the cards question is, again, you mentioned that you wouldn't chase volume and that RoTE is a north star, but equally cards is a scale business. And when the AA book goes, I guess in the next year, I don't suppose the cost base would fall by 20%. So how do you balance between the cost element and the scalability of the card business and sort of not chasing volume for the sake of it?
answer_text: As you would expect I'm not going to talk about any target potential or otherwise. So, I'm not going to talk specifics here, but I will talk about how we feel about M&A generally. So, we've said in the past that where we consider M&A you should expect us to do it in our three highest returning UK businesses. That in so doing we would be looking for either scale or capability. So, Kensington was capability both in terms of its, risk and underwriting capability, but also its securitisation capability. Tesco is both scale and capability. So, as we integrate Tesco, it is an integration and not a migration. So, we are building some of the Tesco functionality into Barclays as we bring those balances across. So, looking for both of those things. And then the third thing is obviously price and return. So, anything that we've done in the past ticks all those three boxes. And anything that we would do in the future would tick all three of those boxes. I won't call out a target RoI, but you should expect that as we look at things, we're also really mindful of our capital hierarchy, which is number one regulatory, and number two, distributions to shareholders. So we don't want to distract the business either from the distribution targets that we've given you already, which are at least £10 billion, nor indeed operationally. We don't want to, have a significant operational lift that we believe would be difficult within the context of the plan, timeframe beyond what we are doing already, we're really execution focused. And then the third thing is investment in the business. So, expect us to remain really disciplined, and as we look at things as a high bar. In terms of US cards, to your point on concentration, look, I talked about previously wanting to be at sort of the 2-4 billion dollars type range. Clearly if there is further consolidation in the market then we'll look at things on a case-by-case basis, I wouldn't give you a conclusion here. The one that we walked away from was obviously American, which would have been in combination, a very large file for us. And not only that, a very large file with a low risk adjusted margin. So that's why we walked away from that business. So, remember as AA exits the business, you're going to see a few things happening. You will clearly see the risk adjusted margin go up. As you say, it does put some economies of scale pressure into the business from a cost perspective but expect us to be working very hard on that even from now. And we do think that growth continues to be both attractive and possible in this business. So, we still remain ambitious to sort of grow balances over time, so we'll just continue to do that. But RoTE is the north star. Okay. Any more questions? Sheel has one.

question_text: Hi, morning Venkat, morning Anna. Thanks for taking the questions. The first one was on the US Consumer [Bank] top line. Clearly very strong up 20% year over year, both non-interest income and then the NIM moving up to 11.5%. Just helpful to understand if there's anything particularly lumpy in there. So, I guess firstly, just to confirm that we should be thinking about growth of that 11.5% NIM base, given the sort of ongoing lending mix actions you've talked to and growth in retail deposit base. And then within that £215 million of non-interest income in Q3, anything lumpy in there, you would point to, to temper us away from analysing north of £800 million before thinking about things like gains on sales or portfolios next year. And then the second question was just on UK Mortgages. From a volume perspective, very strong both net and gross lending. Nearly £10 billion in gross lending is certainly above typical run rates. I'm just interested if that's the level you think you will continue to write at. And then from a sort of competitive perspective, what you're seeing in the market. I know the actions you're taking, and Kensington offers quite a bit of insulation, but are you seeing any competitive pressures on new lending spreads when you look at like for like lending? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thanks Guy. I'll take both of those and thanks for opening the call for us. And just on the US Consumer [Bank] top line, I think what you're seeing coming together now is a real combination of all of the operational actions that we've been undertaking over the last few quarters. And you can see that on a new slide on Slide 24. Because it's drawn from those operational actions, we do have confidence in its sustainability. Really what's driving the NIM is the things that we've talked about before. So, it's the repricing, which remember takes some time to work its way through into the NIM because customers need to draw down on those new terms and conditions. It's also the increase in the level of retail deposits, and retail deposits are about 50 basis points to 60 basis points cheaper than the other sources of funding we've had previously. And then thirdly, there is this increasing proportion of retail balances, which are higher NIM. So I expect over the next couple of quarters, Q4 and Q1 to be broadly at the level of NIM that we're currently running at, around 11.5%. I'm not going to guide you to Q2 and beyond, because obviously, once we exit the American Airlines portfolio, that NIM is going to jump up again. So, I will guide you to that a little nearer the time. In terms of non-interest income, there's a couple of things going on in there. The first is obviously the increase in volume that we're seeing, not just from General Motors, but also the organic growth in this business. So, if you go back to the equivalent quarter just before the start of the plan, we've grown 13% since then. So, you're seeing that coming through in non-NII and you're also seeing some improvement in partner sharing agreements, just reflected in that number. So, we do have confidence in the momentum in the income line. I just remind you that this is a seasonal business and you get that seasonality in NII because of balances, but you also get it in non-interest income. But yes, we're pleased with that progress. In UK mortgages, the UK mortgage market is robust, and we see that across the piece. We see it in house purchase; first-time buyers are up 11% year on year. We're seeing strong levels of refinancing, and the margins in Barclays, if you like, in the more vanilla book, have been broadly stable over the last few quarters. Obviously, we're seeing a margin benefit coming through from Kensington, which is 3x to 4x higher. And really what you're seeing here is our capabilities reaching the marketplace. And by that, what I mean is both the product breadth, because we now got Kensington in play, but also the operational capabilities because we launched a new broker platform, which is working extremely well. The only thing I'd call out for you is we're about to enter a period, market-wide, it's not a Barclays thing, where we've got coming to maturity the five-year business that was written during the stamp duty holiday in FY20 and FY21. That's at relatively wide margins, so you're going to see a little bit of churn compression come through on that, but of course, we've captured that in the guidance that we've already given you around NII progression for BUK. Thank you, next question please.

question_text: Good morning. Thank you for taking my questions. The first one, just looking at competitive conditions in US Investment Banking, we've had some of the peers talk about potentially very significant levels of additional capital that's available for deployment following some of the deregulation and stress test changes. And Prime appears to be one of the places that they may be looking to allocate additional capacity. So, given it's a focus for the bank, could you just talk about whether you think you have additional capital to deploy given the changes in things like stress tests and what you're seeing on product margins and that sort of thing? And then secondly, on the non-bank financial intermediary (NBFI) space, thank you for the additional disclosures. Those are really welcome and it's good to see the impairment charge at a group level below consensus today. Venkat, I wonder whether you could talk a little bit about risks in that industry, how mature the exposures are, whether there are any vintages we should be bothered about. We could observe that the cases we've seen so far all involve fraud, but we have seen very strong growth in the industry writ large. And so, I wonder with your risk management hat on, whether you could just talk about, whether this is an industry that has yet to grind into fully mature loss run rates and how you think about that sort of thing. Thank you.
answer_text: All right. Thank you Jason for both questions. On the first one on capital regulation or disparity, potential disparity in capital regulation between Europe, the UK and the US. Look, it is, I think, an important factor in the industry. We haven't seen ultimately what will be the changes in the US and how much the UK, which is the important jurisdiction for us as a home regulator, makes itself consistent or not. I think what I would point out on things like Prime is, we've got a good and strong market share. We work with a few important and big clients carefully. It is as much a balance sheet business as it is a capital business. And so, we think we've got the wherewithal, and given our current market position, given our product capability, given our client penetration, we've got the wherewithal to compete effectively and continue to compete effectively. Of course, it's all subject to capital rules. We'll have to see where they are, but I'm pretty confident in the strength of that business and how we will adapt overall in the Investment Bank, because ultimately, it's about that. Coming back to private credit and NBFI, so here's what I will say. First of all, I view credit as credit as credit, right? There's a distinction about where it's originated from, and you know, private credit, generally, we at least think of it as the kind of credit that's originated outside of banks and outside of the public debt market. But I think of lending as lending, and through the cycle, you've got to be careful about all the aspects of lending. Client selection, sector concentrations, NIM concentrations, terms, and continuous monitoring, qualifying them initially and monitoring it over the time period. So that's important, and that you've got to do through the period. I'm obviously disappointed that we had Tricolor. The fact that it was fraud is no excuse. We have looked at what lessons we can learn from that and apply that across our portfolios. I will talk a little about that. We did not have First Brands. We were approached a couple of times, and we said no. We said no because our credit officers felt that there was not enough data information to support the financial projections they made. That's how credit selection is supposed to work. Now, at this point in time, and you talk a little about vintages. Less to me a question about vintage, but two questions, one is are there circumstances either because of inflation, tariffs or changes in general economic conditions that put stress on credit performance. So, do companies find themselves stretched? Now fraud can be isolated bad actors, or it could be economic conditions that increase the propensity towards bad acting. And then if you worry about that, you've got to consider very carefully the independence and strength of the financial controls employed within the companies. Now as you can imagine, we consider all of these things over time. But I think what these two instances show is that we will likely be monitoring our portfolios more carefully, particularly understanding the impact of changed economic conditions on companies and looking closely at the strength and independence of financial controls. Hope that answers your question. Thanks.

question_text: Good morning, thanks for taking my question. I have two please. The first one would be on your UK RWA deployment. I think you have deployed the circa £1 billion of RWA during Q3 and it seems to me that the run rate was actually closer to £2 billion per quarter. So especially in the context where you had a good lending performance in Q3. So, just wanted to discuss how we should think about it and whether or not we should have a catch-up in UK RWA deployment a bit later. And then the second one is just to follow-up on the mortgage headwinds coming from the maturity of the mortgage, on the return during COVID. So, what kind of headwinds are you expecting and for how long should we expect this? Thank you very much.
answer_text: Thank you very much. So, we've got a £30 billion RWA target, we deployed £18 billion so far, £11 million of that is organic. It's interesting because when we set out these targets, the RWA growth in the UK is really a shorthand for our desire to lend into the UK. And actually what you find is that in some quarters, RWAs grow faster than lending and that's what we saw earlier in the year and actually in this quarter lending grew faster than RWAs. It's actually the lending that we're really focused on internally, it's the lending, not the RWAs that we generate income from. And we're really pleased with the progress. It's our highest quarter of net lending in mortgages since 2021 and we've now got four consecutive quarters of lending in our corporate book. So, we're happy with the progress, nothing really to call out it's just timing differences between RWAs and loans. In terms of mortgage headwinds and look our churn effects on our book have been broadly stable, neutral for some time, all we're calling out here is there will be a period of pressure. Actually, overall, we expect the product margin impact on BUK as a whole, taking all products into account will be broadly neutral into Q4. So, expect that number to be broadly zero in the NIM walk. But it's really towards the end of 2020 and the first quarter of 2021, there was a Stamp Duty holiday in the UK, and a lot of business was written. That's going to mature. It will compress margins a little as that business flips over onto front book. I'm not going to call out a particular spread that will be different by lender and different by product. But it's just something for you to consider. And as I say, we've already taken it into account in the guidance that we've given you. But thank you for the questions. Next question, please.

Number two, returning capital to shareholders, and number three, investing in the businesses. So, as we reflected over the last few quarters, we've seen the strength and quality and resilience of that capital generation, this is something that we've been thinking about. question_text: Hi, thanks for taking my question. I guess there are two follow-ups. I apologise for another one on private credit. I'm thinking obviously in a post-American Airlines world. Or would you expect more Joint Ventures, more contract wins, and how's the pipeline looking on any further wins? answer_text: Hey, thanks, Alvaro. Let me start with the first one. So, about the review that we took, it's along the three dimensions which I said to you. I also want to be very clear, there's sort of broad financing, there's private credit. The slide we've given you is on private credit. We will look at loans and we will decide. question_text: Good morning. Two questions please. Firstly, if I could just follow-up on the Investment Bank, obviously you had a very strong first half of the year. Q3 has perhaps slightly lagged the growth seen at the US peers. Can you explain how much you think that's just a mix effect, is it a mix effect by business segment, by region, across Equities and across primary. Or are there any gaps that you're still looking to infill there? And then the second question, broader question on the UK, you've obviously seen strong mortgage and corporate loan growth in Q3, but can you perhaps touch upon customer behavior and activity going into the November budget? Thank you.

We are running our own race, we set out targets, we put in an RWA target for the Investment Bank, which was to keep it flat, and we've kept it flat. We also instituted RWA discipline, which Anna just spoke about. And then we had both revenue targets, cost efficiency targets, and overall return targets, profitability targets, all of which we've been meeting. We also put in within that certain areas of focus within Markets and Banking. In Markets, it was European rates, it was Securitised Products, it was Equities, particularly Equity Derivatives. In Banking, it was certain sectors, healthcare and tech, and then it was M&A and ECM. Now, over this long period, we have shown strong progress in all these dimensions. Even if you look at something like Equity Derivatives, we've been growing a couple of percent over this year, less than what the US peers have this quarter. Quarter-to-quarter, there will be variations. Some of that variation is about the amount of capital and balance sheet some of the competitors allocate overtime. Some of that variation is geographical concentration. So, Asia has been strong. We've always been very clear that we have a solid Asian presence, but it's not as deep and broad as others have. There are times when commodities plays a role, there's times when credit plays a role, and that's generally good for us. So, I would view what you've seen in this quarter's results as that kind of normal quarter-on-quarter variation. I don't think when I look at the plans of the Investment Bank, what we've had, what we intend to do, that there are sort of gaps or holes we need to fill. I think we continue to build on technology, continue to build on product sophistication, continue to build on client reach, and we will show the returns that we've set out to, and we've displayed over the last seven quarters. Thanks, Venkat. Andy, here's how I think about the UK landscape. So, I think about it first in how are consumers spending? What does the demand for credit look like? And then thirdly, how is that credit performing? And if you look through these lenses, then you get a pretty good view. So, I mean, UK consumer behavior is slightly cautious, but we continue to see signs of improvement. So, credit spend is higher than debit spend. We've seen a slight increase in nonessential spending, and confidence metrics have grown slightly. So, so far so good. And we also see that flowing into, for example, the demand for credit, and you can see that in terms of our UK momentum. The demand for mortgage credit is good, and as I said that's not just refinancing. So, in a very cautious environment, you see less house purchase. But what we see is house purchase growth, first-time buyer growth, and also refinancing demand. There's good demand from cards, as you can see, and actually the thing we talk about less is demand from corporates, and you can see really good lending in our corporate book. That is coming broadly half and half from existing clients and new clients. We've originated more than 400 new clients this year. That's on top of the 550 that we did last year, and our lending market share is up 70 bps. So, we don't see a lack of demand for credit at a macro level. So, if we're looking for points that were slightly more hesitant, we would say we see a little bit of hesitancy in mid-corporate, but generally speaking, good demand for credit. And then finally, credit performance is good. We see that in mortgages. We see it in cards. I mean, UK cards delinquencies are extremely low, and I would say across all of the portfolios are low and stable and exactly as we would have expected them to be. And the same is true of corporates. There are no significant single names in our corporate book. So, the UK landscape remains pretty robust. Thank you Andy for your questions. Can we have the next question, please?

question_text: Starting with the Best Egg transaction, can you help us a bit on the cost and the impairment side of things? It's a day one integration cost and going forward, how would impairment flow through it? Presumably it's origination, so you don't have a lot of direct holding of the loan. So, does that mean impairment is also going to be quite low [versus revenues]? Number two, I know the 2028 target is something that you would not want to talk too much about right now. With the Best Egg transaction, we have greater visibility as to how we can get to mid-teens for the business, and then the UK businesses, all three of them are easily making greater than 20%. And if the Investment Bank is greater than 12% Group guidance for 2026, mechanically I think we can get quite close to 14%. Is that aligned to the ambition that you have for the business going forward?
answer_text: Okay, thank you Perlie. Let me take those in order. So the structure of Best Egg will be about $11 billion of what we call managed balances. Only about $1 billion we expect to be on the balance sheet. So therefore, the RWA position is relatively low and the direct impact of impairment is relatively low. So that's really what creates the stability of these returns and the relatively high RoTE of the business. So, I'm not going to give you specific numbers now on impairment, but expect it to be a relatively small number just because of the nature of the business model. As relates to costs, clearly, again we'll update you nearer to the time around our expectations on costs. A bit like what we did on Tesco. So, think no later than Q1, we'll give you a much fuller breakdown of what this is likely to look like. But we do expect some opportunities in the future to be able to generate cost synergies. In the immediate sort of short-term period we would expect to run this business somewhat standalone and then integrate it over time, a little bit like what we've done with the other smaller acquisitions. But I think what's really important here, and you can see it I guess from the numbers that we've given you, is that the RoTE of this business is extremely high. And even if you did it on an ROI basis, it remains high, and we expect to be able to grow that over time. On your second question, clearly I'm not going to give you a target now, but just remind you that when we set out the targets, RoTE, distributions, and the way we expect to grow our RWAs, 2026 was the only ever supposed to be a point in time and, and a sort of near term target. What you should be gleaning from us is that we are gaining momentum in the business, that we're gaining confidence in the business, and that's really what's led us to not only upgrade for the current year, but give you an indication that we're going to come to you a year before the current targets expire. But our ambition is to keep growing the returns of the business and really important for me, not just the returns, but the consistency and the stability of those returns. So more in February, I'm afraid. Thank you. Next question please.

question_text: Two questions from me. One again, just on Best Egg, but just more in terms of USCB capital allocation and growth plan. So, I guess this is presented very much as like a replacement for the American Airlines portfolio in combination with General Motors. You've got the same kind of receivables target and talking about the profitability. I'm just curious, if you'd retained the American Airlines portfolio for example, would you still have done this transaction? How are you thinking about allocation to the business going forwards, where profitability has been strong this quarter. The second question is actually just a bit more specific, but just on the deposit business within BUK. Just curious what your thoughts are going into next year, because I think one of your peers was talking about slightly slower growth. So just curious, what you are expecting and whether that has any feed through to the hedge balance? Thank you.
answer_text: Let's just step back a little bit and think about what Best Egg does for USCB. It creates scale and capability, and they are the things that we've talked about sort of repeatedly when we talked about potential acquisitions. So, the loss of American Airlines clearly gave us a question on scale, but the question of capability is somewhat beyond American Airlines. Clearly it's capital light revenue, but I think, you know, this is digital first, [has] superior risk capability in an area adjacent to what we already do. In fact, we are in this business in a small way. So, it's first and foremost a capability purchase, and we've been talking to the business for nine months. That's really what attracted us. Actually, the sort of to-ing and fro-ing in terms of scale, is somewhat an output. However, as you point out, we're essentially taking a relatively low risk adjusted margin, capital heavy source of revenue and replacing it with a capital light, high RoTE source of revenue. Growth from here, we clearly see growth in this particular business because there are potential revenue synergies there. I think that's not only from the Best Egg customers coming to us directly and us being able to sell cards and deposits to them. It's clearly in the opposite direction, being able to take that product into our full partner suite. We do it with about 10 partners at the moment to give you an idea, but it is small. And then there are clearly revenue synergies in respect to funding and also in securing our flow of ABS business, if you like, into the Investment Bank. So, all of these things are in our mind. That said, the core business and our focus on improving the profitability of the core business in USCB remains. So this is in no way a substitute for all of the stuff that we have been doing for a number of quarters now, in which you're seeing in the Q3 results and we would expect to replicate. But if the essence of your question is, should we expect to see a series of these in the US? The answer to that is no. Because essentially this is about, as I said, firmly a capability purchase. And having got that capability, growth from here should be in scaling that business in a capital light way and in continuing to grow our US cards business very much in the way that you've seen us do it before, both organically and inorganically at the same kind of cadence. Deposit businesses, particularly in BUK, I'd distinguish between deposit competition and trends, and the hedge. So, what we've seen in the hedge is clearly deposit stability, particularly in the hedgeable balances. So, the non-interest sensitive balances that we have, and that's allowed us to give you some guidance that we expect to roll a 100% of the hedge from here. That's what we've done for the last few quarters. Contrast that with what we see as competition in the deposit market, which is really a churn in the fixed term deposit book, whether they be ISA or not, and that's really what we saw in Q2. We saw again in Q3, there were some very, very large maturities in the market in Q3 and therefore we saw some intense pricing. Actually we expect that to continue and that's included in the margin expectations that we've given you. Why do we expect it to continue? Well, in part, we can all speculate as to why there's some extra competition in this market. It may be because of concerns around ISAs, there's certainly TFSME (Term Funding Scheme with additional incentives for SMEs) funding coming up for renewal and maybe broader reflections on Quantitative Tightening. So, we see that sort of fixed term competition continuing and that's really why we said to you in the fourth quarter, expect that product margin element in the NII flight path that we gave you, remember it was very positive in Q3, we expect that to be broadly neutral in Q4. And that's because of what we observe in deposits and also the comments that are made on the earnings call in respect to mortgages. Clearly going in the opposite direction to those headwinds, we've got the formation of IELs (Interest Earning Lending balances), we've also got the impact of Kensington. So, for us it's broadly neutral, but we do see those margin impacts in the wider market.

question_text: On the US Consumer Bank, obviously very good performance in Q3 means we look at Best Egg with better eyes. I just wanted to understand better that improvement in performance, you called out improving in loan pricing and also in fees. The revenue share agreements, some of them were renegotiated. Can you maybe give us examples of how much the loan yields or loan spreads might have gone up or how you compare to competition? Something that would give us a better sense of how sustainable that is? I don't know if higher pricing might affect volume? Any examples of those two things that can help us get our head around that? And the second question is on the Investment Bank, you touched on it already, the RWA efficiencies. There's more to go, but if we think about the next plan or going forward, is the philosophy still to keep RWAs flat in the business? And if that's the case, I don't know if you can help us quantify those efficiencies in particular in [Global Markets], because I realise M&A and ECM don't really carry that much capital. Just to get a feeling of how much more room there is.
answer_text: So on USCB, I mean the improvement that you are seeing coming through does come in large part from pricing. So, to give you an idea, the year-on-year improvements in NIM, about half of that comes from the repricing that we did last year, and that repricing was completed by the end of 2024. But the way this works through into the NIM is that consumers have to repay and then draw down on the new terms and conditions for that to really feed through into the NIM. There has been wider repricing across the market. That came initially from the expectations of late fee reductions last year and has not yet reversed. The impact for us in terms of late fees was relatively small, as you can imagine, relative to some of our competitors. And therefore, we don't believe that it's creating any kind of NIM competitive pressure. For some of our competition late fees would be more significant and therefore that might be more of a question. But on another level, one of the things that we established as we prepared for our strategy pre-February 2024, was we were not optimised for pricing, even on a like-for-like basis, even pre the loss of late fees. So, much of this has been a bit of an industry catch up and therefore has not really had a significant impact, in terms of competitive positioning. So, we remain comfortable where we are positioned and we do see it as sustainable in terms of the pricing. I mean the other things that are directly impacting the NIM are the growth in retail deposits. Remember there's a 50 to 60 basis points differential there [versus wholesale lending] and also the general expansion towards retail balances. Now, clearly in the quarter, there's only been one month of General Motors. So revenue sharing arrangements, I'm not going to call any of them out. We never do as a partner matter and they do actually impact both the NIM line and the non-NII line. So that's why you're seeing some improvements there also, as well as there being just generally increased volumes. So, underlying your question, is this sustainable? The answer is yes, we do believe it is, which is why we said we expected NIM to be broadly stable from here. Just remember it is quite a seasonal business, so you get some lumps and bumps particularly in Non-NII. So we're happy with that general direction. If I go onto the Investment Bank, what you've seen for the last six quarters is that the revenue over RWAs continues to improve. So, if you look year-over-year across those six quarters, you can see a step change each time and clearly what we were looking for at the beginning of the plan was the area where revenue over RWAs had declined markedly over time, [which] was really in the Banking business. And that's where we see a lot of the improvements starting to come through in very, very good capital discipline in driving that Treasury Coverage model. So, you can see that in the International Corporate Bank balances that are growing, and the income there, but also really being focused in M&A and ECM and as I called out before, we do feel there's more to go in those businesses. So in terms of the Banking business, you would expect there to be further road to travel in terms of this revenue over RWAs, because of the International Corporate Bank business continuing to perform. Just because we still have ambitions within ECM and M&A, that they remain a focus for us, but also just this kind of real discipline about the maturation of capital and really whether we continue to extend it to that client or not, or choose to put it elsewhere. So much more to go, I think tangibly within Banking. But in the Markets business, clearly that was coming from a slightly different place. It wasn't a situation where we deployed more capital into that business and that it had largely maintained its revenue over RWAs. What you're seeing now is it continuing to improve because it is taking share, and in many instances we'd already given capital to those focus businesses and they're sort of growing into the capital and maturing into that capital. And then the other thing is obviously Financing, a very capital light business, continues to grow, particularly on the Prime side where the balances were 30% up year on year. So, I can't give you a specific target and indeed that's not how we're thinking about this business in particular, because we do think of it in terms of RoTE. So, it's a number of things to get there, but think of us as still feeling like there's room to go in terms of that revenue over RWAs.

When we say it's sort of in alignment with the UK [businesses], I'm being quite penal in that calculation because I'm including the goodwill essentially. This business, whilst adding capability and adding scale, it is relatively small, certainly at this point in time. That's why we've upgraded our Group NII [excluding IB and Head Office] expectation this year. Then the other thing I would just call out is the two businesses where, they've been somewhat of a drag on Group RoTE or earnings, are clearly now making progress. So, I would say the momentum is with us, but obviously we'll guide you more firmly in February.

question_text: Firstly on Corporate lending, you mentioned it earlier about how good the performance has been, and that wasn't just a Barclays story, that's across the UK Corporate Bank. So I was hoping you could unpick some of the drivers of why you think growth has been so good there and to what extent will the underlying continue into the end of this year and into next year. Secondly, on building out the Investment Bank, I think you're looking to go back into Saudi Arabia. If you could just kind of give some colour about what the ambitions are there. You spoke earlier about how your performance was not so good versus peers because of lacking Equity Derivatives in Asia. To what extent you have appetite of kind of rectifying that, either inorganically or organically?
answer_text: On UK Corporate Bank, we are really pleased with the performance and clearly it's taken a while for us to get to this momentum. I think there's a couple of things really underpinning it. One is actually saying that you are open for business with your clients. I think that's really important, because about half of the new lending that we've done has come from existing clients. I think that gives the confidence to those clients, it gives a confidence to the regional teams that are dealing with them directly. So, that's a really important statement. The other piece, however, that's made a real difference, and it's a bit like what we've done in mortgages or what we've done in cards, is there's an adjacent capability build that we've done here. That's not just digital, but actually the speed to the lending decision is markedly improved. So that's a better client experience. But again, I said half of the lending was coming from existing clients. Well, the other half has clearly come from new clients. So, we have been acquiring clients 550 last year, more than 400 this year so far. But there's no particular concentration geographically or by sector or anything. It is just capability build and focus that's bringing that through. So very much the same risk. So, no change in our risk appetite again, like our strategy in cards. I think the other thing that I would call out, and it's in the back of the [Investor Presentation on slide 35] where we talk about the survey, about 43% of our clients say that they expect to make investment decisions beyond the budget. So, there is a slight hesitancy in the market, probably more in the mid-corporate area, not really holding us back, but clearly there are some thoughts from some of those clients there. In terms of Saudi Arabia, I'm not going to make specific comments on Saudi Arabia here. I don't think you should see it as the harbinger of a substantial move eastward. So, I don't see us reestablishing the position that we exited in Asian Equities in the 2010s. Those comments were more of a reflection of the fact, in some quarters, our business focus will help us excel and in some quarters it will be a relative headwind for us. So, it was a statement rather than a statement of ambition. But in terms of Saudi Arabia, nothing I would particularly add beyond what we've put in the press at this point in time.

question_text: The first question, just coming back to Equity Derivatives in Asia, you mentioned, you don't have a retail business, but if I look at the largest players, they don't have a retail business either. These are the Americans who control the market. So, I'm just trying to understand, your position compared to your peer group really, which is mainly doing Chinese corporate offshore/onshore derivative business. That's where the money is rather than retail. Just want to understand what business do you think you're not doing, which leads to a weaker position. The second question I have is on Financing, you've done a great job of growing Financing. Is there any leverage exposure limitations that you think of? In that context, is there any more detail you can give us on Financing in terms of segmentation? What is actually in the Financing book?
answer_text: Okay, let me start, and I might ask Dan to add to the leverage part of the question. On Equity Derivatives, we feel like there were comments out there in the market around Retail and Wealth, that was our broader understanding. Some of them do have Retail and Wealth businesses, so that's clearly helped their businesses. For us, I'll go back to what I said before, don't expect us to have a significant Asian Equities business. Equity Derivatives is one of the focus areas that we called out right at the beginning of the plan. An area where we felt we really wanted to build capability. It's one where we've monetised the market well, when there's been volatility, less so when there hasn't. And that's clearly something we are reflective of Kian, and an area that we, clearly given the Q3 results, need to keep working on. So that's how I'd characterise it. On Financing, here we're talking about our Prime business and our Fixed Income Financing business, predominantly with hedge funds, that's what we're discussing here. The largest part of the growth is really coming through Prime, where our balances have been up significantly year-on-year. There is an Asian element to that growth. Clearly that's a wider margin than we would see on the other side of the business in Fixed Income Financing. And it's an area that we want to continue to grow. As you call out, it's RWA light, but it is leverage heavy. We are very thoughtful really about the interplay between AT1 and the returns on that business. But Dan, you might want to add. Yeah, just to add a little bit more flavour in the business. Obviously, leverage is the lifeblood for that business, but we've got the same focus on efficiency in that business as we do elsewhere on RWAs, so exactly the same principles apply. We're very focused on the return on leverage balance sheet versus the cost, particularly the cost of AT1. In terms of a bit of the flavour of the business, it's also quite consistent. It's very focused on the top clients. That's really where we spend most of our energies and time. It's just extremely high-quality liquid book serving that client base.
