question_text: Two questions please. First, coming back to Best Egg, because it isn't a bank and it's clearly being acquired by a bank. Would the rules have to change with regards to holding an equity slice, or a tranche of the securitisations? Could you speak to maybe how that works, for Barclays? Then secondly, looking at the SRT book, I know you haven't given disclosure for the third quarter, but for the second quarter, it's declined about £7 billion. So, I'm just wondering, is that a timing issue or how should we think about that, and how does that tally with the capital efficiency in the Investment Bank?
answer_text: In terms of Best Egg, you're right, it's not a bank, it does become part of one as this transaction completes. There are implications of that in terms of its funding. Obviously creates some efficiencies. In terms of the regulatory requirements around the slice that it holds, I don't believe that they are significantly different, but we can revert. But I don't believe so, Dan may want to add to that. So, from our perspective, given its business model and given the way we are already embedded in that business model in the Investment Bank, actually we see efficiencies here, because we have the pre-securitisation funding opportunity. We clearly have reduced securitisation costs because there are things that we will be doing in house. We have an ability also to have a flow of consumer credit into that ABS business. So, from our perspective, it's a net benefit in that particular part. Dan, SRT? There's a very consistent level of activity in SRT, so there's nothing I would call out. Maybe we can follow up with you afterwards on whether there's FX or amortisation. There are numbers, but the footprint has been very, very consistent. Again, that's sort of consistent with what we've said before. We do see that Colonnade program in particular as being a mature program and we manage it carefully in terms of its reinvestment cadence. So, I think it's probably in the detail rather than anything deliberate.

question_text: On Tricolor, could you elaborate on the nature of Barclays' exposure to Tricolor? Was it primarily warehouse lending, securitisation, or another form of structured finance? Just a comment on whether you think this is more of an idiosyncratic trend, or are you worried about broader trends in the market? Then on the Investment Bank, you noted in the call last week that there will be differing trends in each quarter. So, this quarter was APAC performing particularly well. I was just wondering if you could elaborate or clarify the trends that you see going forward, and which parts of the Investment Bank have the most momentum?
answer_text: In Tricolor, clearly, we were lenders into that warehouse. We said on the call that it was a client for many years for the bank. It had been a client for 9 or 10 years. So we've been very reflective of really the indicators that had become apparent in that business that might have led us to discover that particular situation. Now clearly from our perspective, the first line of defence is the clients that you choose at the outset. Tricolor had clearly been a client for a long time and a good one for a long time. There are other clients that we have not onboarded. Then once those clients are onboarded, what monitoring do you do? And we've been reflective of a couple of things. Firstly, what are the controls and, in particular the separation of controls within the vehicle itself. So, who's managing the collateral versus managing the business, and the independence of that is something that we've considered. Also, quite frankly, who are the advisors, the accountants, et cetera for that business. So, we've looked across the rest of the businesses with those thoughts in mind, and there's nothing that we've seen that's concerned us. Clearly, we're watchful as we always are. In terms of the broader trends on the Investment Bank, clearly what we've seen is a reawakening of the Banking market, particularly in the US. We've benefited from, as I mentioned in my prepared remarks, the resurgence within DCM, so that's a business that we are well geared to service. We feel like we've made good progress in terms of sponsors generally, but particularly in M&A. The areas where we've been mindful of our relative performance, as I said, were corporates in M&A and ECM. Now in the quarter, we didn't participate in the largest deals. Again, that's something we are reflective of, but as I look forward into Q4 and beyond, really the ECM pipeline looks better, but we are very mindful of government shutdown in the US and the kind of impact that might have on the timing of transactions, so that's the only thing I would say. For the Markets business, it's very difficult to call a trend a quarter ahead and I won't attempt to do so.

question_text: On Best Egg, in terms of the financials here, you've given us the high single digit P/E of something like a £90 million bottom line. I think you've indicated that the ROIC (Return on Invested Capital) is going to be commensurate with the UK businesses, if I've understood you correctly. So, £90m [bottom line] versus your £800m investment seems to imply quite a meaningful amount of cost synergy that you expect to deliver over time. I'm just mindful of that implying potentially a step up in costs in USCB as we look into 2026. I'm just curious if you could give us an indication of the cost base that's attached to this. Appreciate you've sort of indicated the revenues are commensurate with the American Airlines book, but just in terms of the cost, that would be helpful, I think for our modelling. Then in terms of the longer-term capital allocation question, it came up on the call last week. There's obviously market sensitivity around your 50% Investment Bank allocation target. I guess the $40 billion end net receivables target [in USCB], you weren't necessarily expecting quite so much of it to be servicing relationships when you set out the strategic plan. So, the $16 billion card IRB impact, it would just be scaling that down by $4-5 billion for the fact that, out of the $40 billion of targeted balances, over a quarter is now of-balance sheet and therefore presumably be not impacted at all by IRB.
answer_text: You're sort of broadly at the right sort of earnings level. I think as an ROI matter, what we're saying is in time you're right, we do expect to grow the earnings of this business, and I would say probably in the following order. Starting with funding synergies. Again, remember that's what we did in Tesco, they're the ones that normally come through first and I called those out before. Remember, this isn't a bank at the moment. So, there are clear funding synergies in terms of the pre-securitisation position, the cost of securitisation itself. Then you come to cost synergies, for a while we would expect to run this as a business in parallel and then incur the integration over time. So I wouldn't call out any particular integration chunks next year, but clearly, we'll update you on that. But funding is a key point. And I also think those revenue synergies are going to come from a number of different places. So, as I said before, it's cross selling cards and deposits to customers who come to us via Best Egg. It's going in the opposite direction and extending the Best Egg capability across all of our partners into the cards business. It's also actually about our ability to create a forward flow of consumer business into our Investment Bank, so that's also important here. I think funding, revenue and costs will come in time, but we do have confidence that we can get this to high teens RoTE. On the Investment Bank, clearly when we set that 50% [target] out, there was an expectation of timing of regulatory change, and that's clearly changed over time. That $16 billion was therefore related to a level of balances that was not $40 billion. So I think that's the first thing to remember, because we expected to go through AIRB actually in 2025, it seems like quite a long time ago, but I'm sure our original expectation was 2025, by which time the balances would not have been $40 billion. So, I wouldn't necessarily do the kind of scaling that that you're talking about here. That said, you are right, we've replaced capital heavy balances with capital light balances. Although we'll retain a small portion of the loans, the AIRB treatment of loans is relatively much lower than it is for cards. So you're not really going to see a material step change there, both because of the nature of the change and also because of the quantum. But the 50%, or the spirit behind the 50%, remains intact, which was about holding the Investment Bank [RWAs] flat. You should expect us to continue to do that and expect us to continue to grow the UK in particular. And it was really the UK growth that was driving that change. The regulatory change is timing and at the point where we have a better estimate of that $16 billion, we will of course come to you with it. But unfortunately, the quantum and the timing has some regulatory uncertainty around that.

question_text: Just two questions, both on the US. First of all, you mentioned the shutdown, the impact that could have on Q4 revenues. Should we think about that just as, if the shutdowns still there on November 6th, accounts have gone stale, all the ECM has pushed into Q1. Is that the right way to think about it? Maybe also, does that differ for M&A versus ECM? And then on the second side, I think the Federal Reserve has provided its proposals for the simplification or the increased transparency on CCAR. So just any initial thoughts you have with regards to either for yourselves or for your peers in the US.
answer_text: We would see a shutdown as a relative timing point, irrespective of the line in Banking that we're talking about, whether it's ECM or M&A. To the extent that they're strategically important to those clients, we'd still expect them to complete, they just might get pushed. So that's how we'd see it certainly at this point in time, given this length of delay. In terms of CCAR, and I would say more broadly around the US regulatory emergence, what appears to be a general theme as transparency and coherence. By that I mean the way in which the various aspects of the regulations fit together, whether that be CCAR, whether that be GSIB, whether that be leverage, whether it be Basel. And actually the way the Fed is sort of stepping back and reflecting on those things as a coherent whole, we would welcome, and we remain hopeful that the FPC will take a similar approach.

question_text: I wanted to ask about the Financing Business, please. I mean, that's been working well for you. As Dan said earlier, you've been focused on the largest of the hedge funds. But, from what we can see, and I think disclosure across the industry isn't very good here, but from what we can see, your penetration into those very largest hedge funds is now approaching the kind of top three Financing firms to the big US banks. But where you have less penetration is in kind of the next rung down. Is there still a lot more scope, you think to increase penetration further and really kind of catch up or maybe even overtake the biggest players in the industry among that top group of hedge funds? Or are you going to have to start focusing more on the next rungs down?
answer_text: Our Financing business is working well and remember this comes in two parts. So, our Fixed Income Financing business, very much embedded in the heritage of Barclays and Lehman before it. It is typically number one or two in the market. So very, very well-established business. What we've been doing is growing Prime alongside that. We've gone from typically number seven or eight to joint number five. So, we've clearly made some progress there. As you note, our targeting has been with the larger of the hedge funds, that's deliberate, and it reflects both our business model and our view of risk. So by business model, what I mean is we run our Financing business as an integrated business. So Fixed Income Financing and Prime are run under a single leadership. So when we approach a client, that's how we approach them, not as two individual businesses. We also run our technology that way. So, as we're looking at those clients, we look across their business in its totality, and we believe that gives us a better perspective of their risk. That lends itself to the largest global multi-strategy type funds, so that's really why you see that approach. But also, in terms of our own risk positioning, we do believe that, again, the first step in risk management is through the careful selection of clients, and therefore we choose to work with the larger, more capitalised, more liquid clients in the industry. question_text: Two questions. The first question is on the capital return of over £15 billion. If you could just put this in context of capacity to support investment and growth. How should we think about this capacity that you're outlining? It looks like there's quite a bit of buffer. So we would like to understand that. And then secondly, you're one of the few CEOs who actually discusses ledgers and middle office integration, which is not a hot topic. Just what the focus is and how should we think about post 2028 basically in that respect?

It's this chart here that they've just brought up showing that sort of change to 230 basis points. (slide 71) And in the plan, what we've done is we've meaningfully increased the distribution to greater than £15 billion, but we've also meaningfully, in fact doubled the level of investment. But such is the level of capital generation within the plan. The level of generation actually surpasses both of those two increases. What we've done here is we've deliberately created some capacity for us to be able to invest further if and only if we determine that is the right thing for us to do. And I'll just remind you of our very clear capital hierarchy here and specifically the importance of shareholder returns. So, we're going to set a very, very high bar for any additional level of investment. And quite frankly, if we are unable to find such an investment, then the capital hierarchy will kick in and we will distribute more than we have here in the plan or alternatively, we will be investing more than we have here in the plan and we would expect the momentum of the business in the outer years to be higher than we're presenting here. question_text: One of them is kind of a follow-up to the second question maybe for you, Venkat. In one of the slides and you pointed out that 75% of the employees are in support functions. It is an emphasis on fee businesses and also you know, at the right points of the cycle, intermediation.

question_text: The first question was on capital in terms of targets. You got the 13% to 14% target. I think you've talked sort of running at the top end of that range throughout this plan and given this is the plan now to 2028, post Pillar 2A changes, given the constructive tone from the regulator. I'm just wondering what do we need to see to sort of potentially move lower down in that range as sort of a formal way you're running from the business? Is it just getting that Pillar 2A change from the regulator? And [I assume] you [have] got pretty good visibility as to what you're expecting there. So, if things do land as you expect, maybe you could help sort of frame that and we can think about what that means for capital return and RoTE targets? And then he second question was on the mortgage book in the UK. You referred to the headwind in the first half of this year. Can I just check in terms of the definition of that headwind? Is that sort of a gross headwind? Because I'm mindful that with Kensington and the sort of flow of the book, you might be able to offset some of that as you have some higher LTV, higher margin business coming through. So, can you kind of frame the definition of that headwind? Thank you.
answer_text: On the first one, if you go back to the beginning of 2025, what we said was that because we were carrying more Pillar 2 in advance of IRB implementation, you should expect us to operate at the top of the range or towards the top of the range. That's still what we're saying. It's no different to that. And I do expect there to be some pillar 2A offset when we get through Basel 3.1 and IRB. I just don't know what they are right now. What we are trying to do in every single part of this plan is put it in our control. We want our distribution plan to be underpinned by the things that we're doing and that it can't be put of course by the timing of regulatory change or the certainty of that change. That's all we're saying here. So, for us, in the short term, our planning assumption throughout this plan, is that we will be at the top end of the range. Obviously, you should reflect that in the way you think about our distributions, you should reflect that in the way that you calculate our RoTE. But once we get beyond that implementation and we have that clarity, we will, of course, review where we think we should be within that range. We still think that the 13% to 14% range is the right range for Barclays. But at this point in time, we just don't have the regulatory clarity and we want this plan in our control. So that's the reason for it. And on mortgages, I'm specifically talking about a gross impact and it relates to the mortgages that were written at the very end of 2020 and beginning of 2021. As you remember, as we were all coming out of COVID, there was that stamp duty holiday in the mortgage market was very substantial. Those mortgages were written at very widespread, like 160 basis points. That's quite meaningfully different from where we are now. So just as they refinance, you're going to see some relatively short-term pressure across the market as a whole. We think it will be gone by the end of half one [2026]. And then beyond that, you're going to see the kind of progress that you've seen in our NII to date. But it is a growth impact. We're obviously, enjoying very good levels of net lending, driven very much by Kensington and that broker platform. So, it's a short-term hiatus, I would describe it as. And if I may just underline one thing, Anna, whether it's capital or looking at our RoTE, there are potential tailwinds, right? We are planning prudently, but what Anna is referring to, whether it's the new capital rules and what relief we get, there are potential tailwinds. We are not banking on them.

question_text: First one is on Private Banking Wealth Management. What products are you currently missing from your Premier Banking proposition? And how easy is it for you to build those yourself? And then secondly, can you continue on the UK loan book? UK retail banks continue to surprise to the upside on loan book growth relative to GDP. I think your guidance is for 5% loan growth CAGR out 2028. What's driving the growth in excess of GDP? And what's your outlook for volumes in the mortgage market for the next couple of years? Thank you.
answer_text: Let me start on both. We've got a pretty big and complete product suite. There are a couple of gaps in the product suite that are missing, SIPs and Junior ISAs that are coming online. But if you put yourself at a higher level looking at it, starting at the self-directed end of the spectrum, what we've got is Direct Investment, what we used to call Smart Investor, which is you're basically doit-yourself investment buying stocks, bonds. Then you come to the next piece, which is planning and advice. That is where we are doing some work, as I said, to create products, which we will talk to you about soon, which you know clearly constructed, fairly priced, transparently built and efficiently distributed. There we are looking to grow in scale and we've got the basic product set. And then we've got our Private Bank both domestically and internationally. So, I would view it more as a scaling journey than as a completion of product capability. And that is our goal. I think more broadly, the UK is a nation of savers. I think it needs to be more of a nation of investors. I think we're going to have a broader tailwind and support for this. I think it's important role for banks to play and you'll see us emphasise it. Then if I come to loan growth above GDP, let me begin and then Anna should fill in. We've said 5% as you say, loan growth versus nominal GDP of 2%. Basically, there are parts of the business in Corporate Banking, in Business Banking and even parts of personal loans where we were underrepresented in the last number of years. Tesco has given us the capability in personal loans and you can see the increase. You're seeing the increase of 18% growth in lending in the UK Corporate Bank. If you look at the UK Corporate Bank broadly, still loan-to-deposit [ratio of 34%]. So, we have a lot to grow, right, versus what you might normally expect. Simply put, Ben, I think it's a combination of increased capability. So, we've talked a lot about the mortgage platform. Actually, we're doing very similar things within the Corporate Banking environment, making it easier for that customer or client to engage with us and making that journey efficient, quick, giving them certainty, etc, that's making a really big difference. I think also the sort of broader product architecture that Venkat talked about. We see it in cards across multiple products. We obviously see it in our mortgage business. So, we're just going to market with a much broader range and certainly more of a step change than we've had sort of two or three years ago. What it isn't is price, and what it isn't is risk. So, you can imagine as CFO, I've got a very keen eye on those things. If you think about our Corporate lending, it's up by 18% year-on-year. We've got more than 1000 new clients in two years. About half of those are driving some of that lending. But as I look at the risk profile, it's not changed since the beginning of the plan. And as I look at the portfolio margin, it's not changed since the beginning of the plan. So, it's really technology, intention to lend, and I would say breadth of product.

question_text: So on the Investment Bank, if I look at your 2026 targets, previously you had a greater than 12% target. It's now circa 12%, a high-50s cost income ratio is now circa 60%. I'm assuming the change is primarily due to FX, but perhaps you could firstly confirm? Secondly, when I go back two years and think of the original plan, a lot of the revenue growth was assumed to come from market share gains and you actually assumed a fairly flat wallet. Actually, what's materialised is a much better wallet than you expected, but flat market share. So perhaps you could also just talk to competitive dynamics and how that's played out versus what you thought two years ago and how that then fed through to your 2028 assumptions as well. Then on the US Consumer Bank, I just wanted to understand some of the moving parts because you talked about greater than 13% NIM for 2026 full year, but I think in your earlier commentary, you said 12.5% for Q1, 14% for the second half post the [American Airlines] sale. So, presuming it's the 14% you would argue we should be thinking about into the outer years. But then similarly on the loan-loss ratio charge, you're actually assuming that's coming down even as the exit NIM is higher. So perhaps you could just square the circle there. Thank you.
answer_text: Thank you. So, Andy, you are correct. The material moving part between the last plan and this plan is we previously planned on [GBP/USD of] 1.27. We're now planning on [GBP/USD of] 1.35. Now that has no impact on group capital, no impact on our ability to distribute, but in particular, pockets of the bank, you see some concentrated effects and the Investment Bank is one of those, you're going to see it in US Consumer Bank as well. So that movement in FX is worth about 50 basis points. So, all we're doing is we're just truing up our expectations. We're pleased with the progress that it's made so far. I'm not going to mark-to-market that plan every single passing quarter. It's just that as we're resetting targets, we felt like it was the appropriate thing to do. Thank you. I think, on the other side, what I would point to is, on the Investment Bank side, Banking per se, as I said to you, we would like to see greater fee share. What you've seen so far is progress from the hires and the investments we've made, and you've seen greater revenues, obviously and excellent capital discipline. As we make these investments; we hope to see the fee share. On Markets, I would point you to the fact that in the three focus businesses, we've done what we said we would do and we've done it a year early. And as well as the number of our top five clients among the top 100 clients for whom we are top five, that has gone from 30 to 50 to 60. So, there is structural progress being made in these elements. Thank you. So Andy, you're right. There's a lot going on in US Consumer Bank in 2026, specifically being driven by the fact in Q2 we expect to exit the American Airlines partnership and also complete the purchase of Best Egg in the same quarter (slide 96). Firstly, that has a NIM impact. I expect the NIM to go to around 12.5% in the first quarter. What's driving that? Well, it's just the accounting that I called out earlier. It's a movement between non-NII and NII. Then we've always said that because American Airlines was such a high-quality portfolio, the NIM on it is relatively low, but also the loan loss rate on it is relatively low. So taken together, it was a relatively low returning portfolio because it's super prime. So what happens when that leaves the portfolio is the NIM will go up further. So you're right, in the second half of next year, I'm expecting, a clean run-rate of NIM, which looks more like 14%. Now, when I come to loan loss rates, that same impact is going to take us from 400 basis points to 500 basis points, but that will be more than offset by NIM. During 2026 in isolation, what you're going to have is a couple of impairment effects. The first is, if you recall, when we buy something, we bring it all on at Stage 1. So, it has to mature through Stage 2. So, you get what we call stage migration. You're going to get that in the General Motors portfolio. So that's going to elevate impairments slightly. So, I'm just trying to think about why you've decided to do that in the context that obviously, the Investment Bank probably is one of the businesses that has performed above expectations in the last cycle. And increasingly there are questions about with the US peers investing more and putting more capital behind Investment Bank, why would you choose not to do so?
answer_text: So how do we think about product margin in the UK is I think your question. So, look, there's a bit more to go here and you can see that from the, can we go to the structural hedge slide, please? Thank you. (slide 64). We are assuming that we are going to be reinvesting the structural hedge at 3.5%. The maturing yield over the next three years is materially below that. So, 1.5%, 2.1%, 2.7%. So, you're going to have a considerable hedge tailwind across at least this plan, probably beyond. And everything that we've done around the tenure of the hedge and extending it from 3% to 3.5% is only going to increase that momentum for longer. So that remains there as a, if you like an underpin for product margins. Then if you think about lending more and particularly within our credit card business, all of the volume that we've written over the last two years coming to maturity from its promotional balances, that will start to increase the interest-earning lending in the credit card book. So, we expect those things to continue. Now what we're not doing here is planning for any expansion of product margin really though, because what we've said implicitly is that the growth that we're seeing in lending and some of the margin pressure that we're seeing in the UK market pretty much broadly offset. That's our planning assumption. Now it may turn out differently to that, but we are not assuming that product margins in totality, get either better or worse, if that makes sense. You just continue with that hedge grinding in the background, product margin is broadly awash. That's how we think about it or that's how we planned for it. In terms of the Investment Bank, what we're trying to do here is construct a plan that is carefully constructed. We're trying to put as much of it within our control as possible. So, we're planning on a flat wallet. We're not materially expecting any market share change in Markets. We expect some in Investment Banking. The pressure here in the plan is coming more from Transaction Banking, but that's where we're directing our investment. But don't conflate careful planning and lack of ambition because what we will do, of course, if the opportunity presents itself, we will monetise it as we have done to date. I will emphasise that last point. I must say it's nice to be getting a question about why we shouldn't be bigger in the Investment Bank. We've been very clear to you over the last couple of years about where we are roughly targeting the IB as a percentage of the Group. I think what you should expect us to do is exactly what Anna said, which is we're making a plan based on an assumption of a wallet. If there is an opportunity, we've done it in the last number of years, which is we take advantage of it.

question_text: Just a question on the Investment Bank to begin with. Are you able to give any colour on perhaps how much leverage exposure is tied up in the Investment Bank? I know we talk about RWAs, but as we shift towards the growth, you're seeing in the Financing businesses, how relevant that metric is? And when you talk about flat market share in Global Markets, is that a conservative assumption or not given, I guess the deregulation story we're seeing building in the US and also the ambitions one of your European peers has in FICC, specifically in the United States? And then the second question is more broadly on AI. I think or I assume behind the scenes going through all the planning, you've looked at a lot of the opportunity set in that area. It feels as though more generally, there's a narrative that the technologies are becoming more impactful, but perhaps the speed at which you can get them into the enterprise is taking longer than people had expected and maybe at a slightly higher cost. Is that a fair narrative or one that you would agree with when you think about the work you've done behind the scenes on this topic?
answer_text: We don't talk about return on leverage balance sheet a lot with this community, but you can imagine we are very focused on it in the background. And you're right, there are two big parts of the bank where leverage is deployed probably most extensively. One of them is obviously retail mortgages. The other one is Financing within the Investment Bank. So, it's very high RoTE business because it's essentially secured lending, but it does consume leverage balance sheet. That's why we have the AT1 strategy that we have. And we're always thinking about what are those returns on the leverage balance sheet versus the cost of those AT1s. That's how we think about it in the background. We have deployed more leverage in the business over the last few years, but so have our US peers. And our perception to date certainly is that they have not been leverage constrained in the way that they have addressed that. And despite that, we've grown the balances by 60%. It's a business, of course, we're focused on the returns across many lenses, but we're happy with where it's going. I'd also say one of the things about the bank and the way we're building the bank is that we have lots of options and lots of opportunities. So just as you have two areas which consume leverage, you've also got the US cards business, which helps you offset that because it's capital dense, relatively speaking. And what we're doing on the personal and unsecured side in the UK, which is also relatively more capital dense. So, I spoke on one of the slides about balancing product, income type mix, all these factors are coming in to create the portfolio which we have. I think back to me on AI. You're right that I think what people are finding is that it's not just sort of enabling a particular type of model or a particular capability on everybody's computers and then get to work. So, you have human adoption and then you have more importantly, the ability to get it to work in the system. To get it to work in the system requires two things or three things. One is the basic infrastructure, then adding the capability and then the third, the willingness to reengineer your processes. That is what we are trying to convey in the slides we spoke about on technology. So, the basic infrastructure is about both data and computing. Then on top of that, you build the model capability, which exists in some of the computing platforms, but which you might put on your own. And then the third is the commitment to reengineer processes and you've got to really do it end-to-end. So, whether it is BarxBot, whether it is what we are trying to do in credit risk, whether it is what we are trying to do in the US Consumer Bank and customer service, you can't leave pieces of this undone. That's the deep organisational commitment. So, we recognise it. That's what we are finding behind the scenes, as you said, but we're trying to pick the right projects that will have the biggest impact on the bank and see it through from beginning to end.

question_text: I've got two, please. Anna, can you talk about your thoughts on kind of deposit volumes and spreads in Barclays UK, please. answer_text: Okay. So, on UK deposits, you can see that the deposits are up quarter-on-quarter by around £3 billion if we go to this slide. (Slide 17). What we can continue to see there, James, is we do continue to see some competitive pressure in the UK and specifically that move towards fixed or time deposits. Now, seasonally, I would expect some concentration of that in Q1, Q2 just because of the ISA season in the UK. We always see that and it feels like as a market, we're well primed to see that. But we are pleased with that deposit progress. What does that underpin? Well, I think just continued improvements in the business. And I would say that we've deployed our multi brands in deposits this year. We don't really talk about that. We talk about it a lot in assets, but you know, we are going to market with a much more sophisticated product architecture in deposits because we are now deploying the Tesco brand here. So that's really helping us. But we are not assuming from here that there is any real easing in that deposit environment. It may happen, it may not. But as I say, we're trying not to make significant market assumptions. Yeah. So, on the Investment Bank, first of all, investment comes in different ways. Investment comes in people, investment comes in technology, particularly in the Markets business and then investment can come in RWAs. What we've spoken about on the balancing side is basically Investment Bank RWAs as a percentage of the Group, where we set a target of around 50% seems right. We've also indicated flexibility around that number if there's a little opportunity, but 50% seems right. Some of this or a lot of it is going towards things that are relatively capital-light and relatively high in fees. We are prioritising stable income, we are prioritising Corporate Banking and of course, electronic trading, which helps with our Intermediation. And on the capital side, as I've said, there is a balancing act and it's about 50% is where we would aim to target. And to get there right now, Investment Bank RWAs have to be relatively flat.

question_text: So, two for me. One, I guess one of your peers are talking about reinvestment of the equity hedge in gilts. Just curious what you're thinking there, whether you could do that to get a bit more income? Secondly, just in terms of the inorganic kind of growth strategy, obviously, there's potentially a lot of capital build. Obviously, there's the distribution piece. We saw, I think [Barclays] name was at least in the press on the Evelyn Partners potential transaction. So how are you thinking about the inorganic capital deployment? And within that, is that also part of getting the Investment Bank down to the kind of 50% that you now target for 2028 in terms of RWA consumption?
answer_text: Thank you for that, Amit. I will let Dan Fairclough, our Group Treasurer, pick the first one up and then I'll come to inorganic. Yes. We've obviously got a different set of options available to us in relation to leverage compared to some of our retail-focused peers. So, we will generally deploy available leverage balance sheet into the Investment Bank, in particular into Financing and the returns there, we would expect to be significantly higher than us kind of using it in the structural hedge and getting a little bit of deal pickup versus swaps. So, for us, you should expect us to continue to use swaps, and that's what our numbers have been based on. So, Amit, let me just cover of the last point you made first. We are not relying on inorganic to get to that circa 50%. We believe that, that is a continuation of the organic progress that we've made thus far. You've seen us make a number of small acquisitions over the last few years, Kensington, Tesco and now Best Egg, which completes in Q2. And I guess they all have a few things in common. First is that they are deliberately furthering our strategy. So, they're either giving us a bulk volume like Tesco did in unsecured, which was something that we really wanted or they're giving us a degree of capability or both. So, think of them as having to really, really lock into the strategy that we've laid out for you. The second thing is that for us, price is very important. Why is it important? Because we've got a very, very strict capital hierarchy. Firstly, regulation, you can see we're operating at the top end. But distributions are very important to us, very important to our shareholders, whether they be dividends or share buybacks. We don't want to disturb that. And that means that we are focused on anything that we buy adding to the division that it sits within. So, is it RoTE accretive or ROIC accretive, if that's more relevant given the nature of the business? Or if I look at it from a Group perspective, is it EPS accretive? And actually, how do I compare that to the RoTE of a share buyback. So, we're considering those factors as we look at any acquisition. And then the third point is how do we blend it into the organisation. Now we've spoken in the past about the ease of integration. The reason that's important is because we don't want it to distract us. But equally, the harder the integration is, the sort of harder you need to stare at your synergies candidly because it can put some risk into the process. So, we'd be very mindful of that. But what do we mean by blend? Really, how does it enhance what we are doing organically. That's really important to us. Think about how Kensington has added to our mortgage journey. Think about how Tesco has allowed us not only to lean into unsecured lending, but also deploy a more sophisticated range of deposit pricing in the U.K. and think about how we expect to take Best Egg into other partners in the US. So it's really that point around how can you sit it on top of your existing organic strategy and really push the growth. So, things that we are looking for, we'll have to tick those three things of. And if we're not picking them up, then for one or many of those reasons, then we've backed of. But it would be over and above our existing organic strategy.

question_text: Two questions on the UK, please. The first one will be on the fee income. I think you're guiding for flat fee income in 2026. So just wondering what is driving this flat guidance and why no growth in 2026? And what kind of growth should we expect from 2027 onwards? And then on costs, you're guiding for sequential cost decrease over the next two years. Just wondering how we should think about it? Is it a linear trajectory? Or what is the pace of efficiency savings versus investments?
answer_text: Thank you. So, we do expect some fee growth in the UK, but that's largely under construction now. So, I'm not anticipating in 2026, which is why we are guiding you to a broadly flat position of circa £250 million each quarter, about £1 billion over the year. It's not entirely flat because there's a degree of seasonality that comes from kind of interchange and spend. But think of that as a bit of a baseline from which we will build. So the fee-based products will not only hang of the relaunched app, but it will also come from some of the 'Premier' focus that Venkat talked about on [FY25 Results / Progress and Targets Update] Day last week. In terms of costs, we are expecting sequential cost reduction. I wouldn't expect it to be entirely linear though, because clearly, there's a greater fall of that we expect in 2027 just because of Tesco. Think about BUK costs coming or cost savings coming in sort of two flavours. The first is the level that relates more generally to the group, which is coming from IT transformation. So that will build through the plan period. And actually, much of it will extend beyond the plan period in terms of what we're doing. So, platform simplification, AI deployment, change delivery, so really underpinning those more structural cost changes in the IT stack. BUK has done a lot so far, but it's been much more operational kind of customer journey-led product simplification. So, this is a bit of a shift in focus towards technology. Second thing then comes from Tesco. In 2027, I expect not to have the £100 million of integration costs that we've currently got. And also, we expect to see around £100 million of synergy costs coming through. So, there'll be a bit more of a step change then and then continuing from thereafter.

question_text: Just a quick one for me. At the beginning of the remarks, you mentioned UK is more of an incumbent in terms of AI, while in the US, it's more of a disruptor. So, if we're thinking further down the line, which one of the two parts is the most sustainable in that regard. You're thinking being in the US as a disruptor makes sense, would that open risks for the UK from potential disruptors? And how would you react to that?
answer_text: Good question. Thank you. We do think of ourselves on either side of the Atlantic, certainly in retail terms as different things. And originally started as the card business in the US, but now what you've seen is us adding a digital savings platform and now digital unsecured lending. So, pulling that together and being very partner-focused with a broad representation. So, it's not a bricks-and-mortar business. Interestingly, and I don't think we talk about this so much, bigger than Chase in the UK. It's a substantial business. And we do see opportunities to grow it with that sort of framework in mind. So very digitally led. In the UK, we start from a very different place. In UK Corporate or in Barclays UK, you're talking about very, very strong primary banking relationships, which, as you say, is where I started this discussion. So, you're really trying to bring your customer or your client into your ecosystem and do as much for them as possible. That's very different from the kind of disruptive mindset. We see our strategy from here as being very much a continuation of that. That said, in the UK, it's really important that the app and the pricing are as good as those of our competitors and indeed our customer service. We've made a lot of progress over the last few years. We're now pretty much top of the large banks in terms of customer service, but we don't recognise that as the standard that we need to get to because of some of the disruptors around us. I think of it as remaining true to being a disruptor in the US and in the UK using the disruptive elements around you to make your primary relationship better and better and better.

question_text: I'll start with costs. I think probably back end of last year, you were still expecting 2026 costs to be flat to maybe down a little. I think that is no longer the expectation. Is it just front-loading some investments? And if so, sort of what? So, it would be very interested to hear how you're thinking about the investment piece. And do you see any risk of maybe having to increase investments maybe like you have done in 2025, which is good for the business, but just wondering how you're thinking about it. So that's one. And number two is on USCB, the £950 million guidance for next quarter, it's almost£100 million down from Q4. So, I understand £45 million has some sort of one-of in that is to do with the accounting change. But the other £50 million feels like quite a big drop, and we haven't seen that seasonality in the last three years. And also, you're now guiding to high single-digit CAGR in that business. So, I would be interested to hear where is that growth going to come from more tangibly.
answer_text: So if you look at our cost flight path, you will determine that I think most of the increase in costs this year comes from Best Egg. So, if you think about the roll-of of the matters that we said we expected to be a bit more one-of this year. So think Motor Finance, think some of the one-ofs that we took in the fourth quarter, particularly in Barclays UK, a bit of inflation, a bit of investment, that would have taken us to broadly flat, and then you've now got the Best Egg cost. So, I think that's a big difference in 2026. More broadly, sort of as we go out to 2028, really, what we're saying, is that we're expecting about £2 billion of efficiency saves. We are expecting the roll-of of costs that won't exist in 2028. So, by that, I mean Motor Finance and the Tesco things that I talked about before. So, say that's another £2.3 billion. Then going the other direction, you've got a lump of inflation. That's been running at sort of £400 million a year. So say that takes us £1.2 billion of your capacity. That leaves me with a little bit more than £1 billion to invest. And that's really the simple math of how I see it as being sort of broadly flat, if that makes sense. Because that's the sort of increase in run rate of investments that we're talking to you about. If I just move on to USCB, I think there's probably three things going on in there. The first is the £45 million that you called out, which was the Non-NII one-of. The second thing is there has been a bit of a deterioration in the US dollar rate. And so just from sort of Q4 into Q1, we're seeing some weakening in the dollar and clearly, that's going to translate into slightly lower income levels. And I think we feel that the Q4 was particularly strong as a holiday matter. So, there's nothing beyond that in there. So maybe a tiny bit more seasonality than we would ordinarily see. The growth across the plan, we see is coming from a couple of things. The first is obviously continued growth in the balances organically. We've made really good progress both in renewing our partners but also growing those partners through time. Onboarding General Motors, obviously, we'll see a full year of that, and it continued to grow in its balances, which is progressing nicely. The other thing I would say is we typically assume at some point through the plan of sort of partner X, it won't be big, I think, between £2 billion and £4 billion across the three-year position. That's roughly what we do across any three-year plan. And then finally, you do have the benefits of Best Egg obviously coming through. So coming on at around £700 million, but obviously, our intention thereafter is to grow it. What we would expect to see probably sooner than cost synergies is revenue synergies in terms of funding costs. So those are probably the moving parts in terms of USCB.

question_text: My questions are more on the AI sort of CapEx cycle and if you could help us think through it. So, some of the plans in the US of the hyperscalers have humongous sort of numbers behind on the CapEx side, which, I mean, it looks good for business, issuance, etc, presumably deal logic suggests that year-to-date, things are going very, very well. But on the other side, we see a lot of the banks offloading data centre risk and some of these numbers, the share price reaction questioning if it's a good use of money. How are you thinking about it from an underwriting perspective? Are you just intermediating, issuing, helping them issuing the bonds? Or how much risk are you taking from a credit perspective? Or how are you thinking about it? And potentially on the other side, more as you think further down the line as well on the underwriting risk, how do you think about AI affecting the underwriting risk more broadly? I'm thinking also here on the retail side, the risk of disruption sort of efficiencies and ultimately would lead to job losses. Can you help us think through it because that's also doing the round.
answer_text: So let me start with sort of AI / software just as an Investment Bank matter. I mean we don't think of this as differently to other sectors really. So, expect us - and I think it's Slide 100 in the deck, expect us to deal with this type of credit with the same degree of rigor, even though it's had clearly a huge strategic focus, there is a massive sort of build in funding in the US. From our perspective, we would maintain the same kind of concentration limits, the same kind of sector diversification requirements as we would have anywhere else, both in terms of the sector and the counterparties involved. Expect us to deal with parties that are relatively larger and more established, etc. So just a continuation of that really. If we had significant concentrations, you would see it in our disclosures, and you can see that actually it's subsumed within a much larger bucket, the name which I've completely forgotten, but we will come back to you. So it's not an outsized position for us. That said, given the activities over the last sort of four to six weeks, we are extremely focused on it and extremely focused on the levels of risk. And obviously, here, we use SRT as we use elsewhere in other sectors. So, nothing to call out if there were, then we would have done so. In terms of underwriting on personal, we've had some really interesting questions on the road on this actually as to whether or not we should be expecting more of a white-collar recession versus a blue-collar recession, particularly in the US. But we see no movement in credit thus far. We're obviously very watchful as we always are, both in the UK and in the US. It feels a bit early to call the shape of the impact from many of our competitors and many firms across the industry, they're not really talking about headcount reduction. They're really talking about the spending that they're undertaking and perhaps technology efficiency. So, we will watch it very, very carefully. We're also very mindful that AI and sort of data more generally can bring us huge benefits on the underwriting side just because of our ability to ingest data and process that data. That's actually the fundamental basis of Best Egg. So, we do see opportunities to learn here. I think it's on both sides of that particular argument, Alvaro, but very, very watchful.

question_text: If we could stick with Best Egg for a moment. You spoke about bringing the data sort of expertise to other partners or perhaps I was thinking more RWA efficiency gains and so on. So, if you could just talk a little bit about what that might mean and if there are consequences for post Basel IRB RWA density, perhaps where you think that might land once all that's done. Secondly, in the strategy slides, there's quite a lot of talk about the huge growth you've seen in Prime balances and there's interest in the market as to what's happening to margins there. So, if you wouldn't mind just sort of repeating what's happened to balances and revenues, where they live and how you're seeing things evolve in that part of the Investment Bank, that would be great.
answer_text: Best Egg comes from two things really. The first is our desire to be this more sort of rounded consumer disruptor, if you like, in the US. So really looking for a capability around unsecured loans. We were doing some unsecured lending with some of our partners, but it was really quite limited. So really, if you like, purchasing a capability that we really lacked. So it's partly about the products there, but equally about the capital-light model. Now unsecured loans are lower in capital anyway, even under IRB than cards because obviously, it's fully drawn. There's no undrawn element to it. So, it's an inherently more capital-efficient product even if you keep it on your balance sheet. But obviously, the nature of Best Egg is it's a largely originated securitised model. So, from that perspective, we are really mindful of the impact of IRB and potentially the regulatory divergence that we have versus some of our US peers. And therefore, the strategy for this business was both to diversify and to look for more capital-light streams of revenue. And if you recall, way back in 2024, we did that very early trade in terms of securitising the credit card balances. So, I expect us to lean on both things on both the diversification and the capital-light nature of it. We expect to bring cards and savings and Best Egg to our partners. Sort of simultaneously, if you like, so a much fuller relationship for them. We do expect to securitise much of what we are doing in the US. And that's also very attractive because it means that we're originating consumer lending for our markets business, which gives benefits there also. So, it's quite a fulsome integrated strategy if that makes sense.

question_text: I've got two questions, please. First, on the Investment Banking business. You've done a review of the loan book, so 60% of that is done, and you've seen a 150 basis points pickup in income over RWAs. Firstly, can I ask how much of that pickup is due to maybe more penetration on the income side versus the recycling on the RWA side? And secondly, on the remaining 40% how much of a benefit should we expect? Are we thinking that the low-hanging fruit is already done and we're going to be squeezing harder? Or should it be a sort of a symmetrical benefit there? And then secondly, on UK corporates, a lot of these banks in the UK are targeting this segment. Can I ask how asset spreads are looking in this market, particularly as market share gains is a story for a lot of the banks here?
answer_text: So the answer is it's a bit of a combination, and we haven't split that out because essentially, what we are doing here is we recognise that two things were true, and they're drawn from, if you like, our historic strength in Fixed Income across Barclays very, very widely. So we're very good at DCM, very good at Lending, probably not as disciplined as we should have been around the returns on that Lending and very focused on getting the initial piece of debt, the RCF and then assuming that we would get subsequent Banking fees to go with us with that, and that would complete the client returns. Clearly, that's quite difficult for us to control. It didn't always happen, which is one of the reasons we pushed more discipline into that business. So, it's not only about reviewing the returns of those loans as they come up for renewal, but also saying what happens then? Either the returns have to improve or we have to broaden the relationship out into Transaction banking. So it's actually a combination of the we see it as one single discussion with the client, which is why we haven't separated it. But we have seen considerable growth in deposit balances. I want to say our dollar deposits are up by about 140%. And that reflects the particular focus we had on, if you like, our US or US nexus clients. So, they might be UK businesses operating in the US, we might have some dollar debt with them. We also want to have some dollar deposits. So, I would say a combination of the two. The remaining 40%, don't think of it as low-hanging fruit. Think of it as literally the things that came up for renewal during that period. Roughly, the loans have a three-year average life. So, there's no reason to expect that the remaining year will be different to the first two is the way I would think about it. In terms of UK Corporate Banking, so what we haven't seen there is a compression in asset spreads. And from our perspective, it's really because we were coming from way behind. So, we are still considerably below our natural market share in that business. So, our loan-to-deposit ratio is 34%. If you look at our peers, it's going to be anywhere between 55% and 80%. So, we're coming from a really different position. And all we've done is created an expectation that we would lend with the regional teams and improve the process. Now clearly, we would expect to see some momentum there also coming from the fact that we're consolidating everything onto one platform from five in the shape of Portal. But as I look, I'm really happy to see the growth. They've grown their income in the fourth quarter by 18% from lending. We've seen about 100 basis point pickup in market share. I'm really happy about that, but I'm just as focused on the RoTE, which means there's two things that matter. The first is the default grade. The second is the margin. And neither of those two things are moving relative to the portfolio. So, this is not an expansion driven by pricing and risk. It's an expansion driven by capability and willingness to lend with clients we already have in the door. And indeed, going out and getting new clients. So, we've got, I think, more than 1,100 new clients in just two years. So, the business has some momentum now that it has not had for years. And actually, as I look sort of further out in the plan, one of the areas where I think probably consensus and our expectations are a little bit departing is probably the corporate business.

question_text: Thanks for your comments on AI within the deposit book. There's an awful lot of first, as you say, from the challenger banks for the deposits, a lot of term deposit compression, instant access savings compression. AI is kind of building the tech there, even though we've had open banking for ages, it only seems to just be impacting the market. What are the sort of the chances that, that level of deposit spread compression persists forever? And the NII actually comes out at £8.1 billion and flat lines because it's just expensive to run in the deposit market, and this just gets perpetually chipped away by technology. And then secondly, kind of on AI as well, just what impact you see it having in the wealth market, given that's a bit of a focus last week and kind of looking at the reaction that the market has had and investors had to NatWest Evelyn. Does that make you question the reaction that people have had, does that make you question any acquisitions in wealth now?
answer_text: Thank you, Rob. Well, Vim Maru was reminding me yesterday that the first such platform was launched by Bradford and Bingley some time ago. So, this kind of approach has been out there for some time. We've obviously seen it become more sophisticated. But customers are moving their deposits around now. It's pretty much a friction-free market because we're nearly all optimising our deposits on our app, and it's pretty easy to do. That said, we are not seeing a significantly higher level of term deposits than we saw immediately post crisis. So there seems to be a sort of natural level, if you like. That said, we can't rely on that, which is why we're investing so much in the app because actually, what you want to do is bring your customers into your environment and for them to find everything that they need there so that they don't need to go. And obviously, that means that you know them better because you have the primary banking relationship, you can give them the kind of nudges that it's much more difficult to do on a sort of open banking basis. So we think that's the way to address this. Clearly, we are also assuming that deposit margin pressure does not ease. So that was back to the question from Ed. So we're not assuming that we find out of this by the end of the year and that there's any difference in the margin pressure in this business. You then need to think about what happens sort of if rates continue to go lower, then you make less and less money out of deposits anyway and you start to make more and more out of assets. That's why it's really important for NII longevity, that there is some diversification within NII. We're very, very focused as an industry, I guess, as a sort of investor group at the moment on the margins within deposits. But we have to grow NII from assets now because the rate cycle will tell you that in low rates, you make more in assets, less in deposits. That will come. And so for those challengers, that is quite a challenge to the model. You can't just be a deposit taker. What do you do with those deposits? How are you going to lend them. So, we do think about it through the cycle, we do think about it on a more holistic basis and technology is really, really important, not only engaging the customer on the deposit side, but also ensuring that we are lending to them and deepening that relationship. In terms of wealth and AI, it depends on what you mean about wealth. So, there's a huge continuum here around how people think about their wealth and how they place it. So, if you go from our Private Banking business, -it's very high touch, very human-led. If you remember that slide that Venkat had, it was the one that's over on the left-hand side, and we would probably see that persisting. So, if you're looking at a Private Banking model, it's going to be predominantly human-led. If you're at the other end where you are an execution-only model like Smart Investor, now renamed Direct Investing, I think, that has to be execution only, completely digital, etc. Then wealth is somewhere in the middle. So, you are going to want to have your customers dealing with you digitally, getting digital prompts. And that's why that advice guidance boundary piece of work that the government is doing is so important because at the moment, the boundary to receiving advice is quite a high one. I give you advice, you pay me. That's what RDR requires. But actually, in advice guidance, it becomes a bit more like people like Rob, looks at things like this. So it's much more prompting guiding. In that kind of environment, you would expect AI to be much more relevant, the kind of nudges and understanding that you have of our customers. That's why we think this link between our 'Premier' and our 'Affluent' customers and that digital link from the app back to the point I made about you get in the app and you stay in that ecosystem and extending that all the way over into wealth, we think is really important. That does not exist in the UK at this point in time. That doesn't exist. So, you can come at it in a couple of ways. You can either buy a predominantly adviser-led wealth business and sort of try and push it right to left or you can go the other way. And obviously, that's what we're trying to do.

question_text: So in the Investment Bank, you're only assuming a flat market share. I'm just wondering what assumptions are underlying this across FICC and Equities? And how do you see the competition playing out versus US peers? Then the second question is on the US Consumer Bank. How much underlying NIM improvement do you think there's left to go? Because I think you mentioned that there's going to be a NIM improvement to 14% post the AA exiting the portfolio in Q2 2026. And how much of that is an underlying NIM improvement versus just AA coming out of the portfolio? And then a secondary question to that, just on US cards. Any sort of update to commentary on the APR cap? What sort of solution do you think will appeal to the Trump administration over this 10% cap?
answer_text: So, we have a planning assumption of flat share. And for us, the number that we give you is basically the top 9 Investment Banks and our share of that combined revenue. It's a pretty rough indication because it includes things and territories that we do not operate in. So, there are times when we would expect to outperform and times that we wouldn't. So, we're not in commodities. We're largely not in Asian equities. So, it's a bit of a broad brush and it's a planning assumption. Basically, what we're saying on markets in particular, is that we've made really good progress. We expect to continue to make progress in our focused businesses and Financing in particular. So I won't give you a split between FICC and Equities, but think of us leaning on European rates, Securitised Products, Equity Derivatives and also continuing in Financing. So, they are the businesses that we're going to continue with there. So more of the same really. The market share is an output, and it tends to just move around because it's such a rough measure. You do get coalition data, which is much, much more specific, but it tends to come out with a huge lag, which is why we rarely report it out to you. On USCB, the simple answer is before we take AA out in Q1, we expect our NIM to be 12.5%. Then it goes to sort of 13% in the second quarter because we're taking AA out relatively late, and then it goes to 14% when it's fully out. So, I would say roughly 12.5% beforehand, roughly 1.5% impact of taking AA out. And if you remember back to our original Investor Day [in February 2024], we did say that we expected to be at a NIM of greater than 12% [in 2026]. So, we're broadly where we expect it to be and this extra pop, if you like, in the NIM is because of the portfolio change that we didn't plan for. I do expect it to continue to grow just because our strategy around more retail deposits doesn't change. Our strategy around continuing to rebalance the portfolio between retail and travel doesn't change. You're not going to see the same kind of step changes, but I would expect it to continue to sort of move on. And then finally, on the APR cap. Firstly, well done, everyone. We got nearly all the way around the table without someone asking that question. It's a little quiet. From our perspective, we share the broader views of the industry that afordability is really important. It's important in any form of lending, whether that be unsecured or secured. So it's the right focus. It may not be the right way of going about it because actually what it would do is lead to a withdrawal of credit in the US. So, we might expect there to be further discussions around things that really sort of lean into afordability in the US. Maybe some of the things that have been on the table and come of like late fees, etc. So, we're just sort of watchful and waiting for that. In the meantime, the best thing that we can do is drive the profitability of the business and do what we've done with Best Egg, which is diversify it. So retrospectively, Best Egg looks better and better.

question_text: Two questions. One, just quickly on some numbers you may or may not be able to give us, but just the average current account balances. And those are, I guess, period end. So how different do they look like on a sort of intra-month average versus end of the month just as people have been paid? And how much lower would the median be than the average on this? And then secondly, you've talked about AT1 costs being sort of a hurdle rate for returns on the leveraged balance sheets in FICC Financing and in Prime. Do you think about that across customer relationships? Obviously, let's say, an institution using repo and prime, do you aggregate the two to think about the hurdle? Or do you think about it specifically within FICC on one side, Prime on the other? And then your AT1s are just, it's a very low hurdle rate right now, right? AT1, let's say, 5% to 6%. So that's obviously not the hurdle rate you think about managing the group towards. So how much would you sort of be willing perhaps to work on that AT1 hurdle rate compromising your group return, but maintaining market share, etc, within the financing businesses?
answer_text: Why don't I start of on that? I'm not going to be able to give you all the numbers that you want but let me help you think about it. And then I will invite Dan to make some comments on AT1 costs. So, remember, there are two types of current accounts that we think about in the Group, and they actually move differently. So, in retail, customers get paid at the beginning of the month. And then typically, what happens is they start paying their bills, their mortgages, etc, balances drop of quite quickly. So, you get an intra-month loan. Corporates are exactly the opposite. So pre-Barclays UK, when we used to have something called Personal and Corporate Bank (PCB), which some of you will remember, the current account balances were actually relatively stable because you have these two waves going in opposite directions. That makes sense. You're right, in retail, there is that intra-month dip, but there is the opposite in Corporate. And to a lesser extent, Business Banking, it's not quite extreme. But we don't disclose the sort of top to bottom drop in either of those. And obviously, they sit in different legal entities. Dan, why don't you talk about AT1 costs, and then I'll pick up how we think about the financing relationship. Yes. I mean exactly right. We do look at the AT1 cost, and we use it as a hurdle rate for the returns we would expect to get in the Financing business. We don't really think about it on a coupon level. We would always need to have the total capital level anyway. So, the way we think about it really is the spread differential between AT1 and Tier 2 because we weren't issuing more AT1 than we need, we would be issuing Tier 2 instead. So that's the way that we think about it. In terms of sort of analysing the hurdle return for the business, just from a simplicity perspective, I think about it is that we should be clearing that return in our lowest returning bits of the complex. So extremely liquid fixed income where you've got the very highest quality government securities, that's generally the lowest margin business. We should be returning more than the cost of AT1 in that business and it's extremely liquid. So we've got a high degree of confidence that we can move it around. We would expect that the client return is obviously higher than that because if we're dealing with a client, they'll be dealing across multiple products and they are clearly profitable, then we are comfortable overall. And the last thing I would say is we do think about the clients as a single client across both platforms. So, as we deal with them, as we look at them, as we risk manage them, we are looking at them across Fixed Income Financing and Prime together. And that's really important if you like, the strategy of that part of the franchise. So, I think that probably brings us to the end. Thank you very much for coming in. Really appreciate your time. Really appreciate your interest in Barclays. We will see you in an expectingly short period of time because this is the shortest quarter. So, we'll see you at Q1 very, very soon. And until then, stay well. Thank you.

question_text: Good morning. Alvaro Serrano from Morgan Stanley. Thanks for taking my questions. Venkat, maybe this one's for you. You made the comment that you've reduced the risk appetite or pulled back (I can't remember the exact words you used) on slightly higher leveraged and some structured products. Can you give us a bit more colour of the concrete measures you've taken and maybe speak to slide 45 (and thanks very much for that disclosure). In which areas have you pulled back a bit, and how should we think about any impact on revenues from that sort of reduced risk appetite? And the second question is on the UK or [more] broadly NII outlook. Obviously, rates are high now and you've locked in the outer year extra hedge income as you've disclosed and spoken to. When you think about the high yield [environment] versus slowdown in loan growth and volume growth, do you think there's upside to NII if you were to mark-to-market to current curves? Maybe you're more thinking of flexing your NII guidance. Thank you.
answer_text: Yes. Hey, Alvaro. Good morning. So, let me start with your first question and I'll hand it over to Anna for the second question. So, we said in the statement that the impact is not material, either today or a foregone income in the future. On slide 45, in that third box is where you'll see the £17 billion lending to business models that are basically themselves asset-backed lenders. That is [one area] where we have [in the past] seen more vulnerable business models where we may not find the strength of financial controls we'd like to see them demonstrate. That's really the place where in the structured financing exposure, we would expect to see some limitations. But as I said in the prepared remarks, it's not material now as a source of income, nor foregone income in the future. Anna? Thanks, Alvaro, for the question. Given the experience that we've had in Q1, we are more confident now on NII than we were at the full year, because the actual experience that we've had in Q1 is either positive or neutral. And I'm very comfortable with consensus for '26, both for the Group and for Barclays UK. As I look a little further out into '27 and '28, that consensus looks light. We said the same at full year, it looks very light in '28. So what we've observed in Q1 is actually a good deposit performance. So current accounts in BUK have been broadly flat. Ordinarily, we would see a seasonal decline in Q1. We've had a good ISA season where we grew faster than the market. You can see good lending growth across the piece, 5%, pretty much on the [UK lending] target that we've given you. Our USCB NIM is a little higher than we guided to at 12.8%. And of course, as I said, we've topped up the hedge by £6 billion, and we've rolled it in the quarter at around 3.9%. Now, this change in rates is really about the future years. We are still basing the guidance that we're giving you on 3.5%. To the extent that we see rates remaining higher, obviously that will build through time, and you'll see the impact a little further out. And I'd just remind you that our hedge income for 2026 is 95% locked in already. So, our confidence is really coming from the real factors that we see in both deposits and in lending. To your point about slowdown in lending, we have not seen a slowdown in lending. We see it growing strongly both in BUK across the products, also in [UK] Corporate. And for the first time, we're seeing some really good signs of growth within Business Banking. That's driven by our own actions. We're not reliant on the market. So, at this point, I wouldn't say that we would adjust our NII guidance for any change in lending. It's more the experience that we've had in Q1 just gives us greater confidence to deliver [against] the consensus numbers. Thank you for the questions. Perhaps we can go to the next question please.
