question_text: Hello, good morning. A couple of more questions on NII, please. So, the product margin side of things, can I just dig a little bit deeper [on] that? So, I think previously you said that the mortgage compression from the COVID-era mortgages rolling of would be about £100 million. How far are we in that? Because presumably, as you said, some of the volumes that might be rolling of in Q2 probably got pulled forward in Q1. And then with swap rates volatility, can you comment on what you're seeing in terms of front-end margins as well? And then on the deposit side, I suppose the competition has been maybe a little bit higher, partly reflecting seasonality as well. So, when you said that you expect product margin to be similar next quarter, is that more mortgages or is it more deposits? If you could just help us understand that a little bit better. And then on the USCB as well, you commented that margins were quite high this quarter, there's a big improvement. Obviously, there will be some mechanical improvements further from the American Airlines exit. But how much more sort of underlying improvement can we expect from pricing and from deposit mix, et cetera?
answer_text: Okay, thank you, Perlie. I will take both of those. So, our product margin impacts in Q1 are as we guided and they're in line with our expectations. And I'm going to merge your two NII questions, if I may Perlie, because actually that product dilution is coming from both mortgages and from deposits. In mortgages, we are seeing the impacts that we called out at the full year, and that's the maturation of the COVID-era loans coming through as expected. Somewhat offsetting that, we are seeing better performance from more recent vintages, where we are seeing better retention. So that's a slight positive impact in mortgages. And we are seeing the impact of deposit margin compression coming through in there. I expect it to be broadly similar in Q2, Perlie, with all of those factors continuing. And that's simply because of the timing of the maturity of mortgages. But also, very importantly, remember deposit competition in the UK tends to be concentrated in Q1 and Q2 because of the ISA season. Thereafter, we would expect that product margin compression to ease of a little. What's different from when I spoke to you at the full year is we now do expect NII growth in Q2. We expected it to be broadly flat previously. Now we expect growth into Q2, and then to continue growing quarterly thereafter, and to grow year-on-year in every single quarter of the year. When I think about what's happening in the mortgage market, we have seen a pull forward of applications, but they have not yet completed. So, March was a very, very large month for applications, and I think that just speaks to the volatility in the rate environment and customers seeking to lock in. To give you an idea, for our June maturities, we've seen roughly double the number of customers lock in by this stage than we would ordinarily. But that hasn't completed yet, it's going to complete through Q2 and Q3. Margins remain fairly robust. Clearly rates are moving around, but so are swaps, and they tend to move in alignment with one another. So that's what's happening in terms of BUK NII. In terms of USCB, the net interest income there is a little higher than we anticipated, but not significantly so, and I wouldn't call out anything in particular. The repricing impacts have worked their way through now, but we will continue to see ongoing beneficial, both NIM impacts and net risk-adjusted margin impacts from continuing to rebalance the book from just travel and entertainment towards a bit more retail. So you're obviously going to see a step change over the next quarter, but that will be an ongoing impact. And I just call out here also our progress in deposits. Really pleased with that, our retail deposits are now 76% of our overall funding. That's higher than the target that we gave you of 75% by the end of '26, and that has been disproportionately driven by some of the partnerships. So, you're going to continue to see margin accretion, but obviously it will be more pronounced over the next quarter or so. But thank you for the questions. Can we go to the next question please?

question_text: Hello, good morning. So, I was going to ask you about share awards, but I nearly fell of my chair when you made the comment on 2028 net interest income. And I don't know whether you can give us a bit of colour as to where you think we're wrong at a divisional level. Tying into that, just a quick question on the hedge. Are you taking advantage of the fact that the yield curve is markedly higher today? I mean a one-year forward starting seven-year is offering you 4.4% today. I'm just wondering if you're pre-hedging maybe a bit more of your future maturities than you might have done in the past? Thanks.

It doesn't relate to the movement in the yield curve and the guidance that we are giving you is still based on a 3.5% reinvestment rate. We have not changed that number. And it's the Group number [excluding IB and Head Office] that I'm referring to as I look at that. So, this is no change from what we've said before. If I can point you to where I think the difference is, I think it arises in two areas. The first is UK Corporate Bank. And you know, we see considerable momentum in UK Corporate Bank. We've seen it for consistent quarters now. It has grown its lending in the first quarter by 15%. And it continues to make great progress, even before we land the capabilities that we are due to land through this year in iPortal. So that's the first thing I would call out, I think we don't discuss it a great deal on these calls. The second thing would be US Consumer Bank, where you've really got three things starting to come together here. You've got cards balances, which are up [9%] year-on-year in the first quarter. We will, in the next few days, complete the purchase of a top five unsecured direct-to-consumer loans business in the US. And that gives us the opportunity to take that capability directly to our customers and to our corporate clients. And then the third piece is our deposits, which, as I said, are now at 76%. And a meaningful part of that growth has come from our partnership with AARP. So, we are really learning in this business about how we can take the full suite of products to our partner base. And that's what gives us the confidence in that business' ability to grow. Venkat, anything you would add on the USCB in particular? Yes. So, I mean, you asked about NII, Jonathan, and Anna's given you the various dimensions of it. But in the USCB, in addition, what you see is continued improvement in digitisation, continued improvement in cost, leading to the higher RoTE that we've shown this quarter, 18% plus. You're seeing performance in the way we said we would demonstrate it 2.5 years ago and reiterated three months ago. And just to remind you, Guy, we do these post-management adjustments (PMA) for two reasons. The first is where we're doing some work on the models, and to anticipate what that model work will show, we very often take a PMA. And then the other reason that we take a PMA is when we are faced with a degree of economic uncertainty and we feel like consensus may not be effective. The point that you're talking about here is the former. So, actually what happened is prior to this quarter, the General Motors impairment was not modelled. We were essentially using our expectation and our existing portfolios to anticipate what that was going to be, and we put it in as a post-model adjustment. Now what's happened is, we've updated the model, and so General Motors [impairment] is a modelled number. So, you're not going to see any change in the total number. It just jumps from being in the PMA to being in the modelled number. The real changes in PMAs that we've done, and the ones we've spoken to you about, really speak to economic uncertainty and relate to US Cards, UK Cards, and the IB. Thank you, perhaps we can go to the next question please.

question_text: Hi there, if I could just pivot the conversation to capital. Just intrigued on two things. One, there's been a lot of press coverage about your comments around the leverage ratio proposal to potentially exclude unencumbered gilts. Perhaps you could just touch more broadly on where you see the leverage ratio as a binding constraint now. For which product, which divisions, do you believe the leverage ratio is a binding constraint for? And then secondly, I want to talk about Basel endgame. Overall, a 5% release is expected for the Category 1 and 2 banks on the change in the GSIB methodology. But arguably more important from a competitive standpoint is the output floor has been dropped. And when I look at the risk weight, I think under ERBA, it's 75% on retail loans, 45% for credit card transactors. So, can you just talk about what you think Basel endgame means for the competitive dynamics with the US Consumer division and for the Investment Bank? Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, Andy, why don't I start on leverage and then I will hand to Venkat on the second part. So yes, like the broader consultation might suggest, there is an ongoing discussion in the UK about the leverage ratio and really leverage being a backstop, and we would support that. You're noting that we have published a piece of work that talks about the opportunity in the UK, really for the treatment of unencumbered gilts, and we do think that that's important. As we make that statement, it's more about the opportunity for UK PLC and the reduction in costs that that would have for the government, and we called out around £2.5 billion per annum on an ongoing basis. We are not leverage constrained. Clearly, we have considerable leverage usage within our Financing business, within the Investment Bank. That's why we are a significant issuer of AT1s in the market. And as we do so, we're clearly mindful of the relative cost between those AT1s and the kind of margin that we get in the Financing business. So, the two things are somewhat unconnected. One is more of an observation on UK PLC. Venkat? Yes. So, Andrew, on the capital side, we clearly are watching very closely what's happening in the US, not just in terms of capital ratios proposed under the Basel endgame, but the way supervision is itself changing and stress testing is changing. You've got to look at all three together, and we would advocate very strongly for the UK numbers to be relatively consistent. And for the UK approaches also to adopt a greater transparency in the way in which add-ons are determined both for banks and for investors. The particular things on the Investment Bank and credit cards, let me begin with credit cards. So, in the credit card space, you're right that if there are no changes, then the UK numbers will, at a parent level for us, holding company level, add on more capital per unit risk than a US bank would face. Now, what we're doing to adjust our business is obviously running it more efficiently and also diversifying it. And the purchase of Best Egg and the direct-to-consumer loan business should be seen as a part of diversifying our cards business into other places which are less penalised in terms of capital. And then on the Investment Bank, the point I would make is, we have already for some time been facing US banks which have been putting more capital and more balance sheet. And you know, at least the way we have done the analysis, and you should probably replicate it, is if you look at returns per risk-weighted assets, a form of capital efficiency, I think we've done pretty well. And as you know, over the number of years, we've made structural improvements in the way the Investment Bank is performing. We've had eight successive quarters of strength in year-on-year income growth on positive cost jaws, on income over RWAs, as I said. And we beat consensus [income] for eight consecutive quarters in the IB. This is all deeply structural, and what we are trying to do with these structural changes, with the increase in Financing as a portion of our total revenue, et cetera, is finding our own ways to be competitive and to be efficient. Now, on top of that, do I want to row against the current of capital disparity between the UK and the US? I wouldn't. But we've made our views known, but we will continue to operate the bank in the way we have and show the progress we've done quarter-over-quarter. Thank you Venkat, could we go to the next question please?

question_text: Good morning, thanks for taking the questions. If I could come back to this topic around competition from US players. And the second small one on corporate lending in the IB, that looked quite soft this quarter relative, even with the fair value marks adjusted for you. It looked like a soft quarter. What should we be expecting there going forward, noting that you're looking to the ICB as an area of growth? And I know transaction banking is doing well, but if you could comment on that [Q1] print for corporate lending, that would be appreciated. Thank you.
answer_text: Okay, Chris, why don't I start? So, I'll talk about leverage and then I might hand to Venkat and then I'll pick up on corporate lending. So, look, clearly Financing has been an area of growth for both us and for the US banks. And we've seen that over a number of quarters now. We're pleased with our performance, which is up 31% year on year in dollar terms. And we don't perceive that the US peers have been leverage constrained up to this point. And indeed, it's not just this quarter. If you look back over successive quarters, as Venkat has said, you see increasing levels of balance sheet generally being deployed into the business. But Venkat, you might want to comment on the competitiveness of this product generally. Yes. Look, first of all, as Anna said, we've been seeing this for a number of quarters. We've adjusted our business for a number of quarters. Second, especially when you come to things like Financing and Prime, there is a competitiveness element to it, but there's also a client service and stickiness element to it. Our rankings have been growing consistently because of the services we provide to our clients in Equity Financing and in Fixed Income. We're a top [three] Fixed Income financier, and we have been for a long, long time. So, it's these capabilities that we bring to bear that make us very competitive and make us attractive to clients. So, I would view it on a much more holistic basis. I mean, and as Anna has said, and I said earlier, over a number of quarters, you've seen the US banks put in both capital and balance sheet much more than we have. We've been very disciplined on both, minor fluctuations quarter to quarter, but keeping it stable. And yet we've continued to show the results in our Investment Bank that I spoke about in terms of continuous quarters of improvement. And it's coming from building in the foundations to generate repeatable, improved performance. Anna? Yes, thank you Venkat. Chris, the corporate lending line, I appreciate it's very difficult to forecast because what you've got there is an underlying level of corporate lending. That's not really changing. We're clearly cycling through this process of reviewing the book. We're sort of a little more than two thirds of the way through that now. So that number is fairly consistent at around £50 million a quarter, so, nothing really happening there. You've obviously got this swing in Leverage Finance marks year on year. It was up more than £100 [million] last year. It's down £40 [million] this year. So, you've got nearly 150 basis points of RoTE impact on the Investment Bank just in that line alone from those Leverage Finance marks. And then the other two things that flow through there are cost of hedging and cost of SRT. Nothing really notable to call out there. You should imagine in the current environment we do a little bit more hedging, but there's nothing particular I would call out for you, Chris. Thank you, can we go to the next question please?

question_text: Yes, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. Just one, actually. I just wanted to go back to discuss your cost of risk guidance, which is now at the top of the 50 to 60 basis point range. Just wanted to know, what are your assumptions regarding especially the Middle East situation? Does your guidance capture any improvements in the geopolitical situation or status quo, or maybe at the other end of the spectrum, maybe a potential increase in inflation because of the situation? Anything you can give us regarding this new guidance, thank you.
answer_text: Okay, thank you, Nicolas. And I mean, we have called out that we expect to be around the top end of our 50 to 60 basis point points range. That's purely because of the single name [charge] that we took in the first quarter, and we do not see any other signs of credit deterioration in the UK, in the US, in corporate or in consumer. And so, from our perspective at the moment, if you do the math, then you'll see that we are broadly in the midpoint of the range for the remaining quarters of this year. I can see that consensus is already at the position that we've guided to today, so I think that's probably what the market was anticipating. At this point, we don't see any significant impact from the situation in the Middle East, other than the revenue impacts which have been broadly positive to date, so the rate impacts and, obviously, our ability to capture the cyclical opportunity in the IB. In terms of credit, we don't perceive any deterioration at this point. However, we have taken three, I would say, relatively modest adjustments in our IFRS 9 modelling, as we look at future potential risks. So, the first of those relates to UK and US cards, where we have been slightly more conservative with the unemployment rates that we have used predominantly, and we're just recognising those that clearly consensus is moving on over time, and those two particular books are highly, highly sensitive to unemployment and the rate of change in unemployment. The second thing that we've done is, to Venkat's prepared remarks, we're a little bit more mindful of some of the Investment Bank exposures. And on that basis, we have put a little bit of downside bias into the Investment Bank calculation, essentially weighting it more heavily to the downside one scenario. That was very consistent with what we've done in previous periods, where we faced uncertainty. So, we're not trying to make a prediction here. We're really just recognising some of the uncertainty around us. Now, clearly, if the situation were to persist, and we started to see real economic effects coming through in terms of higher inflation, then that may have some impact on credit, but there's a few things I would say, hopefully, to reassure. The first would be, we've clearly had recent experience of this in 2022, where we saw a sharp inflationary environment, and we saw a sharp increase in rates, and we saw very, very resilient consumer and client behaviour. Corporate balance sheets remain strong. Consumers remain in a very robust position. And whilst we've added lending since then, there's been no meaningful change in our risk stance since that point in time. So that gives us confidence. The second thing is that we see, I would say, rational changes in behaviour from both clients and consumers. So, being mindful of the uncertainty and perhaps paying back their credit cards a little faster than they otherwise might. We think that that's really positive for credit. And it's something that we observe. But overall, nothing additional that we've taken so far other, than those three PMAs. IFRS 9 is highly pro-cyclical. So, if we were to see a real deterioration, then really that might lead us to make some changes. But of course, we'll call that out if it occurs. But thank you for the question. Could we go to the next question please?

question_text: Morning, thanks for taking my questions. You sound very, very bullish on the outlook, with only kind of a small PMA taken and the implied rate benefit to the top line and calling out consensus, even on lower rates being too low. Is it not a bit perverse that an energy price shock that causes higher interest rates and lower economic growth outlook is actually a positive for bank earnings? So, I guess is there any negative risk in there from growth? Which parts of the book from a growth perspective would you be most worried about in this type of environment?
answer_text: Yes. So, look, you raise a very good question, Rob, and I think there are two issues here. There's one of timing, and then there's one of certainty or knowledge. Clearly inflation risk has increased with what's going on in the Middle East, and you can see it in the UK inflation numbers, speaking just in the UK, and over time, there are worries in the US as well. For a variety of reasons, it's not hit employment, and growth in the UK at least until February was strong and growth in the US remains strong, and there are important sectoral reasons for why that is the case related a lot, of course, to tech. And we said to you, Anna said that we are not seeing any impact on our retail or corporate credit portfolios in the UK or the US, especially the smaller companies. So, all of that put together, explains why credit conditions are generally good. I mean, we said that we expect impairment to be at the higher end of our cyclical range of 50 to 60 basis points. And we've discussed NII, and we've discussed the interest rate income of the bank. The longer this thing goes on in the Middle East, and the more inflation feeds into the economy, then there is a risk of growth, or lower growth, and then there's a risk potentially of the implications of lower growth, including on credit. But we are not seeing it yet. And I don't think it's fed through to consensus, which is what we follow. That's the reason. What you're seeing from us is prudent risk management in the forms of the way we've talked about credit lending, or our approach to credit, and the way Anna described a slight emphasis to weaker scenarios in calculating IFRS 9 related impairment. So, what you're seeing from us is a little more prudent positioning, a little more prudent weighting of impairment scenarios. But it's not yet played through mainstream consensus numbers, or of course, into what we experience in the portfolio. Anna? Yes. Thank you, Venkat. I think the other thing I would call out, Rob, is that our confidence is drawn and relates to the plans that we continue to execute. And this is another quarter of execution. And of course, we're mindful of the environment, and Venkat's called out a few examples. But our focus is on executing the plan, as it has been over the last few quarters. And that's really what's delivering the momentum that you can see today. Also, the diversification that we have in the book, both geographically and between different types of business, allow us to be resilient in quite a range of environments. But we're clearly mindful of the outlook. Thank you Rob. Perhaps we can go to the next question, which I believe is the last question?

question_text: Thanks very much. Yes, I had two sort of related questions, and I guess you partly covered it in the answer to Rob's. I guess what we're all struggling with is the contrast between people like the Deputy Governor of the Bank of England saying the markets are ignoring risks, there's an awful lot of volatility going on, people are not focusing on it. And the message from you, which is there aren't really any problems. And so, I'm just trying to get a sense, I suppose the way I'd ask the question is, what has to happen for there to be a problem? You know, you must sensitise your book. Is it that the Middle East [crisis] continues for much longer than expected? Is it the oil price of $150 is the big question mark? Because obviously $100 is not a problem. So, what is an environment which would have you guys thinking, this is a problem for our book, and we're going to have to start taking some material numbers? I guess that's the first question. And then just related to that, I was struck both by the size and the high proportion of write-ofs you took on the one-of impairment or the one-of exposure. And I'm just wondering, could you give us a sense, I mean, is this like a normal exposure to you? Would this be like a top 10% [exposure]? I mean, how many of these sort of size single name exposures do you have on your book? Would this be a very material one? And then I guess secondly, related, I guess you've been through all of them now. Can you give us some flavour as to why this was a one-of? Because it was an extraordinarily big number in itself and a big percentage write-of, if that makes sense. Thanks very much.
answer_text: Okay, why don't I start, Venkat, and then I will hand to you. So, Ed, I'll just reiterate, we are very mindful of the environment around us, and that's why we are managing risk and capital very, very carefully. But we go into this kind of environment with a resilience that would not have been there a few years ago. So, we are operating with greater proportion of our capital focused on more stable returns. We have higher operating leverage, which gives us greater resilience. And of course, we have much higher levels of absolute capital. So, if there is a deterioration, then we would face that in a completely different position as a bank. So that's number one. Number two would be, as Venkat has said, we continue to manage our risks carefully. He's talked about some changes that we are making around how we approach lending. I would also call out the way that we've managed the volatility in markets in the first quarter. So, you can see both the VaR and the single day trading loss that tells you how we are approaching risk in this kind of market. But you know, you're right to the extent that the situation intensifies either in terms of inflation or indeed time, we might see that start to flow through into the real economy. But that's how we are positioning ourselves to manage those things robustly. Venkat? Yes. So let me just continue on that question for a second and then I'll come back to your second question. So, what Anna said, we are managing our risks, we take a view to the future, but also look at the structural composition of the business, right? What you've seen in this quarter is an anticipation of greater volatility and greater economic weakness. That has led to volatility in the financial markets themselves, which [our] trading businesses have been able to do well and because of the help that they're providing to clients and the intermediation that they did. So, the question I always ask is, if on the first day of the quarter, you knew how the quarter would fold out, what results would you expect? And at the last day of the quarter, did you get the results that you thought you would expect, right? And if you look at our businesses, because of the structural changes which we are doing, A, what you see in each business is what we would have thought. B, the way the businesses interact, also gives us protection. So, coming back to the question that, I think it was Rob who asked it, on the one hand, you're getting an advantage from interest rates. On another hand, you're getting an advantage from trading and trading related activity. On yet another hand, you're getting the advantage in the Investment Bank from people seeking capital markets transactions and IPOs, right? And then credit conditions still remain strong. If that changes, which it could over time, the longer these things go on, then yes, you would have some issues or impairment, but you may still continue to get benefits from other sides of the portfolio, right? And then we've not spent some time on this call, but we do have fee businesses, transaction businesses, all of which will be important and relevant as people look to hedge financial exposures. So, it's a diversified bank, diversified sources of revenue, and it's important to focus on one or the other, but you've got to look at it holistically. And this quarter's results show you the importance of that. Then coming to the second question, first, I would take you to page 45, where we've gone through the history of our exposures to these things, and what we've said is, as a credit matter, we've had no losses or negligible losses across all of this. That's the first important thing. When fraud happens, right, and depending on the extent and sophistication of the fraud, the numbers are appreciable. I'll say two things. I don't like to lose a single dollar or a single pound to fraud. On the other hand, this business has been structured, [and] has been performing well over the last number of years. It has been structured in such a way, and we've made fundamental improvements to it that we are able to absorb it. It doesn't mean I like it, it doesn't mean we won't take steps, in which we are taking steps to reduce that likelihood, minimise it, and so on, but we can absorb it. In a credit lending business, there's always the chance of that. We look to reduce it and minimise it by good risk management. There are obviously lessons which we have learned from watching these two situations, and those lessons we've put in, and that's what I would say. The last thing, I know this is the final question, if I may close on this. The message I'd like to leave all of you with, first of all, thank you for joining us. Thank you for being on this journey with us. Thank you for the excellent feedback you give us on this call and between calls. What you're seeing is yet another quarter of the demonstration of the fulfillment of our strategy. Quarter after quarter after quarter, we've been improving this bank structurally in the ways we said we would, and delivering in the ways we said we would, across the bank. In the Investment Bank, an increase in RoTE now to double digits, it's 15% this quarter. In US [Consumer Bank], an increase in RoTE, when we started this plan it was 4%, we've just printed an 18% [plus] quarter. The [Group's] RoTE itself is at 13.5%, we are reiterating all our targets. [We have] strong capitalisation, we're at a 14.1% CET ratio, which is a little above the high end of the range. That shows you prudent planning, prudent stewardship of capital, and with a view to what might come in the future, which some of the guys you have asked questions about. The growth in NII, the strength of our deposit base, the increase in UK corporate lending, fulfillment of our RWA promises in the UK, increased client engagement in the Investment Bank, and so on. So, we've laid out our strategic plan, we've laid out the structural improvements, we look to deliver upon it quarter after quarter, and to report to you that way quarter after quarter. That's our aim. Thank you very much for joining us. Thank you, everybody. We look forward to seeing you on the road, and of course, we'll see some of you at the analyst breakfast, but thank you for your questions.

question_text: I guess if we start maybe with UKCB. So I guess there, the loan growth has been picking up in recent quarters. But I guess the question becomes what's the margin that you expect going forward in that business? I mean there is some increase in terms of going back to your natural market share, but how tough is it to actually do that without compromising margin? And then a second one on that, what's the through-the-cycle cost of risk? I think it's 35 basis points [is] what you're expecting now. But I guess on a bigger book with a bigger push, maybe that should be going up? And then a second one, maybe on the overall cost efficiencies. When those were issued, I guess, inflation expectations were arguably lower. Do you see any risk on that and whatever levers you would pull to maybe offset that?
answer_text: Okay. Thank you, Michael. Let me start with UKCB. So, our objective here is to lend more and it forms a really key part of our £30 billion commitment and the [>5%] CAGR in lending beyond that. As I look at the lending that's being put down there, Michael, I see no deterioration in margin, and no deterioration in the risk profile. The thing that we look at is the delinquency grades, [there is] no change in that at all. And really, that's because of two reasons. The first is, clearly, we're coming from a situation where our loan-to-deposit ratio is so low. We have actively not lent to many of our clients in the past. And this is about really having a clear intention and determination to lend where appropriate. So roughly half of our lending is coming from new clients, half of it is coming from existing clients. And as those new clients come on board, they're not meaningfully changing any of the kind of risk profile that we see and the portfolio margin remains static. So what's driving that? Well, firstly, it's that intention and secondly, it's the capability that we are landing. So the thing that we've done so far is materially changed the loan process, and what that does is it gives both the client and the regional teams confidence in our ability and intent to lend. That's really improved the lending pipeline. The other thing that we have actually seen is that as we engage with those clients more fully, what we're seeing is [that] they're getting to a higher number of products much faster than we would have expected. So the 2024 cohort, as I look at them now, are actually exhibiting the same number of products that would have taken previously four to five years to get to. So just that increased engagement with the client is really helpful. All of this, of course, is before we land iPortal, so all of the technology is there. We expect to migrate the corporates through this year, and that really gives us the opportunity to digitally engage. And it's what really that gives us the confidence that we continue this kind of momentum. Your second point on loan loss rate. So on the basis that we're not changing the portfolio mix in any meaningful way, we wouldn't expect to change that loan loss rate guidance. On cost efficiencies, we've gone through a period from 2024 to 2026 where we actually experienced fairly high levels of inflation because inflation reaches us typically on quite a lagged basis. If you think about our major stripes of cost: people, property, technology, you don't see an immediate inflationary transmission through to those costs, Michael, they tend to sort of lag a little. So actually, 2024 and 2025 were relatively high levels of inflation for us, 2024 in particular. So we'd expect inflation to come through on a lagged basis, and what we've done before is try to lean more into the growth efficiency targets that we have to try and manage that position. So at this point, I wouldn't change our targets. I would expect us to go harder after efficiencies to try and manage it wherever possible.

question_text: The first question was on [Investment Bank] capital. There's been a lot of discussion around where some of your US peers are prepared to put more capital to work now given some of the regulatory changes. I know on the call, I think Venkat said that its landing broadly as expected, but I guess it's only now we're starting to see how people react and what the behaviours are. So does that worry you at all from a competitive dynamics and market share perspective, especially if we don't get any dramatic changes in the UK on that side, what do you think might happen? And in terms of some of the stuff more in your own control, if you like, is there much more you can do in terms of recycling RWAs around the Investment Bank from an efficiency point of view? I know you've done some pretty good stuff in the last couple of years, but I don't know if we're towards the end of that journey as it were. I guess I'm really trying to get a sense as to how difficult it will be to hold market share, grow market share whilst holding RWAs flat certainly from the outside, it looks like quite a challenging objective. And the second question was around U.K. politics, which I appreciate you might try to dodge. But I guess it wasn't that long ago that Barclays talked about the UK political backdrop being the best it's been in a long, long time. Presumably, that informed the renewed push into the UK, particularly on the corporate side. So if we do see a meaningful shift to the higher taxes, be that personal, corporate, banking taxes, whatever it might be, could that change the strategy? Or frankly, is the bar just so high before you pivot from here?
answer_text: Okay. Thank you very much for that. So what Venkat was really getting at on the [Barclays Q126 Results] call was that if you go back over the last few quarters, it's not just in Q1 that we've seen a change in either capital or leverage deployed across the industry more broadly. It's actually been several quarters now. So probably more marked in the first quarter just because of the market environment that we saw in particular. So perhaps more of a step change there. So you're seeing both a seasonal step-up and you're also seeing, if you like, that volatility impact. But we've seen it sort of quarter in, quarter out for quite a few quarters now, and I'd encourage you to go back and look at that. It's certainly something that we are focused on. From our perspective, we still think that there's more to go. And our choice here is to run the IB in a very, very disciplined way. So we did put more RWAs into the IB in the quarter. And we felt we did that in an appropriate way. You can see that our Markets results in particular, are broadly in the pack, if you look at them in dollars. FICC, you have to recall, has got no commodities in it. So ex commodities, we think that's a good performance. Equities was right in the middle of the pack. And we did so while still increasing our revenue over RWA, went up to 8% in the quarter. We had one loss day and the VAR was flat. So across risk and across capital deployment, our choice is to be disciplined. Because fundamentally, our goal with this business is to get to a sustainably higher level of RoTE. So expect us to keep going down that route. We still think there's more to go on the optimisation of RWAs. Not least there's another year to go, because remember, at the beginning of the story, we said there was three years' worth of banking to work through. So we're only sort of two years and one quarter through that. So still a bit more to go there. And we continue to learn. And obviously, in this kind of environment, capital moves quickly. The velocity of capital goes up. So your risk management needs to be very good. That's where the discipline comes in. But we remain confident that we can continue to do this. And of course, much of the areas of growth that we are focused on, we'd either put capital into already or are inherently capital-light. And I'll just take you back to the sort of guidance that we gave you on the 10th of February [2026], we said that our market share would be broadly stable, and we are expected to see some growth in [Investment] Banking. Now [Investment] Banking, remember, is capital light. So we're already mindful of this environment when we give you the targets that we have. So expect RWAs to be broadly stable. Expect us to lean in and out depending on what the market opportunity is and to retain that very strict discipline, both around risk and around capital. Let me move to UK politics. So when we announced our strategy in 2024, that was a year in the making. So we had concluded before the change of government that it was the right thing to lean into the UK. And we believe that deeply for a couple of reasons. The first is that we believe the Bank should be rebalanced. The Investment Bank has the right waterfront, and therefore, our choice is to grow, particularly in the UK. That's a more stable source of returns for us, that's the highest returning part of the business. So that drove our choice, but also, a reflection as we look at universal banks across the globe, the really successful ones are very strong in their home market. And we felt that we needed more emphasis there. So it was driven by that. The political environment then changed and was then consistent with that. We would hope that whatever happens, the political environment is still geared towards growth. That's what the UK needs. It needs growth, it needs productivity. We believe that what we are doing is important as a part of that. And so we will continue that strategy. Of course, if the credit environment changed markedly, you would expect us to look at that, but the change in government alone would not be sufficient.

question_text: The first question is really me trying to understand Private Credit a bit more. And I appreciate you probably don't want to give us any specific numbers, so the question really is just on [a] strategy level. For example, [when it comes to Private Credit] do you have a target balance between your fee expectation and your balance sheet risk consumption? I guess, more specifically, what level of returns and your capital efficiency would determine whether you'll hold or distribute them? I guess that's my first question. If I can quickly throw in, are you seeing any meaningful changes right now in terms of changes in the lending discipline in Private Credit or risk management overall [for] Barclays and other banks, if that's okay. And then the second one will be on income mix really. I know you've previously talked about more stable returns and higher quality income mix. So, reflecting on Q1, FICC was amazing. But I just wonder how sustainable that performance will be, and when you talk about shifting towards this more stable and capital-efficient return and income, where do you think we are now versus what you ultimately want to achieve by 2028?
answer_text: Okay. There's a lot there. So I will attempt to step through it. So for Private Credit, look, we've given you new disclosure, on Slide 45. So that's our entire NBFI stack. Private Credit is obviously part of that. It's a relatively small part, as you can see. Just to level set everybody, what we previously showed you was a number of £20 billion. That was the committed lines. Actually, as we've gone through Q1, we noted that most of our peer banks were disclosing drawn facilities. So that's a drawn facility, that £15 billion. That's the difference between the two, just so that everybody is clear. Look, we don't have a target balance. We have grown, I would say, broadly in line with the market over time. As we've done so, we've remained very focused on larger managers, areas where we have clear look through to the collateral for that collateral to be, in our view, higher quality, higher EBITDA businesses. We have strict concentration limits by sector, by geography, et cetera, as you would expect us to. And really, the way we think about this, Elise, is no different to if we had a direct relationship with those corporates. So that's the kind of analysis and requirements that we have. So I wouldn't call out any specific numbers, but just to say that we would anticipate that it's no different other than obviously, you've got the benefit of that being in a pool of collateral. But for us, no meaningful changes in our credit risk appetite other than the two things that Venkat called out, which don't specifically relate to that bucket. The first was more highly levered sub-investment-grade businesses. And really there, our reflection is less about Private Credit per se, more about the geopolitical instability, the risks of inflation that we've talked about, risks of higher rates, perhaps the impact of AI, we feel that those businesses, some of those businesses are perhaps a little bit more exposed. But again, it's not a meaningful part of our portfolio either in exposures or income. And then around the sort of [Asset Backed Securities] business, smaller lenders where their financial control or the control environment is more generally less obvious to us from the outside. But they are the only two areas where we are taking a differential stance. There's nothing I would call out in terms of the industry more widely. In terms of income mix, there are two things I would call out. The first is we've given you some ideas about how we expect this to shape over time. In that the sort of differential income CAGRs between the two sides of the business, if you like, the Investment Bank versus the lending side that we're more focused on. So we are, if you like, on one hand, diversifying our NII, that's really important because we have this considerable support for NII into 2029, maybe beyond, let's wait and see, from the structural hedge. But when the rate cycle does eventually turn, we want to ensure that we've got a reasonable proportion of our NII that's coming from lending. That's one of the reasons why we made the decision that we did. So diversifying NII is really important and continuing to do that through our [>]5% CAGR [UK lending] target. Then leaning more meaningfully into fees in those businesses. So think about everything that we're doing with iPortal, think about the Premier focus that we have within the BUK, the link between Premier and Wealth in the PBWM business. All of those are designed to increase the fee pool on that side of the business. Again, more sustainable through-the-cycle revenue, very stable, et cetera. And we really feel that those investments will help us build that up. On the [Investment Bank] side, this is more a story of Financing and the International Corporate Bank. Now the International Corporate Bank benefits from all of the technology that we're putting down in corporate. It's one set of technology. And the way I think about it is you're building it for your most sophisticated clients in the ICB and then everybody else gets the benefit of it. So we've done a good job in growing deposits in the ICB. We expect to follow that with increased levels of fees associated with our Treasury Coverage model facilitated by the iPortal implementation. And then when you get into Financing, look, that's a business that's grown, the whole industry has grown. We've seen particularly in Q1, more revenue from Asia. That's basically our global clients seeking access to Asia. That's how we think about it. That's how we access that market. Typically, that business is very stable, given the nature of it, it's secured lending to hedge funds essentially. What we do see is that the income will go up and down with leverage in the system. Clearly, there's a lot of leverage in the system right now. But if you look back over the last few quarters, you can see just that continued progress. So we're confident in it. But all of this is designed to make the organisation higher returning, more stable and really goes back to Guy's question about how do you create an Investment Bank in particular, that has a higher, more sustainable RoTE and then elsewhere in the bank, make it less rate sensitive.

question_text: A couple of questions from me as well, please. One on Markets business, another one a follow-up on Private Credit. On the Markets business, in Financing obviously has been a big source of growth. To what extent the sort of the tighter credit standards in Private Credit could slow that down? And where I'm coming from is we've now had quite a good few quarters of very strong trading. With Financing, it may slow down, last year you had Liberation Day. Are we going to run into sort of pretty tough comps, and we're going to see year-on-year declines at some point? Just sort of general thoughts as we think about sort of the revenue outlook in that business, admittedly difficult to predict. And the second question on Private Credit. We've seen another competitor in the UK that had issues with fraud in the quarter. When I've listened to you and if I've interpreted correctly and other banks, the explanation around Private Credit exposures were like, look, it's a diversified book, where there's concentration, we've got recourse to the sponsor, bulge bracket sponsors. The recourse doesn't seem to have worked in this case of your competitor and apparently, is a bulge bracket, so you raised a question about their underwriting capabilities despite this is bulge bracket. Can you sort of help us think through when you look at your book, why you think your recourse does work and why sort of that wouldn't happen to you?
answer_text: So if I just pick up Financing in particular, I mean, most of the growth in our Financing income is liquid financing. So not the structured financing that you see within that disclosure. So quite different. So I take your point around tougher comps, Alvaro. We definitely saw at the end of this quarter, we saw more volatility. We are comping against a period of quite considerable volatility last year, but it's difficult to give you a forecast on that, nor would I give you a trading update. But just to say, the Financing business, in particular, more reliant on the demand from hedge funds for that liquid financing in terms of the growth that we've seen. And therefore, we would hope to see that continue. I'd just remind you that it does have slight seasonality of that business. So, it tends to be bigger in Q1 and Q2 than the back end of the year just because of when dividends are paid. So just remind yourself of that. In terms of the second part of your question, we're speaking here specifically about Back leverage. From our perspective, we have very limited exposure here, not to the particular fund that was called out. And we are confident in the terms and conditions that we have and therefore, our recourse.

question_text: Firstly, on UK mortgages. I feel like some of your peers have spoken a little bit more about customer mortgage journeys. Are you making any significant changes in that space? And specifically on mortgage tokenisation, when do you expect that to be a commercial reality for Barclays? And do you think that, that will come with higher spreads? And then secondly, when I look at my model, I find it difficult to not generate excess capital for Barclays, particularly when I get into 2028. Should we expect that you continue to be comfortable to run above the 14% [CET1 ratio] as we move through next year? Or as you start building excess capital, will we hear you talking more about more investments into the business?
answer_text: Okay. So I think it's too early to talk about tokenisation and what that might do within mortgages. Dan may have a view, I can ask him to add, but it feels like that's a little way off. Where we are very focused, however, is in the customer journey, both directly and via the broker. So we talked a lot about what we did last year and that new broker platform that's really helped us. It meant that March was definitely the highest applications we've ever seen. And we're also seeing much higher levels of retention because of some of the customer journey changes that we've made around people coming to maturity. But Dan, do you want to talk about tokenisation? That specific use case you probably know is in the retail section of the regulated liability network. So it's something that the UK banks are collaborating on as a kind of proof of concept. I mean it's a long way away from it being a proper reality, but steps are being made on a proof-of-concept basis. Yes. I'd just remind you, it's such a competitive market that maintaining any kind of spread advantage is very difficult in mortgages. In terms of capital, our position remains as it was in February. The capital generative capacity of the business is greater than is accounted for in both the distribution plans and the investment plans of the business that we've set out for you. So there is excess capital in the plan, if you like. What we've said is that we expect to run around the top end of our capital range until we have regulatory clarity. We will get that, we believe, in two chunks. The first will be the Basel implementation at the beginning of 2027, and then the second chunk will be IRB whenever that goes live. And again, we expect that to be in 2027. Until then, it's very difficult for us to say where in the range we will move. I guess why did we keep that level of excess capital, in part because we do see that there are opportunities for us to invest further. That may come as a result of organic or inorganic opportunities. You've seen us do sort of small tuck-ins over time. We've also increased the amount of technology that we are spending. And in the current environment, you can imagine we and others are learning more all the time about what is possible. So we wanted to give ourselves the flexibility to do that whilst still just putting down a meaningful change in the distributed amount, both in terms of the dividend and the buyback. Of course, if we don't see the opportunity to do that, we will return it to shareholders. And we'll be very clear about what our intentions are. It's quite difficult to be clear sort of this far out because clearly, we're only one quarter into that new plan. But what you're calling out, which is the opportunity for increased investment or deployment of that capital is exactly what we talked about in February.

question_text: A couple of questions, one on US consumer, one on the UK. On US consumer, thank you for the opening remarks and the comment around non-NII as a percentage of total revenues. I guess just to drill down into that, you talked about AA being broadly offset by Best Egg's $700 million. Best Egg's predominantly non-NII. Can you give us an idea of the split of the AA revenue mix that's dropping out just for our modelling purposes? And then linked to that, you obviously talked about US consumer NII being too low for consensus. I'd argue part of that is because consensus has taken out the bulk of AA through the NII line. So perhaps I can just invite you to comment on consensus non-NII for US consumer as well. And my second question on UK, completely different bit of strategy. Vim [Maru, CEO BUK] in April was in the press talking about actually potentially increasing branch numbers as opposed to cutting branch numbers, which obviously is a big step change, albeit consistent with what a couple of the peers have also said now. Do you think we're in a different environment now where the branch network is going to be more stable? And if so, what does that mean for cost opportunity going forward?
answer_text: Okay. So I'm not going to be drawn on the split of AA between non-NII and NII. We've tried to give you sort of firmer guidance about total income and tell you how it will be split in totality. There's just so many moving parts here, Andy. Clearly, as we get more into the pattern of Best Egg being underway, we'll be able to guide you more firmly. But at this point, what we're saying is that the total income is going to be replaced both by Best Egg, which will have a portion of NII in it, but largely non-NII and the growth in the portfolio, the organic growth in the portfolio. I actually think what's going on is, yes, there'll be a bit of loss of AA in the NII consensus gap, if you like. But I think there's also this piece around just the ongoing organic momentum of that business and the way it's coming through. So I'd really encourage you to think about it as a total income and use the split that we've given you to model it. As I go to the second part of your question, when I got to Barclays in 2013, there were 1,800 branches, and there are now a little over 200. And we said a couple of years back that we weren't intending to close more. And what we need to think about here is the branch network is a retail network. It needs to reflect demographic changes in towns and cities that we operate in. It needs to reflect our regional strategy. And so it's a living, breathing thing. So when [Vim] talked about having more branches in February, it was a reflection of that. It was a reflection of the fact that we feel like we've been at a point of stability for a while. And now we see some opportunities to improve that network. And that's not only in opening a few new ones, but it's also in refurbishing the ones that we have because we think that alongside landing or relaunching the app at the end of the second quarter of this year, the interaction with our customers is both digital and human. We see opportunities for both. We think they're both equally important. Of course, as a transactional matter, most of our customers want to use [a] phone. But for many, they also want at times to speak to somebody. And therefore, the types of technology that we have in branch, the types of meeting space, et cetera, et cetera, are all really important. So expect us to see refurbished branches as well as putting down some new ones, and we'll talk to you about that as they occur. So it's more of an organic sort of reflection of what we see happening in towns and cities. You might actually see us relocate some. So we're in a particular street that's no longer where we want to be, we might want to be somewhere else. So it will morph over the next few years. [Can I just add one thing to be helpful Andy on AA. The only thing which is worth pointing out, and I think you're getting there, is the American Airlines income was more weighted towards non-NII given the high quality transaction book, so more of a weighting to fees versus NII relative to the rest of USCB.]

question_text: I'll stick to the two questions. And the first is back to the Private Credit again. And obviously, thanks for the extra disclosure. And I guess the main question is no doubt in five years time, it's going to be a net benefit in terms of the cost line for the bank. answer_text: Okay. Thank you. So we set out Page 46 in response to an investor request actually for us to just be really clear with the market how this type of Private Credit works. We have a low loan-to-value. For us, in particular, what we're also calling out is the way we manage the credit. So in other words, we are very focused on managers who create a collateral pool of very high-quality corporate credit. So its EBITDA is typically higher than $200[m]. We retain revaluation rights in most cases. We are in a position where we can require more collateral to be put in and also approve that collateral. And obviously, it's a very high RoTE business and one that we think has considerable opportunity to grow. So we think that's the right decision. question_text: Good morning everybody, two questions from me. You talked about a commensurate improvement in Group efficiency in 2027 from the £300 million of additional SCA (Structural Cost Actions) spend in H2. So, could you comment then on how you feel about the £18.2 billion of [total operating expenses] that consensus has in for next year? Does that feel too high or too low when you think about the SCA tailwinds on the one hand, versus some of the higher compensation costs on the other hand? And then second, on Equities, I get the mid-40s print that looks a bit low versus peers, but it's basically in line on a two-year stack. I just wondered if you could give any colour on regional trends, growth in the US and APAC, whether how much that would have been higher versus what we see here in EMEA. And in Financing, I was surprised that was flat quarter-on-quarter. It seems like Prime was really strong across the street in the second quarter. So, if you could unpack that Financing sequential evolution a bit, maybe it's Fixed [Income] Financing versus Prime, maybe it's balance sheet discipline, just anything you have to say there on that topic as well please. Thank you.
answer_text: Okay Chris, I will start and then I will ask Venkat to make some comments. So, what we have said is that we expect to take up to a further £300 million of structural cost actions in the second half because we see compelling opportunities to get a good return on investment and drive the long-term sustainable returns of the business. In so doing, we expect a commensurate improvement in the gross efficiencies next year. Now what we haven't done is given absolute targets in costs. The way we think about costs is because returns are our north star, cost: income ratio is our north star, because to the extent that the business has a degree of momentum around it, we may incur further absolute costs. So that's what's really important to us. We believe that the cost: income ratio in 2028 will continue to be a low 50s print, and we expect 2027 to be a meaningful step towards that from the high 50s cost: income ratio that we expect in the current year. But we're fully expecting a commensurate increase in gross efficiencies, and you will see that coming through in terms of cost: income ratios. In terms of the Equities print, that is very much driven by the investments that we have made in the business. What we see all the way across the Investment Bank is that we are growing in the areas that we expected to grow within. So particularly within Equities, what you're seeing is a strong print in Equity Derivatives and also a strong print in Prime. We have some exposure to the Asian market through our Prime business, where we're essentially satisfying the demands of our global clients and we noted that about 80% of that growth is coming from our top 100 [Markets clients].So it's just reflective of that global strategy. Venkat anything you would add? Yes, and I think just to add on to that you should view this picture in terms of the longer term of what we said about the Investment Bank. So, one is just starting big and then coming small. We said that we are going to operate with a stable capital base of around £200 billion, give or take, and we've been there. Second, is we expected that [the Investment Bank] would be a smaller fraction of the overall bank, which it is. Third, that we'd be increasing top-line revenues, increasing returns, which means costs fall relative to revenues, and increasing capital efficiency and we've shown you a number of 7.7% return on RWAs [in Q226]. So, all of those things have been achieved over the full period, and I believe in nine [consecutive] quarters [of year-on-year improvement]. Within that, we also said we would diversify the business, both in terms of stable sources of income versus Intermediation, and then the role of Equities versus Fixed Income. So, there are slides here which sort of indicate that. Page 41, for instance, shows you the rising stable sources of income from Financing in the International Corporate Bank. Equities is now 30-odd% of the bank's revenue in Markets, and that is to be desired. This is the house that Fixed Income built. I'm very happy, I'm fond of saying. But it's increasingly a house on which we lean on Equities. And as Anna said, the regional shift has gone a little bit towards Asia, helping our large clients access the Asian markets. Our balance sheet has grown a little to take advantage of that, but you should continue to see this business operate with the principles and the guardrails which we've set out two and a half years ago. Stable capital, increasing capital efficiency, revenue improvement, disciplined cost management, higher returns, and a more diversified business in terms of stable sources of revenue versus Intermediation, Equities versus Fixed [Income], Financing versus the rest.

Now, most of our maturities were actually in the first quarter. Most of the market maturities were in the second quarter. And that allowed us to somewhat stand back and price very selectively and use our Premier proposition to really defend and maintain our market share, which is what we have done and about 85% of the growth that we've seen in the ISA balances year-on-year are driven by our Premier customers, which is exactly what we want. So, we think we've done a good job, but that said, you can see some marginal pressure in that product margin. We have seen mortgage margins somewhat recover after the compression that we saw in the Q1 swap volatility. And very importantly, in relation to deposits, a couple of things. Firstly, you've got the concentration of the ISA market behind you. But secondly, remember that term deposits are in large part one-year products. And we saw the start of this more intense competition in the second half of last year. So, as we go forward from here, what you're going to see is that the maturing margin and the prevailing front book margin are somewhat converging in the second half of the year. That was not true for the market in the first half. If pricing stays where it is, they'll be broadly neutral by Q4. So, we're taking all of that into account, Alvaro, and we expect sequential growth in BUK NII into Q3, and then again into Q4. So, moving into USCB. So in the quarter, we've seen two impacts that relate directly to the elevated level of rates versus what we expected. And I should say that the underlying business is performing as we anticipated. So we're seeing good underlying cards growth, particularly, for example within our General Motors portfolio, we're seeing good volumes within Best Egg. It is around platform modernisation. It is around process optimisation. It is around change delivery modernisation and in so doing making the organisation simpler on a permanent and enduring basis. So clearly what that investment does is it gives us greater confidence that we will be able to achieve our results in the short to medium term. So these are exactly the investments that we anticipated that we would be making, but two things have really changed since that Investor Update in terms of timing. I mean our earnings per share are up 43% [year-on-year] in the second quarter and that allows us to make these investments whilst balancing our primary two commitments, which are progressive returns and progressive distributions. That's why we have the conviction in the ROI. From our perspective, it gives us more confidence about a RoTE target which is open-ended for 2028. Actually, just as importantly, beyond that point, because we said what we were doing here was somewhat deliberately not optimising the short-term ROI of the business, but to be looking forward and creating, yes, a progressive ROI pathway, but a sustainable and higher level of ROI in 2028 and beyond, what we called an all-weather RoTE. So sorry to focus on consensus and guidance. The second question is the dividend. Nice increase in the dividend in the first half. answer_text: So Jonathan, let me take your first clarification points. So, I'll just repeat what I said. I'm not going to mark-to-market. As we look over the first half in totality, it looks completely fine and actually broadly similar to the previous year. Let me just deal with mortgages, and then I'll hand to Venkat on PBWM more generally. What we've seen is a strong quarter in Mortgages. As I mentioned before, we've seen somewhat of a recovery in application margins in Q2 after the compression that we experienced in Q1. Actually, the gross completions were very strong, we had a £10.0 billion quarter, that's the biggest quarter we've ever had, and June in particular was a very significant month for us, so no signs as yet. There's real wage growth in the economy and good demand for mortgages as we see it across the bank. Our gross share has exceeded our stock share now for many, many quarters, and clearly, we have quite a breadth of proposition now with Kensington in place. Firstly, people are remortgaging quickly given, if you like, that uncertainty in the market, and secondly, we're seeing a move to lower tenors and more tracker products, relatively speaking, just as customers are seeking to secure, if you like, a lower rate in a slightly more uncertain environment. Our investment comes not just in technology, but in the way in which we are constructing products, making them more accessible. Our broad goal for the Wealth Management and Direct Investing part of this, which is much more of the mass market in the UK, is to make available low-cost, transparently constructed and priced, risk-appropriate options to the investment public. We want them to invest in their financial futures. And in this quarter, we've done two things to make that easier. One is that we removed custody charges for all customers in Barclays Direct Investing. So with that removal of custody charges, we've got the most competitively priced alternative for those who seek full-service investment with the security of dealing with a large provider, particularly a bank. Another thing we did as part of our Premier product in retail, is that we've launched something called Planning and Advice, which allows Premier customers to access human-led advice through our app, again, with no upfront fee. So, all of this is a form of investment in the future of financial planning. And we expect to see the results of this investment over time. But you're absolutely right to point out that this is an important area of focus here and hopefully a long-term growth area for us.

question_text: Yeah, thanks very much. Good morning, everybody. I just had two questions. The first one, in terms of this additional investment in the second half, I think previously you were committed to BUK costs falling every year for the next three years, I think that's the way you articulated it. Is that still your commitment? So even with that additional investment, will costs in BUK still be down each year for the next three years? That was question number one. And then the second question was a slightly broader question. I get what you're saying about the NIM in the second half and the product margins will stabilise or even improve a little bit, but if I look at the totality of Barclays NII, it seems that volumes have taken of way faster than I think certainly consensus and certainly I expected. But your NII guidance is broadly the same, or even a little bit, maybe a tad lighter, which implies obviously that the margin is going to be lower than we were all expecting. Firstly, is that broadly a fair representation? And secondly, are we talking about margins being there or thereabouts now going forward? I get what you're saying about the structural hedge momentum, but that actually if you're going to keep this sort of momentum growth in volumes, you're actually going to have to share most of that gain with customers going forward, if you're going to keep your share in the deposit market. Is that a sort of fair understanding? Thanks so much.
answer_text: Okay Ed let me start and I will then pass to Venkat if he's got any comments. So the answer to your first question simply is yes. So, in incurring additional structural cost actions and in incurring some costs in quite frankly responding to regulation and getting to a more flexible pay mix for our MRTs (Material Risk Takers), these are not permanent elevations in the cost base. That's not what they are intended to do. They're intended to drive the returns of the firm and they are intended to create optionality and efficiency in the cost base. For BUK, we still expect sequential falls year-on-year during this plan and for the Group as a whole, I expect positive jaws in every year of the plan. So that remains completely unchanged. That's what we meant when we said it's the momentum that allows us to do this, without disturbing the commitments that we have to the outside world. And then on your second question, I think about it slightly differently, Ed. So we committed that we would put down £30 billion of RWAs in UK business growth across '24 to '26. And at the end of the second quarter, we are at £25 billion. That is exactly where we expect it to be. So, the pathway between balance growth and NII growth is as we anticipated it. And the thing that's driving the growth in NII across Barclays is not price, it's capability build. And that's true of every single product that we have. So if you go to mortgages, it's Kensington and it's the mortgage portal. That's what's allowing to drive our market share up, so that the gross share is higher than the stock share. If you go to cards, it's Tesco and it's the customer journey. If you go to corporate, it's about the capabilities that we put down in terms of, speed to market, speed to lending. And I could go on, but this is capability led, it's not price led. So, we don't feel like we are under margin pressure. Now that said, the UK market and indeed the US Consumer Bank markets are extremely competitive, but they always have been. And there's no real intensification of that beyond the comments that I've already made. We're confident in that progress, because we feel it's being driven by capability builds, and quite frankly, in some areas building back to a level of share that is more natural for us, particularly in something like corporate.

question_text: Hello, good morning. So we've talked a lot about cost. So it sounds like you want a balance between distribution, growth, various different things. Well, I think at this point, it looks like in the guidance, income is now £500 million higher and incremental cost is £450 million higher. So if there is another quarter of very strong IB income, et cetera, would a lot of this incremental income be spent on SCAs? Because obviously, if you are having opportunities to invest in things that give you 100% ROI, that probably suggests that you have many other opportunities to invest and improve the long-term efficiency of the company. Is that the right way to think about it? Obviously, distributions is probably not in a bad place, and you are already on track to meet all of that. And then the other question is just quickly on deposit mix in the UK. It does look like there's a bit more of a shift towards time deposit. Is it just a function of the ISA seasonality or is the fact that the market is a bit more competitive and therefore rates a bit higher? And I suppose if you look at the swap rates, looks to be probably staying higher for a period of time. Should we expect a little bit more of a mix shift towards time deposits from here?
answer_text: Okay, thank you, let me take those. So what we're saying on SCAs is that we normally do £300 million. We've actually undertaken about £100 million in the first half. That means that in an ordinary course of business, we'd be telling you we expect to spend about £200 million in the second half. Actually, we've added up to £300 million to that. So we're talking about undertaking around £0.5 billion worth of structural cost actions in the second half. In terms of an operational list and the level of investments that we can deploy wisely on behalf of the shareholder, we think that's the right sort of level. So clearly, as we look forward from here, Venkat and I have at least as much confidence in the RoTE of the firm as when we started the year for 2026. And you can see that in the fact that we have upgraded our income twice, first to £31 billion and then to circa £31.5 billion. So we think there is momentum in the business, but this will be a big operational lift for us in the second half. And we are very focused on ensuring that we deploy that absolutely wisely. So yeah, that's our primary objective here. And then in terms of your second question, well, our current accounts are broadly stable. We are, if anything, slightly better than the market. What we're really looking at here is some churn within the time deposit market and customers seeking yield. We say we feel like we've progressed through the ISA market well. I think what's really important, because we've had some comments this morning about the structural hedge in relation to this. So what's really important to the structural hedge is to realise, number one, the structural hedge in no way relates to time deposits. They are, by definition, interest rate sensitive and are excluded from the hedge. So all of this churn has no impact on that for us or, indeed, for others. It's really the stability of the relationships overall and the current accounts. So, everything that we see in the deposit market is very rational from customers and doesn't undermine our long-term expectations in terms of NII. Okay, thanks Perlie. Perhaps we could take the next question, please.

question_text: I've just got a few questions, first on the US deposits, [with core deposits around 82% of total funding]. I know the ambition is to grow this model, where could this grow to? The last quarter saw some tighter pricing as well, so with that in context, are you looking to step into that on a more gradual basis or see a step up? answer_text: Okay, thank you Sheel. So on US deposits, as you noted, we've clearly seen a step up in the quarter. Much of the growth we've seen is from AARP. Now clearly that is predisposed to good deposit growth, but some of the products that we've launched there have been very successful. So we would seek to deploy those more widely with other existing partners. And then with Samsung, well you'll hear a bit more about that in time, but we do feel that could be an important platform for us to develop our deposit business further, and you will see that in the other platform that I referred to.
